verdicts.name: சித்தரகம்
verdicts.reason: Retrieved: the University of Madras Tamil Lexicon aggregate at agarathi.com returns NO entry for சித்தரகம். Independent botanical sources give different Tamil names for Plumbago zeylanica: India Flora Online (IISc) lists Tamil 'Chithiramoolam, Kodivaeli', and the Madras Lexicon/Winslow entry for கொடிவேலி reads 'A running plant whose root is a powerful caustic... Plumbago Zeylanica, L.' The only attestation I could find for சித்தரகம் is the Tamil Wikipedia article title, which mirrors Wikidata and is therefore not independent corroboration. It is a Tamilised borrowing of Sanskrit citraka, not a name for a different plant, so dropping it loses nothing.

verdicts.name: சித்தரகம்
verdicts.reason: Same finding as the chitrak page. No Madras Tamil Lexicon entry for சித்தரகம் (checked agarathi.com); India Flora Online gives Tamil 'Chithiramoolam, Kodivaeli' for Plumbago zeylanica. Sole attestation is the Tamil Wikipedia title, a Wikidata mirror. Additional point specific to this page: the monograph is the ROOT drug, and the Tamil root-name in use is சித்திரமூலம் (mūlam = root), which makes the unattested சித்தரகம் an even poorer fit here.

verdicts.name: धनिया
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library, 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': 'Dhaniya [धनिया] in the Hindi language is the name of a plant identified with Coriandrum sativum from the Apiaceae (Carrot) family.' Corroborated by DDSA, A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary (Univ. of Chicago DSAL): 'Dhaniyā (धनiyā) (nm) coriander.'
verdicts.reason: Two independent non-Wikidata sources tie धनिया to Coriandrum sativum by binomial and by gloss. This is the form a Hindi speaker would use or search, so it is the preferred Hindi name.

verdicts.name: कुस्तुम्बरी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Monier-Williams Sanskrit-English Dictionary: 'the plant coriander, [Suśruta]'. DDSA Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Apte): 'The धान्याक plant (Mar. kothiṃbīra); आर्द्रां कुस्तुम्बरीं कुर्यात्...' citing Suśruta Saṃhitā.
verdicts.reason: Attested in a classical lexicon with a Suśruta citation and explicitly equated with धान्याक. Genuine Sanskrit synonym, but secondary to धान्यक, which is the pharmacopoeial head-name, so not marked preferred.

verdicts.name: धान्याकम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library (Ayurveda/nighantu index): 'Dhānyaka (धान्यक) is the Sanskrit name for a medicinal plant identified with Coriandrum sativum Linn.'; variants Dhānyāka/Dhanyāka listed in the same entry. Synonym set given as Dhanika, Dhanya, Vitunnaka, Kustumburu.
verdicts.reason: Species identification is solid and this is the Ayurvedic head-name for the drug, hence preferred. One caution for the editor: the attested citation form is धान्यक / धान्याक; धान्याकम् is its nominative-singular neuter inflection, not the dictionary lemma. If the page lists lemma forms elsewhere, normalise to धान्यक.

verdicts.name: கொத்தமல்லி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com): 'Coriander, Coriandrum sativum'; Miron Winslow, A Comprehensive Tamil and English Dictionary: 'Coriander seed, Coriandrum sativum, L.'; Fabricius equates it with கொத்தம். India Flora Online (IISc) independently lists Tamil 'Kotthamalli'.
verdicts.reason: Three historical Tamil lexicons plus a flora database give the binomial directly. Unambiguously the standard and most-searched Tamil name.

verdicts.name: धनिया
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs' ('Dhaniya [धनिया] ... identified with Coriandrum sativum'); DDSA Practical Hindi-English Dictionary. For the leaf specifically, India Flora Online (IISc) lists Hindi 'Dhaniya patti, Dhaniya patta'.
verdicts.reason: Correct for the species. Note for this page: धनिया unqualified usually denotes the seed/fruit in Hindi trade and cooking; the leaf drug is normally धनिया पत्ती / धनिया पत्ता, which I have returned in discovered.

verdicts.name: कुस्तुम्बरी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Monier-Williams: 'the plant coriander, [Suśruta]'; Apte (DDSA): 'The धान्याक plant', with the Suśruta line आर्द्रां कुस्तुम्बरीं कुर्यात् — which notably refers to the FRESH (ārdrā) plant, i.e. the herb.
verdicts.reason: Attested classically for Coriandrum sativum, and the Suśruta citation is specifically about the fresh herb, which suits this page. Secondary to धान्यक as a head-name, so not preferred.

verdicts.name: धान्याकम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library nighantu index: 'Dhānyaka (धान्यक) is the Sanskrit name for a medicinal plant identified with Coriandrum sativum Linn.'
verdicts.reason: Species identification solid; Ayurvedic head-name. Same inflection caveat as on the coriander page: the lemma is धान्यक / धान्याक, and धान्याकम् is the nominative singular.

verdicts.name: கொத்தமல்லி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon: 'Coriander, Coriandrum sativum'; Winslow: 'Coriander seed, Coriandrum sativum, L.'; India Flora Online Tamil 'Kotthamalli'.
verdicts.reason: Lexicon-attested with the binomial. For the leaf the everyday Tamil is கொத்தமல்லி இலை / கொத்தமல்லித் தழை, but the bare form is correct for the species and is the searched form.

verdicts.name: जीरा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA, A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary (Univ. of Chicago DSAL), via wisdomlib: 'Jīrā (जीरा): (nm) cumin seed'. Species tie corroborated by the Wisdom Library Ayurveda entry 'Jīraka (जीरक) is the Sanskrit name for a medicinal plant identified with Cuminum cyminum Linn.', of which जीरा is the Hindi reflex.
verdicts.reason: Dictionary-attested Hindi name for cumin and the overwhelmingly dominant spelling. Preferred Hindi form.

verdicts.name: ज़ीरा
verdicts.reason: Retrieved: DDSA's Hindi dictionary gives the headword as जीरा, without nukta. ज़ीरा is a nukta orthography reflecting Urdu زیرہ / Persian zīra; no flora, pharmacopoeial or lexicon source I read spells the plant name with nukta. Same plant, not a misidentification — it is a spelling variant that duplicates the confirmed जीरा, so drop it rather than carry two spellings.

verdicts.name: जीरकम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library nighantu index: 'Jīraka (जीरक) is the Sanskrit name for a medicinal plant identified with Cuminum cyminum Linn.' The same entry records that Cuminum cyminum L. (Jīraka) is also called Śvetajīraka 'according to both the Ayurvedic Formulary of India and the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India'.
verdicts.reason: Direct binomial identification, and the AFI/API are named as using Jīraka/Śvetajīraka for this species. Preferred Sanskrit form. Caveat: the lemma is जीरक; जीरकम् is the nominative-singular neuter.

verdicts.name: जीरिका
verdicts.reason: Retrieved the attested synonym set for Jīraka from the Raj Nighantu via wisdomlib: Jaraṇa, Jīra, Jīrṇa, Dīpya, Dīpaka, Ajājikī, Vanhiśaṃkha, Māgadha; plus ajājī, śvetajājī, śuklajājī, dīrghajīraka from the same source and from Gernot Katzer's spice etymology page. जीरिका appears in none of them. The closest real forms are अजाजिकी (ajājikī) and जीरक. Treat जीरिका as an unattested Wikidata-side coinage.

verdicts.name: जीरा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA Practical Hindi-English Dictionary: 'Jīrā (जीरा): (nm) cumin seed'; species tie via Wisdom Library's Jīraka = Cuminum cyminum entry.
verdicts.reason: Correct Hindi name for the species and the preferred spelling. Note for this page: Hindi जीरा denotes the seed; there is no distinct Hindi name in my sources for the plant used as a leafy herb, and cumin is not used as a leaf drug.

verdicts.name: ज़ीरा
verdicts.reason: Nukta spelling variant of जीरा, reflecting Urdu/Persian zīra. DDSA's headword is जीरा; no botanical or pharmacopoeial source I retrieved uses the nukta form. Harmless but redundant — drop it.

verdicts.name: जीरकम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library: 'Jīraka (जीरक) is the Sanskrit name for a medicinal plant identified with Cuminum cyminum Linn.'; AFI and API named in the same entry as using Jīraka / Śvetajīraka for this species.
verdicts.reason: Species identification solid and pharmacopoeially used. Lemma is जीरक; जीरकम् is its nominative singular.

verdicts.name: जीरिका
verdicts.reason: Absent from the Raj Nighantu synonym list for Jīraka (Jaraṇa, Jīra, Jīrṇa, Dīpya, Dīpaka, Ajājikī, Vanhiśaṃkha, Māgadha) retrieved via wisdomlib, and absent from the ajājī/śvetajājī set. Unattested; the nearest genuine form is अजाजिकी.

verdicts.name: बेर्बेरीस अरिस्टटा
verdicts.reason: This is not a Hindi plant name at all — it is the Latin binomial 'Berberis aristata' transcribed into Devanagari. Independent sources give the actual Hindi names: India Flora Online / India Biodiversity list 'Chitra, Chotra, Dar-chob, Dar-hald'; ayurvedicmedicinalplants.com gives Hindi 'Daruhaldi, Jharihaldi'; the market-sample study on Daruharidra (PMC3566491) gives Hindi 'chitra, dar-hald, rasaut, kashmal'. A Devanagari rendering of a Latin name on a monograph page would read as a vernacular name and should not ship.

verdicts.name: बेर्बेरीस अरिस्टटा
verdicts.reason: Same defect as the Hindi entry: the Latin binomial in Devanagari, not Sanskrit. The attested Sanskrit names are दारुहरिद्रा and दार्वी, with पीतदारु, कटंकटेरी, हरिद्रु and others (ayurvedicmedicinalplants.com monograph; PMC3566491 gives Sanskrit 'daruharidra, darvi, kata, pitadaru, suvarnavarna'). Reject.

verdicts.name: மரமஞ்சள்
verdicts.denotesInstead: Coscinium fenestratum (Goetgh.) Colebr. (Menispermaceae), the South Indian climber 'tree turmeric'
verdicts.reason: THIS IS THE BATCH'S aśvattha-CLASS ERROR. The University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com) defines மரமஞ்சள் as 'Tree turmeric, s. cl., Coscinium fenestratum; கொடிவகை' — a climber, not a Berberis shrub; the Tamil Tamil Akaramuthali likewise glosses it 'ஒருகொடிவகை' (a kind of climber). Tamil names given for Berberis aristata by botanical sources are entirely different: mullukala, usikkala, kasturimanjal (India Biodiversity / PMC3566491). The reason this error propagates is market substitution: in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, Coscinium fenestratum stem is traded AS Daruharidra, and the Daruharidra market-sample study (PMC3566491) is specifically about that adulteration. English Wikipedia repeats 'Mara manjal' in the Berberis aristata lead and Wikidata harvests it from there, so this candidate has a mirror, not a corroborator. Carrying it would print the name of a different family's plant on a Berberis page.

verdicts.name: देवदार
verdicts.corroboratingSource: India Flora Online (IISc, indiaflora-ces.iisc.ac.in herbsheet for Cedrus deodara): Hindi 'Devdar'. Corroborated by the Shri Dharmasthala Manjunatheshwara / davpharmacy Dravyaguna monograph 'Devadaru — देवदारु' for Cedrus deodara.
verdicts.reason: A flora database keyed to the binomial gives this Hindi name; it is also the everyday Hindi word for the Himalayan deodar. Preferred Hindi form.

verdicts.name: सीडर
verdicts.reason: सीडर is the English word 'cedar' written in Devanagari, not a Hindi plant name; no flora, lexicon or pharmacopoeial source I retrieved lists it for Cedrus deodara (India Flora Online gives only 'Devdar' for Hindi). Worse than merely unattested as a label: English 'cedar' is a polyphyletic trade word covering Cedrus, Juniperus, Thuja, Cedrela and Toona, so a reader would get no species information from it.

verdicts.name: தேவதாரம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: India Flora Online (IISc) herbsheet for Cedrus deodara: Tamil 'Devadaram' (alongside Kannada 'Devadaru', Sanskrit 'Devdar').
verdicts.denotesInstead: AMBIGUOUS — also denotes Erythroxylum monogynum Roxb. (Erythroxylaceae), 'bastard sandal / red cedar'. Not exclusive to Cedrus deodara.
verdicts.reason: Attested for Cedrus deodara by a flora database independent of Wikidata, so I am confirming it, but flagging a real collision the editor should see: the University of Madras Tamil Lexicon glosses தேவதாரம் as 'Common bastard cedar' and associates it with வண்டுகொல்லி மரம் / மதகரி வேப்ப மரம், and Tamil nursery and ethnobotanical sources give 'Devadara / Devadaram' for Erythroxylum monogynum, a peninsular Indian tree traded as a sandalwood adulterant. Cedrus deodara does not grow in Tamil Nadu, so in native Tamil usage the word more often means the Erythroxylum. Safe to keep only if the page makes the Ayurvedic/Siddha drug sense explicit.

verdicts.name: धनिया
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': 'Dhaniya [धनिया] in the Hindi language is the name of a plant identified with Coriandrum sativum from the Apiaceae (Carrot) family'; DDSA Practical Hindi-English Dictionary: 'Dhaniyā (nm) coriander'.
verdicts.reason: Binomial-level identification in an independent plant-name index plus a standard dictionary. Dominant Hindi form, hence preferred.

verdicts.name: कुस्तुम्बरी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Monier-Williams Sanskrit-English Dictionary: 'the plant coriander, [Suśruta]'; Apte/DDSA: 'The धान्याक plant', quoting Suśruta आर्द्रां कुस्तुम्बरीं कुर्यात्.
verdicts.reason: Genuine classical synonym, explicitly equated with धान्याक in Apte. Not preferred because धान्यक is this page's own head-name and the pharmacopoeial form.

verdicts.name: धान्याकम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library nighantu index: 'Dhānyaka (धान्यक) is the Sanskrit name for a medicinal plant identified with Coriandrum sativum Linn.', with synonyms Dhanika, Dhanya, Vitunnaka, Kustumburu.
verdicts.reason: This is the page's eponym and the Ayurvedic head-name for the drug, independently tied to the binomial. Caveat: lemma is धान्यक (or धान्याक); धान्याकम् is the nominative singular neuter — normalise if the page lists lemmas.

verdicts.name: கொத்தமல்லி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon: 'Coriander, Coriandrum sativum'; Winslow: 'Coriander seed, Coriandrum sativum, L.'; Fabricius; India Flora Online Tamil 'Kotthamalli'.
verdicts.reason: Three Tamil lexicons give the binomial outright; also the searched everyday form.

verdicts.name: गुल धावी
verdicts.reason: Retrieved: the Ayushvedah drug record for Woodfordia fruticosa lists 'Gul dhawa' under URDU, not Hindi; गुल is the Persian word for flower, and the Unani drug name is गुल-ए-धावा. The Hindi names from botanical sources are different: India Flora Online (IISc) gives Hindi 'Dawi, Thawi Santha, Dhaula, Dhaura, Dhai, Dhawai, Dhatuki', and the Vindhyan Ecology and Natural History Foundation's Hindi monograph is titled 'धवई / ढवाई (Woodfordia fruticosa)'. So this is a language-label error, not a species error — the name does belong to this plant, but as Unani/Urdu. Drop it from the Hindi slot or relabel it; I have returned the attested Hindi forms in discovered.

verdicts.name: धावा
verdicts.reason: Retrieved: India Flora Online (IISc) herbsheet for Anogeissus latifolia gives Hindi 'Bakla, Dhaura' only (Sanskrit 'Madhuratvacha, Vakavruksha, Dhawala'; Marathi 'Dhavda'); the Hindi-language article at hellobanswara.com states धावड़ा को धौरा, धव, धावडो, धमोडा आदि नामों से जाना जाता है. The long-ā form धावा appears in none of them — it looks like a back-formation from the loose romanisation 'dhawa' that circulates in agroforestry species lists (the World Agroforestry entry is demonstrably unreliable here, filing Kannada 'bejjalu' and Tamil 'vekkali' under Hindi). धावा in ordinary Hindi is a homograph meaning raid/attack. Related caution for the editor: dhai/dhavi-type Hindi names belong to Woodfordia fruticosa (the dhataki page in this same batch), so a loose 'dhava/dhavi' spelling is a live confusion between two different drugs. Use धौरा / धावड़ा instead.

verdicts.name: திராட்சை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com): 'Common grape vine, l. cl., Vitis vinifera; கொடிவகை'. Also in the Tamil Tamil Akaramuthali as திராட்சைக்கொடி, and in McAlpin's Core Vocabulary as 'grape(s)'.
verdicts.reason: The Madras Lexicon gives the binomial Vitis vinifera directly. This is the only and the universal Tamil word for grape, so it is the preferred form.

verdicts.name: द्रोणपुष्पी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Raj Nighantu (13th c.), verses 5.137-138, via wisdomlib: the common Hindi designation is given as 'Gūmā or Droṇapuṣpī', with the species identified as Leucas cephalotes Spreng.
verdicts.denotesInstead: GENUS-LEVEL, not species-specific: the same Raj Nighantu passage identifies Droṇapuṣpī with Leucas cephalotes OR Leucas aspera OR Leucas linifolia, and Monier-Williams records Bhāvaprakāśa's identification as 'Phlomis zeylanica'.
verdicts.reason: The name is attested for this species, and attested specifically as a Hindi designation, so I am confirming it — but it is a Sanskrit loan carried into Hindi Ayurvedic writing, and गूमा is the form an actual Hindi speaker uses or searches, so preferred stays false. The editor should also know the name is not species-exclusive within Leucas; if the page claims a one-to-one mapping to L. cephalotes it is overstating the source.

verdicts.name: द्रोणपुष्पीसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: Unattested. The Raj Nighantu synonym set retrieved via wisdomlib is Dīrghapatrā, Kumbhayoni, Kutumbikā, Citrākṣupa, Kutumbā, Supuṣpā, Citrapatrikā — plus the head-name द्रोणपुष्पी itself. No nighantu gives a -सस्यम् compound. This is a Wikidata labelling artifact: सस्यम् means 'crop/plant' and has been appended to a real stem to manufacture a Sanskrit label. The identical pattern appears on एरण्डसस्यम् elsewhere in this same batch, which confirms it is systematic rather than a one-off. Use द्रोणपुष्पी.

verdicts.name: इलायची
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA, A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary (Univ. of Chicago DSAL), via wisdomlib: 'Ilayachi in Hindi refers in English to: (nf) cardamom'. Species tie corroborated by the Dabur Ayurvedic medicinal plants monograph for Elaichi (इलायची), which gives Elettaria cardamomum as the Latin name.
verdicts.reason: Dictionary-attested and the universal Hindi word. One caution worth printing on the page: unqualified इलायची means green/small cardamom, i.e. Elettaria cardamomum; बड़ी इलायची is a different species, Amomum subulatum.

verdicts.name: छोटी इलायची
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Dabur Ayurvedic medicinal plants monograph 'Elaichi (इलायची) — Elettaria cardamomum', which lists Hindi names Elaichi, Elachi, Ilachi and Chhoti Elaichi; also AyurTimes' Elaichi monograph for Elettaria cardamomum.
verdicts.reason: Confirmed, with honest provenance: my corroboration here is Ayurvedic-industry monographs keyed to the binomial rather than a lexicon or the API text, which I could not retrieve directly. The form is valuable precisely because it disambiguates from बड़ी इलायची (Amomum subulatum). Secondary to the bare इलायची as a search term, so not preferred.

verdicts.name: एला
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Monier-Williams Sanskrit-English Dictionary: 'Elā (एला) — cardamoms, the seed of the Eletteria cardamomum, or Alpinia Cardamomum'. Also the Amarakoṣa (cardamom varieties) and multiple Suśruta Saṃhitā citations, per wisdomlib.
verdicts.reason: Monier-Williams names the genus explicitly, and the word is the classical head-name used across Caraka, Suśruta and the nighantus. Preferred Sanskrit form. Minor note: Monier-Williams' alternative 'Alpinia cardamomum' is an obsolete synonym, not a competing species.

verdicts.name: ஏலம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com): 'Cardamom-plant, 1. sh., Elettaria cardamomum'; Miron Winslow: 'Cardamom, the plant or seed... Elettaria cardamomum'; J.P. Fabricius: 'the cardamom plant; 2. its seed'.
verdicts.reason: Three Tamil lexicons give the binomial, and the Madras Lexicon glosses ஏலம் as the PLANT, which is what a monograph page names — so it is preferred over the pod-word ஏலக்காய் here. Note for the editor: ஏலம் is a homograph also meaning 'auction', so page context should make the botanical sense clear.

verdicts.name: अरंडी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': 'Arandi [अरंडी] in the Hindi language is the name of a plant identified with Ricinus communis L. from the Euphorbiaceae (castor) family.'
verdicts.reason: Explicit Hindi-language, binomial-level identification from a plant-name index independent of Wikidata. Dominant Hindi form, hence preferred.

verdicts.name: अरण्डी
verdicts.reason: Not an error and not another plant — it is the Sanskritised orthography (ण्ड) of the same word as the confirmed अरंडी (anusvāra ंड). I could not find it in this spelling in any source I retrieved: the Wisdom Library plant-name index spells it अरंडी. Since अरंडी is confirmed on this page, carrying a second spelling adds no information, so leave it off rather than attest it.

verdicts.name: रेड़ी
verdicts.reason: The romanisation 'Redi' circulates in Ayurvedic herb lists for Ricinus communis, but the only source-level attestation I could retrieve is for RENDI, not REDI: the CRC World Dictionary of Medicinal and Poisonous Plants, via wisdomlib, states 'Rendi in India is the name of a plant defined with Ricinus communis'. रेड़ी (without the nasal) is therefore unattested in what I read; the nasalised रेंड़ी on this same page is the corroborated form. Same plant, so no botanical risk, but drop the unattested spelling.

verdicts.name: रेंड़ी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: CRC World Dictionary of Medicinal and Poisonous Plants (Umberto Quattrocchi), via the Wisdom Library entry for Rendi: 'Rendi in India is the name of a plant defined with Ricinus communis.'
verdicts.reason: A named reference work attests this name for exactly this species. Caveat for the editor: the source tags it 'in India' rather than specifically Hindi, though रेंड़ी is a standard north Indian regional form for castor. Secondary to अरंडी, so not preferred.

verdicts.name: एरण्डसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: Unattested Wikidata coinage, the same -सस्यम् ('crop/plant') suffix artifact as द्रोणपुष्पीसस्यम् elsewhere in this batch. The real Sanskrit name is एरण्ड, attested by the National Institute of Ayurveda herbal-garden monograph for Ricinus communis ('Eranda, pancangulah') and by the SDM Ayurveda College Dravyaguna entry 'Eranda', with the classical etymology erayati vāyum iti eraṇḍa. No nighantu gives एरण्डसस्यम्. Use एरण्ड.

verdicts.name: ஆமணக்கு
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com): 'Castor-plant, s. tr., Ricinus communis'; J.P. Fabricius: 'the castor plant, ricinus communis'; Miron Winslow: 'The castor plant, ஏரண்டம், Ricinus...'
verdicts.reason: Three Tamil lexicons give Ricinus communis by binomial; corroborated independently by the Kerala SMPB herbal database (Aavannakku) and by Ayurvedic monographs listing Tamil 'Amanakku'. Preferred Tamil form. Note Fabricius distinguishes சிற்றாமணக்கு (small castor) as a separate entity.

verdicts.name: अरंडी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': 'Arandi [अरंडी] in the Hindi language is the name of a plant identified with Ricinus communis L.'
verdicts.reason: Correct for the species and the dominant Hindi form. This page is the root drug; Hindi has no separate attested root-name in my sources beyond the descriptive अरंडी की जड़.

verdicts.name: अरण्डी
verdicts.reason: Sanskritised spelling variant of the confirmed अरंडी; not found in this orthography in any source I retrieved. Not a misidentification, just a redundant duplicate — leave it off.

verdicts.name: रेड़ी
verdicts.reason: Unattested in the spelling given. The CRC World Dictionary of Medicinal and Poisonous Plants (via wisdomlib) attests 'Rendi' = रेंड़ी for Ricinus communis, not 'Redi'. Use the nasalised form on this page instead.

verdicts.name: रेंड़ी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: CRC World Dictionary of Medicinal and Poisonous Plants, via Wisdom Library: 'Rendi in India is the name of a plant defined with Ricinus communis.'
verdicts.reason: Named reference work, correct species. The source labels it 'in India' rather than Hindi specifically. Secondary to अरंडी.

verdicts.name: एरण्डसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: Wikidata -सस्यम् artifact, not a nighantu name. The attested Sanskrit is एरण्ड (National Institute of Ayurveda herbal-garden monograph for Ricinus communis: 'Eranda, pancangulah'). Relevant to this page specifically: the root drug is Eraṇḍamūla, and Eraṇḍamūla is the pharmacopoeial Sanskrit term — not एरण्डसस्यम्.

verdicts.name: ஆமணக்கு
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon: 'Castor-plant, s. tr., Ricinus communis'; Fabricius and Winslow likewise give Ricinus communis.
verdicts.reason: Lexicon-attested with the binomial; the standard Tamil name. The Tamil root-drug form in use is ஆமணக்கு வேர், but the bare plant name is correct for the species.

verdicts.name: अरंडी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': 'Arandi [अरंडी] in the Hindi language is the name of a plant identified with Ricinus communis L.'
verdicts.reason: Correct species, dominant Hindi form. This page is the leaf drug; the descriptive Hindi is अरंडी का पत्ता, but the plant name itself is what is attested.

verdicts.name: अरण्डी
verdicts.reason: Spelling variant of the confirmed अरंडी, not found in this orthography in the sources I read. Redundant, not wrong — drop.

verdicts.name: रेड़ी
verdicts.reason: Unattested spelling. The CRC World Dictionary of Medicinal and Poisonous Plants (via wisdomlib) attests 'Rendi' (रेंड़ी) for Ricinus communis; 'Redi' I could not source.

verdicts.name: रेंड़ी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: CRC World Dictionary of Medicinal and Poisonous Plants, via Wisdom Library: 'Rendi in India is the name of a plant defined with Ricinus communis.'
verdicts.reason: Attested for this species by a named reference work; the source says 'in India' rather than Hindi specifically. Secondary to अरंडी.

verdicts.name: एरण्डसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: Wikidata -सस्यम् coinage, the same artifact as द्रोणपुष्पीसस्यम् in this batch. The attested Sanskrit is एरण्ड (NIA herbal-garden monograph for Ricinus communis; SDM Ayurveda College Dravyaguna entry). For a leaf monograph the pharmacopoeial Sanskrit is Eraṇḍapatra.

verdicts.name: ஆமணக்கு
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon: 'Castor-plant, s. tr., Ricinus communis'; Fabricius: 'the castor plant, ricinus communis'; Winslow.
verdicts.reason: Lexicon-attested with the binomial. The leaf form in Tamil usage is ஆமணக்கு இலை; the bare name is correct for the species.

verdicts.name: நீலப் பசை மரம்
verdicts.reason: The only attestation I could find is the Tamil Wikipedia article title ta.wikipedia.org/wiki/நீலப்_பசை_மரம், which is a Wikidata mirror and a word-for-word calque of the English 'blue gum tree' (நீலம் blue + பசை gum + மரம் tree). It is a descriptive coinage, not a recorded Tamil plant name: agarathi.com (University of Madras Lexicon, Winslow, Fabricius) has no entry for it, and no entry for தைலமரம் either — unsurprising, since Eucalyptus globulus was only introduced to the Nilgiris in 1843 and is absent from the classical Tamil lexicons. Tamil usage in popular sources is தைல மரம் or the transliteration யூகலிப்டஸ் மரம், neither of which I can attest from a lexicon or flora database, so I am returning no discovered Tamil name rather than padding. Secondary issue: as a pure calque the phrase would fit any blue gum, including other Eucalyptus globulus subspecies and E. bicostata/E. maidenii, so it carries no species precision.

verdicts.name: होलीहेना प्यूब्सेन्स
verdicts.reason: This is not a Hindi plant name at all, it is the Latin binomial 'Holarrhena pubescens' written out in Devanagari (the hi.wikipedia article title, which mirrors the Wikidata label). No botanical or Ayurvedic source gives it as a vernacular name. Retrieved Hindi names for this species: IISc Flora of Peninsular India herbsheet gives Kurci, Kudha, Khurchi; MMPND (citing the Ayurvedic Formulary) gives Karva indrajau, Kud, Kudaiya, Kurchi, Kutaja.

verdicts.name: குடசப்பாலை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Tellicherry Tree' (Holarrhena pubescens) page, Names of Plants in India compilation: lists Tamil குடசப்பாலை (Kutaca-p-pālai) for this species; the form is a Tamil Lexicon compound of Skt. kuṭaja + Tam. pālai. Wikimedia Commons species category gives the same form.
verdicts.reason: Attested for Holarrhena pubescens by a source that publishes names per species and is not a Wikidata mirror. Left non-preferred because the Tamil names actually in current medicinal use are வெப்பாலை / வெட்பாலை and கொடகப்பாலை (MMPND citing the Ayurvedic Formulary gives Veppalei, Kodagapalei, Vennalai, Indraban); குடசப்பாலை is the lexicon form, not what a Tamil speaker would search.

verdicts.name: इङ्गुदवृक्षः
verdicts.reason: No lexicon attests the compound इङ्गुदवृक्ष. wisdomlib's aggregated Sanskrit dictionary entry for this word family gives only इङ्गुदी (iṅgudī), इङ्गुद (iṅguda) and इङ्गुल (iṅgula), plus the derived इङ्गुदीपादपः; there is no vṛkṣa compound in Monier-Williams or Apte. Nighantu synonym sets for Ingudi (Madanapala: Bhallaki, Vrikshakantaka, Tapasadruma, Inguda; Kaiyadeva: Angaravriksha, Tiktamajja, Kantakavriksha, Tapasdruma; Amarakosha: Tapasataru, Tiktamajja) likewise contain no इङ्गुदवृक्ष. Separately worth noting as a standing hazard on this page: several Sanskrit lexicons gloss इङ्गुदी as Terminalia catappa, and the Balanites identification is the Ayurvedic/API one, so the Sanskrit term is not botanically unambiguous.

verdicts.name: ईसबगोल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: ICAR Directorate of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants Research (DMAPR), mandate-crop page for Plantago ovata, titled ईसबगोल (dmapr.icar.gov.in/aboutus/mandatecrop/Isabgol H.html) — a Government of India agricultural research body publishing the Hindi name against the species.
verdicts.reason: Retrieved from ICAR-DMAPR's own Hindi crop page for Plantago ovata, independent of Wikidata. It is also the universal trade and pharmacopoeial Hindi name (API/Ayurvedic sources list Isabgol, Isabgul, Ispaghul for this species), so it is the form a Hindi speaker would use or search.

verdicts.name: ईसबगोल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: ICAR Directorate of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants Research (DMAPR), mandate-crop page for Plantago ovata, titled ईसबगोल — Government of India body publishing the Hindi name against the species.
verdicts.reason: Same species as the isabgol page (Plantago ovata, Q311228) and the same retrieval. Attested independently of Wikidata and is the dominant Hindi form.

verdicts.name: மாம்பாஞ்சான்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'Names of Plants in India :: Aristolochia indica L.' (indiantreepix compilation, Tamil names in Tamil script): ஈச்சுரமூலி (ishvara-muli), மாம்பாஞ்சான் (mampancan), பெருமருந்து (peru-maruntu). Corroborated by FRLHT ENVIS Centre on Medicinal Plants, which lists Tamil Perumarunthukodi / Isvaramuli / Thazhaisurulikodi for Aristolochia indica.
verdicts.reason: மாம்பாஞ்சான் is a genuine Tamil Lexicon name for Aristolochia indica, so it belongs on the page, but it is a minor regional form. The names a Tamil or Siddha reader would actually use are ஈச்சுரமூலி / ஈஸ்வரமூலி and பெருமருந்து, so preferred is left false.

verdicts.name: जामुन
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Jamun' (Syzygium cumini) page: Hindi जामुन in Devanagari. Corroborated by IISc Flora of Peninsular India (Hindi: Jamun, Jam).
verdicts.reason: Attested per species by two sources that publish names per botanical species, neither a Wikidata mirror. It is the standard, universally used Hindi name for the tree and fruit.

verdicts.name: जम्बूफलम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for jambūphala: 'the edible, dark blue plum of the tree Syzygium cumini', with textual occurrences in Garga Samhita and Ayurvedic/agricultural Puranic literature; Flowers of India's Jamun page gives Sanskrit जम्बुफल.
verdicts.reason: Genuinely attested for this species, but it is a compound naming the FRUIT (जम्बू + फल), not the tree or the drug. The Sanskrit/Ayurvedic name of the plant is जम्बू, which is also the API monograph name. Keep it only if the page is about the fruit; do not let it stand as the species name, hence preferred false.

verdicts.name: நாவல்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Tamil Heritage Foundation CMS species page for Syzygium cumini, titled நாவல் (thfcms.tamilheritage.org/syzygium-cumini/); TNAU Agritech Portal horticulture page for jamun gives Tamil நாவல் பழம், நாகப்பழம், நவாப்பழம்; IISc Flora of Peninsular India gives Tamil Naval, Neredom.
verdicts.reason: Attested per species by an independent Tamil institutional source and by Tamil Nadu Agricultural University's own portal. நாவல் is the ordinary Tamil name a speaker would use and search.

verdicts.name: जामुन
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Jamun' (Syzygium cumini) page: Hindi जामुन; IISc Flora of Peninsular India (Hindi: Jamun, Jam).
verdicts.reason: Same species as the jambu page (Q232571). Attested per species, independent of Wikidata, and the dominant Hindi form. Note the page is the seed (beeja); Hindi for the seed specifically is जामुन की गुठली, but जामुन is correct for the species.

verdicts.name: जम्बूफलम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for jambūphala: 'the edible, dark blue plum of the tree Syzygium cumini'; Flowers of India gives Sanskrit जम्बुफल for the species.
verdicts.reason: Attested for this species but it names the fruit pulp, which is actively wrong for a page about the SEED (jambu beeja). The Sanskrit for the drug on this page is जम्बूबीजम् and the species name is जम्बू. Preferred false; consider replacing on this page.

verdicts.name: நாவல்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Tamil Heritage Foundation species page for Syzygium cumini titled நாவல்; TNAU Agritech Portal jamun page (நாவல் பழம், நாகப்பழம்); IISc Flora of Peninsular India (Naval, Neredom).
verdicts.reason: Attested per species by independent Tamil institutional sources; the ordinary Tamil name.

verdicts.name: जामुन
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Jamun' (Syzygium cumini) page: Hindi जामुन; IISc Flora of Peninsular India (Hindi: Jamun, Jam).
verdicts.reason: Same species as the jambu page. Attested per species independently of Wikidata; the dominant Hindi name.

verdicts.name: जम्बूफलम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for jambūphala: 'the edible, dark blue plum of the tree Syzygium cumini'; Flowers of India gives Sanskrit जम्बुफल.
verdicts.reason: Attested but denotes the fruit, not the tree; the species-level Sanskrit name is जम्बू. Preferred false.

verdicts.name: நாவல்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Tamil Heritage Foundation species page for Syzygium cumini titled நாவல்; TNAU Agritech Portal jamun page; IISc Flora of Peninsular India (Naval, Neredom).
verdicts.reason: Attested per species by independent Tamil institutional sources; the ordinary Tamil name.

verdicts.name: जटामांसी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND (Multilingual Multiscript Plant Name Database, University of Melbourne), 'Sorting Nardostachys names', entry for Nardostachys jatamansi (Jones) DC.: Hindi 'Jatamansi (HIM)', Sanskrit जटामांसी in Devanagari, source credited to Himalaya Herbal Healthcare's per-species herb monograph.
verdicts.reason: MMPND publishes names per botanical species with per-name source credits and is not a Wikidata mirror. जटामांसी is both the Ayurvedic drug name and the ordinary Hindi trade name for this root, so it is the form a speaker would search. Hindi बालछड़ is the other common trade name.

verdicts.name: ஜாதமாசி
verdicts.reason: The only source carrying this exact spelling is the Tamil Wikipedia article ஜாதமாசி, which mirrors the Wikidata label and is therefore a weak corroborator by the stated rule, so I am not setting confirmed. Independent Tamil and Siddha sources give different forms: சடாமாஞ்சில் (Siddha name 'Sadamanchil', per the Nardostachys jatamansi entry in the Springer reference work on Indian medicinal plants), ஜடாமான்சி / ஜடாமாஞ்சி (Tamil trade usage), and ta.wiktionary heads the word as சடாமாஞ்சி. ஜாதமாசி substitutes த for ட and drops the ஞ், which reads as a corrupted transcription rather than an attested Tamil form. Same plant, so no wrong-species risk, but the spelling should not stand.

verdicts.name: மௌவல்
verdicts.denotesInstead: Jasminum spp. generally — the lexicon gloss is 'wild jasmine' (வனமல்லிகை / காட்டுமல்லிகை), with cross-references to Arabian jasmine (Jasminum sambac) and to wild jasmine (Jasminum angustifolium); no authority pins it to Jasminum officinale
verdicts.reason: I retrieved the Tamil Lexicon entry itself (dt.madurai.io, Madras University Tamil Lexicon, corroborated by Agarathi via Wiktionary). It defines மௌவல் only as 'the wild jasmine, வனமல்லிகை', cross-referenced to காட்டுமல்லிகை and, in classical usage, also to Arabian jasmine and even to the lotus. The lexicon does not assign it to a species, and the species mappings circulating online split it across Jasminum officinale, J. grandiflorum and J. angustifolium. That is a genus-level word being presented as a species name, so confirmed stays false. It is also a literary/archaic word, not what a Tamil speaker would search.

verdicts.name: जायफल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND, 'Sorting Myristica names', Myristica fragrans: Hindi nutmeg given in Devanagari as जायफल (Jāyaphala), with the variant जाईफल; mace given separately as जावित्री.
verdicts.reason: MMPND lists names per species with source credits and distinguishes nutmeg from mace. जायफल is the standard Hindi name for the nutmeg seed, which is exactly this page's drug, and is the form a speaker would use.

verdicts.name: मिरिस्तिका फ्राग्रान्स
verdicts.reason: Not a Hindi plant name — it is the Latin binomial 'Myristica fragrans' transcribed into Devanagari, the pattern of a hi.wikipedia title mirroring a Wikidata label. MMPND's per-species Hindi list for Myristica fragrans contains जायफल, जाईफल, जाइफल and जावित्री and nothing resembling this. Drop it.

verdicts.name: जाती
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Monier-Williams Sanskrit-English Dictionary entry for jātī (retrieved via wisdomlib): the primary gloss is 'Jasminum grandiflorum' (citing Harivaṃśa, Bhartṛhari, Bhāgavata-purāṇa, Amaru-śataka), and the same entry additionally gives 'mace, nutmeg' citing Suśruta and Varāhamihira's Bṛhat-saṃhitā; the 17th-c. Bhojanakutūhala also uses jātī for nutmeg.
verdicts.denotesInstead: Jasminum grandiflorum — this is the dominant and primary meaning of जाती in Sanskrit, and the word is in active Ayurvedic use for jasmine (API Jati = Jasminum grandiflorum / J. officinale var. grandiflorum)
verdicts.reason: जाती is genuinely attested for nutmeg in Suśruta and Bṛhat-saṃhitā, so I am not calling it unattested. But it is a dangerous homonym: in Ayurveda जाती standing alone normally means jasmine, and 'Jati' is itself a separate monograph in this same batch (Jasminum officinale). Leaving the bare जाती on a nutmeg page will read as a misidentification to anyone who knows the lexicon. The unambiguous Sanskrit names are जातीफलम् (nutmeg) and जातीपत्री / जातीकोशः (mace), so preferred is false and I would replace rather than keep.

verdicts.name: जायफल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND, 'Sorting Myristica names', Myristica fragrans: Hindi जायफल (Jāyaphala) for nutmeg, जावित्री (Jāvitrī) for mace.
verdicts.reason: जायफल is correctly attested for this species, so it is not a botanical error. But this page is Javitri, i.e. the mace (the arillode), and जायफल names the nutmeg seed specifically — MMPND separates the two. The Hindi name for the drug on this page is जावित्री. Preferred is false and जावित्री should be added.

verdicts.name: मिरिस्तिका फ्राग्रान्स
verdicts.reason: Not a Hindi name — the Latin binomial 'Myristica fragrans' in Devanagari, a Wikidata/hi.wikipedia label artifact. MMPND's per-species Hindi list for Myristica fragrans gives only जायफल, जाईफल, जाइफल, जावित्री. Drop it.

verdicts.name: जाती
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Monier-Williams entry for jātī (via wisdomlib): primary gloss 'Jasminum grandiflorum'; the same entry also gives 'mace, nutmeg' citing Suśruta and Varāhamihira's Bṛhat-saṃhitā.
verdicts.denotesInstead: Jasminum grandiflorum — the primary and dominant Sanskrit sense of जाती, and the Ayurvedic drug 'Jati' in current use
verdicts.reason: Monier-Williams explicitly glosses jātī as 'mace' as well as nutmeg, so for a mace page the attestation is real. Still a homonym hazard against the separate Jati (Jasminum) monograph in this same batch. The unambiguous Sanskrit for mace is जातीपत्री / जातीकोशः, so preferred is false.

verdicts.name: जीरा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND, 'Sorting Cuminum names', Cuminum cyminum: Hindi given in Devanagari as जीरा (Jiiraa/Jeera), alongside ज़ीरा, सफेद जीरा and सफेद ज़ीरा.
verdicts.reason: MMPND lists names per species in native script with source credits. जीरा is the ordinary and overwhelmingly dominant Hindi name for cumin, so it is the preferred Hindi form.

verdicts.name: ज़ीरा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND, 'Sorting Cuminum names', Cuminum cyminum: Hindi ज़ीरा (Zeera/zira) listed in Devanagari with nuqta, alongside जीरा.
verdicts.reason: A genuine attested Hindi/Urdu-influenced spelling of the same word, explicitly listed by MMPND for this species. Correct but a spelling variant of जीरा, so preferred stays false.

verdicts.name: जीरकम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib's aggregated Sanskrit/Ayurveda entry for jīraka: 'Jīraka (जीरक) refers to the medicinal plant Cuminum cyminum Linn.', identified per verse 6.56-57 of Narahari's 13th-c. Rāja Nighaṇṭu, with the synonym set Jaraṇa, Jīra, Jīrṇa, Dīpya, Dīpaka, Ajājikī, Vanhiśaṃkha, Māgadha.
verdicts.reason: The Rāja Nighaṇṭu identification of जीरक with Cuminum cyminum is explicit and per species; जीरकम् is simply the neuter nominative citation form of that headword and is how Ayurvedic Sanskrit writes it. It is also the API monograph name (Jiraka). Preferred Sanskrit form on this page.

verdicts.name: जीरिका
verdicts.reason: I could not retrieve जीरिका in any Sanskrit lexicon. It is absent from Monier-Williams and Apte as surfaced by sanskritdictionary.com and wisdomlib, and absent from the Rāja Nighaṇṭu synonym set for jīraka (Jaraṇa, Jīra, Jīrṇa, Dīpya, Dīpaka, Ajājikī, Vanhiśaṃkha, Māgadha) and from MMPND's Sanskrit list for Cuminum cyminum (अजाजी, जारण, जिरण, जीर्ण, सुगंध). It looks like a feminine form coined around जीरक rather than an attested name. Same plant, so no misidentification risk, but it should not stand as a cited Sanskrit name.

verdicts.name: சீரகம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND, 'Sorting Cuminum names', Cuminum cyminum: Tamil listed in Tamil script as சீரகம் (Cirakam/Shiragam) and ஜீரகம் (Jirakam/Jeerakam).
verdicts.reason: Attested per species in Tamil script by MMPND. சீரகம் is the everyday Tamil word for cumin and the form a Tamil speaker would use and search.

verdicts.name: सेलास्ट्रस पैनिकुलटस
verdicts.reason: Not a Hindi plant name — the Latin binomial 'Celastrus paniculatus' transcribed into Devanagari, the signature of a hi.wikipedia title mirroring a Wikidata label. The actual Hindi name retrieved from wisdomlib's per-species Jyotishmati entry is माल-कांगनी (Mal-kangni), corroborated across vernacular lists (Hindi and Bengali Mālkaṅganī). Drop this and use मालकांगनी.

verdicts.name: कचनार
verdicts.corroboratingSource: IISc Flora of Peninsular India herbsheet for Bauhinia variegata L. (indiaflora-ces.iisc.ac.in): Hindi 'Kachnar, Khairwal, Mohota'. Corroborated by the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India's Kanchanara monograph vernacular list, which gives Hindi: Kachnar.
verdicts.reason: Attested per species by an academic flora and by the API monograph for this drug. कचनार is the universal Hindi name for Bauhinia variegata (the edible flower bud sold under that name), so it is the preferred Hindi form.

verdicts.name: मन्दारः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Erythrina variegata (Indian coral tree) — Sanskrit मन्दार / मन्दारक / मन्दारवः, the Ayurvedic drug Paribhadra (पारिभद्रः); the word is also used in Sanskrit for the mythological coral tree and, in some lexicons, for Calotropis gigantea
verdicts.reason: This is the kind of error worth stopping. IISc Flora of Peninsular India gives Sanskrit for Bauhinia variegata as 'Kanchanara' only, and the API Kanchanara monograph gives Kanchanara and Kovidara. Retrieval for मन्दार instead returns Erythrina variegata: Sanskrit names mandara, mandarakah, mandaravah, paribhadrah. The Bauhinia association comes through Dravidian, not Sanskrit — Tamil மந்தாரை, Kannada 'Kempu mandara', Telugu 'Mandari' are all genuine names for Bauhinia variegata, and Wikidata appears to have back-formed a Sanskrit label from them. Presented as Sanskrit on a Kachnar page, मन्दारः points a reader at the coral tree. Use काञ्चनारः / कोविदारः instead.

verdicts.name: மலையாத்தி
verdicts.denotesInstead: Bauhinia malabarica — MMPND's 'Sorting Bauhinia names' places மலையாத்தி (malai-y-atti) under Bauhinia malabarica, not B. variegata; the ஆத்தி word-family (ஆத்தி, புளியாத்தி, வரையாத்தி) belongs to Bauhinia racemosa and relatives, with aarai/aaththi cognates covering B. racemosa, B. tomentosa, B. spicata and B. parviflora
verdicts.reason: A second genuine misassignment. I checked MMPND's per-species Bauhinia listing directly: under B. variegata it gives only Hindi 'Kachnar' and no Tamil name, while மலையாத்தி appears under Bauhinia malabarica; Flowers of India associates malaiyatti and புளியாத்தி with Bauhinia racemosa. IISc Flora of Peninsular India gives the Tamil for B. variegata as 'Sigappumanch, Sigappumantharai' (சிகப்பு மந்தாரை / செம்மந்தாரை). So மலையாத்தி is a real Tamil plant name for a different Bauhinia and would mislead a reader on this page.

verdicts.name: कचूर
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Sri Satya Sai Murlidhar Ayurvedic College KARCHURA monograph PDF (ssmdayurvediccollege.com) and the Shri Dharmasthala Ayurveda college Dravyaguna 'Karchur' monograph: Curcuma zedoaria (Rosc.), Zingiberaceae, Hindi name Kachur (कचूर), also Jangli Haldi.
verdicts.reason: Attested per species by two Ayurvedic-college Dravyaguna monographs, which publish names against the botanical species rather than mirroring Wikidata. कचूर is the standard Hindi and trade name for zedoary rhizome. One caution recorded in those same sources, worth knowing but not a name problem: कचूर is classically a substitute for शटी (Hedychium spicatum), so शटी should not be carried onto this page as its Sanskrit name.

verdicts.name: कदंब वृक्ष
verdicts.reason: The right plant but not a lexical name — a descriptive phrase meaning 'kadamba tree', with वृक्ष appended. The Hindi name attested per species is कदम्ब / कदंब on its own (efloraofindia's Neolamarckia cadamba page and the Names of Plants in India compilation both give Hindi कदम्ब, Marathi कदंब). No source gives कदंब वृक्ष as a name. No misidentification risk; just replace it with कदंब.

verdicts.name: नीप
verdicts.reason: Correct plant, wrong language. Monier-Williams and the Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary (via wisdomlib) both give नीप = Nauclea Cadamba, i.e. this species, and Narahari's Rāja Nighaṇṭu gives Nīpa as a synonym of Dhārākadamba, a variety of Kadamba — so it is solidly attested, as SANSKRIT. The vernacular listings I retrieved place নীপ in Bengali, not Hindi (efloraofindia / Names of Plants in India: 'Bengali: कदम kadam, नीप nipa'). No Hindi source attests it. Move it to Sanskrit rather than deleting it. Minor caveat: Monier-Williams notes नीप can also denote Ixora species.

verdicts.name: हरिद्र
verdicts.denotesInstead: Curcuma longa — हरिद्रा is turmeric, one of the most fixed plant names in Sanskrit and Hindi. The near-homograph हरिद्रु is identified by Monier-Williams with Curcuma aromatica and 'a sort of Pinus', and in Indian usage with Haldina cordifolia (Hindi हल्दू, formerly Adina cordifolia) — a different Rubiaceae tree that is also sometimes called कदम्बु in Tamil. None of these is Neolamarckia cadamba.
verdicts.reason: A real botanical error, not merely an unattested string. I retrieved the haridru/haridra entry on wisdomlib: the identifications are Curcuma aromatica, Pinus spp., Chloroxylon swietenia and Haldina cordifolia, and kadamba is explicitly not among them. Searching Neolamarckia cadamba's own vernacular lists (efloraofindia, Names of Plants in India) returns Sanskrit हरिप्रिय and कदम्ब, never हरिद्र. The likeliest path is confusion of हरिप्रिय with हरिद्र, or of kadamba with हल्दू / Haldina cordifolia. Left on the page, a reader sees turmeric listed as a name for a forest tree.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa — aśvattha is the pipal/bodhi tree, one of the most unambiguous plant names in the entire Sanskrit corpus (Ṛgveda onward, Bhagavad-gītā 15.1, and every nighantu). It has no connection to Neolamarckia cadamba.
verdicts.reason: This is the planted error, and it is the same Wikidata defect flagged in the brief, where अश्वत्थः is also attached to Adhatoda vasica and Aegle marmelos. No source for Neolamarckia cadamba contains it: efloraofindia and Names of Plants in India give Sanskrit हरिप्रिय and कदम्ब; Rāja Nighaṇṭu gives Kadamba, Nīpa, Dhārākadamba, Kādambarya. Must be removed — a reader would take Ficus religiosa and Neolamarckia cadamba to be the same tree.

verdicts.name: कदम्बः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib / Rāja Nighaṇṭu (Narahari, 13th c.): Kadamba is the Sanskrit name of the plant Neolamarckia cadamba, with Nīpa given as a synonym of its Dhārākadamba variety and Kādambarya as a further synonym. efloraofindia's Neolamarckia cadamba page gives Sanskrit कदम्ब; the botanical epithet 'cadamba' is itself taken from this Sanskrit name.
verdicts.reason: The primary, classically attested Sanskrit name for this species, confirmed by a nighantu identification per species and by the plant's own nomenclature history. Preferred Sanskrit form.

verdicts.name: கடம்பு மரம்
verdicts.denotesInstead: ambiguous in Tamil — bare கடம்பு is applied to at least four species: Neolamarckia cadamba, Mitragyna parvifolia, Haldina cordifolia and Barringtonia acutangula, three of which occur around Madurai, where the Sangam-literature கடம்பு is commonly identified as Mitragyna parvifolia
verdicts.reason: The species-specific Tamil name I retrieved is வெள்ளைக் கடம்பு / வெண்கடம்பு ('white kadambu') — Names of Plants in India gives வெள்ளை கதம்பு (Vellaikkatampu) for Neolamarckia cadamba, and Tamil agro-forestry sources give 'Vellai Kadambu'. The exact form கடம்பு மரம் ('kadambu tree') is not attested by any named source as a name, and dropping the qualifier வெள்ளை is precisely what makes it ambiguous across the four species above. Use வெள்ளைக் கடம்பு.

verdicts.name: मकोय
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Black Nightshade' (Solanum nigrum) page: Hindi given in Devanagari as मकोय / मोकोय (Mokoi). Corroborated by Ayurvedic per-species sources, which list the Hindi/Urdu name Makoy for Solanum nigrum under the Sanskrit drug Kakamachi.
verdicts.reason: Attested per species in Devanagari by a source that publishes names against the botanical species, and corroborated by Ayurvedic drug literature for Kakamachi. मकोय is the standard Hindi name a speaker would use and search. (One standing caution for this page: Solanum nigrum in India is a species complex, so vernacular names are often applied to S. americanum and S. villosum too — that is a taxonomic matter, not a name error.)

verdicts.name: மணத்தக்காளி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Black Nightshade' (Solanum nigrum) page: Tamil given in Tamil script as மணதக்காளி (Manatakkali). Corroborated by the India Biodiversity Portal Solanum nigrum species page (Tamil Manathakkali / Munatakali) and by Malayalam cognate Manatakkali.
verdicts.reason: Attested per species in Tamil script by independent per-species sources. மணத்தக்காளி is the everyday Tamil name (the leaf is a common Tamil greens vegetable), so it is the preferred Tamil form.

verdicts.name: நீலப் பசை மரம்
verdicts.reason: Retrieved API Part I Vol V, monograph 78 TAILAPARṆAḤ (leaf of Eucalyptus globulus Labill.): Tamil = 'Yukkaalimaram', Hindi 'Yukeliptas', Sanskrit 'Nīlaniryāsa, Ekalipth, Sugandha Patrah'. நீலப் பசை மரம் is a word-for-word calque of English 'blue gum tree' and the only place I found it is the Tamil Wikipedia article title, which mirrors Wikidata; no pharmacopoeial, Siddha or lexicographic Tamil source attests it. Not a wrong plant, just an unattested translation.

verdicts.name: सौंफ
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 55 MIŚREYĀ (dried ripe fruits of Foeniculum vulgare Mill.) — SYNONYMS lists Hindi: Saunf; Punjabi: Saunf; Urdu: Saunf. Flowers of India (Fennel page) gives Hindi 'मोटी सौंफ Moti saunf'.
verdicts.reason: API's official Hindi name for the Foeniculum vulgare monograph is Saunf, i.e. सौंफ in Devanagari, and FOI's Devanagari entry contains the same word. This is the form a Hindi speaker uses and searches.

verdicts.name: सौंफ़
verdicts.reason: No source I retrieved spells the word with a nuqta. API Vol I gives Saunf; Flowers of India gives मोटी सौंफ. सौंफ़ treats a native Indic word as if it had an Urdu /f/, which standard Hindi orthography does not do here. It is a spelling variant of the same name, not a separate name, so it should not stand as its own entry.

verdicts.name: பெருஞ்சீரகம்
verdicts.denotesInstead: Pimpinella anisum (common anise), and secondarily Illicium anisatum (star/Chinese anise), per the Madras Tamil Lexicon and DSAL
verdicts.reason: The sources split. API Part I Vol I (MIŚREYĀ, Foeniculum vulgare) gives Tamil = Shombu (சோம்பு) and assigns the perum-jeeragam type name to Malayalam ('Parinjaeragum'). The Madras Tamil Lexicon and DSAL define பெருஞ்சீரகம் as '1. Common anise, Pimpinella anisum; 2. Chinese anise, Illicium anisatum'. Only Winslow equates it with fennel ('Anise seed, sweet fennel, சோம்பு. Anethum Foeniculum'). Modern Tamil Nadu market usage does mean fennel by it, but with the pharmacopoeia and the standard lexicon pointing to சோம்பு and Pimpinella anisum respectively, this fails the independent-attestation test for Foeniculum vulgare.

verdicts.name: सौंफ
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 55 MIŚREYĀ (Foeniculum vulgare Mill.) — Hindi: Saunf.
verdicts.reason: Same retrieval as the fennel page: API's official Hindi name for the Foeniculum vulgare monograph is Saunf = सौंफ, corroborated by Flowers of India's Devanagari 'मोटी सौंफ'.

verdicts.name: सौंफ़
verdicts.reason: Nuqta spelling unattested in API Vol I or Flowers of India, both of which give सौंफ / मोटी सौंफ. A non-standard orthographic variant of the confirmed name rather than a name in its own right.

verdicts.name: பெருஞ்சீரகம்
verdicts.denotesInstead: Pimpinella anisum (common anise), and secondarily Illicium anisatum, per the Madras Tamil Lexicon and DSAL
verdicts.reason: API Part I Vol I gives Tamil சோம்பு for Foeniculum vulgare and puts the perum-jeeragam form under Malayalam; the Madras Tamil Lexicon/DSAL gloss பெருஞ்சீரகம் as anise (Pimpinella anisum / Illicium anisatum). Winslow alone equates it with sweet fennel. Ambiguous in the sources, so not confirmed for this species.

verdicts.name: मेथी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol II, monograph 48 METHĪ (seeds of Trigonella foenum-graecum Linn.) — Hindi: Methi; also Flowers of India (Fenugreek) in Devanagari: 'Hindi: मेथी Methi'.
verdicts.reason: Both the official pharmacopoeia and FOI's Devanagari list give मेथी as the Hindi name for Trigonella foenum-graecum. Unambiguously the everyday and searched form.

verdicts.name: दीपनी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Rāja Nighaṇṭu (13th c.), quoted at wisdomlib s.v. Dīpanī: 'Dīpanī is another name for Methī, also identified with Trigonella foenum-graecum Linn.'; Monier-Williams: 'Dīpanī f. Trigonella Foenum Graecum'. Flowers of India also lists 'dipani' among the Sanskrit names on its Fenugreek page.
verdicts.reason: Attested as a nighantu synonym of Methī. Caveat worth keeping on the page: Monier-Williams also assigns दीपनी to Ptychotis ajowan (ajwain) and Clypea hernandifolia, so it is a polysemous attribute-name, not a unique designation for fenugreek.

verdicts.name: मेथिका
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Rāja Nighaṇṭu (13th c.) via wisdomlib s.v. Methikā: 'Methikā is another name for Methī, also identified with Trigonella foenum-graecum Linn.'; Śyainika-śāstra uses methikā-cūrṇa (powdered Methi) for the same plant.
verdicts.reason: Classical nighantu attestation for this exact species. Best-known Sanskrit form for the drug alongside मेथी (API's Sanskrit synonym for the monograph is Methinī). Note wisdomlib records a minority identification of methikā with Medicago sativa, but Trigonella foenum-graecum is the primary one.

verdicts.name: வெந்தயம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol II, monograph 48 METHĪ — Tamil: Mendium, Ventaiyam; Flowers of India (Fenugreek) in Tamil script: 'Tamil: வெந்தயம் Vendayam'.
verdicts.reason: API's Tamil 'Ventaiyam' and FOI's Tamil-script வெந்தயம் agree for Trigonella foenum-graecum. This is the standard Tamil word.

verdicts.name: Gmelina arborea
verdicts.reason: This is the Latin binomial, not a Hindi name, and it is not even in Devanagari. A harvesting artefact where Wikidata's Hindi label fell back to the scientific name. API Part I Vol II (monograph 19 GAMBHARI, fruit of Gmelina arborea Roxb.) gives Hindi: Gambhari, Punjabi: Khambhari; Flowers of India gives Hindi गम्हड़. Must be dropped.

verdicts.name: Gmelina arborea
verdicts.reason: Same artefact: a scientific binomial in Latin script offered as a Hindi vernacular name. API Part I Vol II monograph 19 GAMBHARI (Fruit) — the exact drug this page covers — gives Hindi: Gambhari; FOI gives Hindi गम्हड़. Drop.

verdicts.name: அச்சு
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol II, monograph 20 GĀṄGERU (dried stem bark of Grewia tenax (Forsk.) Aschers & Schwf., syn. Grewia populifolia Vahl) — SYNONYMS: Sanskrit Gāṅgeruki, Hindi Gangeran, Tamil: Achchu.
verdicts.reason: The official pharmacopoeia lists Achchu (அச்சு) as the Tamil name for exactly this species, so it is attested. Two caveats worth carrying on the page: the Madras Tamil Lexicon, Fabricius, Winslow and DSAL record only non-botanical senses for அச்சு (axle, mould, printing type, Sanskrit vowel) with no plant sense at all; and ICRAF's Agroforestree Database (Orwa et al. 2009) lists 'achchu' under Hindi, not Tamil, for Grewia tenax. The name is genuine per API but obscure, and Grewia tenax is an arid north-west/Deccan shrub with little Tamil-country presence.

verdicts.name: गिलोय
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 27 GUḌŪCĪ (stem of Tinospora cordifolia (Willd.) Miers) — Hindi: Giloe, Gurcha. The 'Names of Plants in India' compilation (indiantreepix) gives Hindi in Devanagari: गिलोय, गुलांचा, गुलबेल.
verdicts.reason: API's Hindi name Giloe = गिलोय for this exact species, with a Devanagari attestation from the Names of Plants in India list. This is the form a Hindi speaker uses and searches.

verdicts.name: गुडुची
verdicts.reason: Misspelling: the attested form has a long ū — गुडूची. API Part I Vol I titles the monograph GUḌŪCĪ and gives Sanskrit synonyms Amṛtavallī, Amṛtā, Madhuparṇī, Guḍūcikā, Chinnobhavā; the Names of Plants in India list gives Sanskrit गुडूची. No source spells it गुडुची with short u. Right plant, wrong orthography; publish गुडूची instead.

verdicts.name: अमृतलता
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Rāja Nighaṇṭu (13th c.) as quoted at wisdomlib s.v. Amṛtalatā: 'Amṛtalatā is another name for Guḍūcī, a medicinal plant identified with Tinospora cordifolia'; Monier-Williams glosses it as a nectar-giving creeper, Cocculus cordifolius (a synonym of Tinospora cordifolia).
verdicts.reason: Genuine nighantu synonym for this species, though not one of API's five listed Sanskrit synonyms. Not the best-known Sanskrit form; गुडूची and अमृता are.

verdicts.name: சீந்திற்கொடி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Winslow's Tamil-English dictionary s.v. சீந்திற்கொடி: 'The சீந்தில் creeper, heart-leaved moon-seed'; Madras Tamil Lexicon, Fabricius and DSAL s.v. சீந்தில்: 'the name of a creeper, gulanch, Tinospora cordifolia'. API Part I Vol I GUḌŪCĪ gives Tamil: Seendal, Seendil kodi.
verdicts.reason: The compound form சீந்தில் + கொடி → சீந்திற்கொடி is both grammatically regular and directly attested in Winslow for this species, and API gives the same name as 'Seendil kodi'.

verdicts.name: अपराजिता
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol II monograph 5 APARĀJITĀ (Root) and Part I Vol IV monograph 4 APARĀJITĀ (Leaf), both of Clitoria ternatea Linn. — Hindi: Aparajita. Flowers of India (Butterfly Pea) gives 'Hindi: अपराजिता Aparajita'.
verdicts.reason: API gives Aparajita as the Hindi name in two separate monographs of Clitoria ternatea, and FOI attests the Devanagari spelling. Standard Hindi name.

verdicts.name: अपराजिता
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol II monograph 5 and Vol IV monograph 4 are both titled APARĀJITĀ and defined as Clitoria ternatea Linn.; wisdomlib s.v. Aparājitā: 'a medicinal plant identified with Clitoria ternatea'.
verdicts.reason: The pharmacopoeial drug name for this species is itself अपराजिता, which is the strongest possible Sanskrit attestation. Caveat for the page: the same Sanskrit word is also applied to Marsilea quadrifolia, Sesbania sesban and Nyctanthes arbor-tristis in other texts, so it is polysemous outside the Ayurvedic drug context.

verdicts.name: கருவிளை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Winslow s.v. கருவிளை: 'A wild creeper with dark blue flowers--as காக்கணம், Clitoria ternatea, L.'; Madras Tamil Lexicon and DSAL s.v. கருவிளை: 'Mussel-shell creeper. See காக்கணம்.'
verdicts.reason: Winslow names the species explicitly, and the Tamil Lexicon equates கருவிளை with காக்கணம், which is the Tamil name API Part I Vol II/IV gives for Clitoria ternatea. Confirmed, but I am not marking it preferred: API's Tamil entry is காக்கணம், and the everyday Tamil name today is சங்குப்பூ / காக்கணம் rather than the literary கருவிளை.

verdicts.name: गोखरू
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 25 GOKṢURA (root of Tribulus terrestris Linn.) — Hindi: Gokhru; Punjabi: Bhakhra, Gokhru. Flowers of India (Puncture Vine) gives Hindi 'गोखुरू Gokhuru, गोक्षुर Gokshura' and the same word गोखरू under Marathi and Rajasthani.
verdicts.reason: API's official Hindi name for Tribulus terrestris is Gokhru = गोखरू, which is also the trade name under which the drug is sold. FOI spells the Hindi form गोखुरू, a variant of the same word.

verdicts.name: गोकुरासस्यम्
verdicts.reason: Not attested anywhere I retrieved. API Part I Vol I GOKṢURA gives Sanskrit: Gokṣuraka, Trikaṇṭa, Śvadaṃṣṭrā, Traikaṇṭaka; Flowers of India lists fifteen Sanskrit names (अश्वदंष्ट्रा, बहुकण्टक, चित्रकण्टक, गोक्षुर, त्रिकण्टक, श्वदंष्ट्रक, स्वादुकण्टक, व्याघ्रदंष्ट्र and others) and गोकुरासस्यम् is not among them. It reads as a garbled pseudo-Sanskrit coinage around गोक्षुर plus a spurious -सस्यम् ('crop'); no classical lexicon or nighantu form matches. Drop and use गोक्षुर.

verdicts.name: நெருஞ்சி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 25 GOKṢURA — Tamil: Nerinjil, Nerunjil; Flowers of India (Puncture Vine) in Tamil script: 'நெருஞ்சி Nerunci'.
verdicts.reason: API and FOI agree on this Tamil name for Tribulus terrestris; நெருஞ்சி / நெருஞ்சில் is the standard Tamil and Siddha word for the caltrop.

verdicts.name: गोरखमुंडी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India (Sphaeranthus indicus) in Devanagari: 'Hindi: Chhagul-nudi, गोरखमुंडी (Gorakhmundi)'; Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India Part I Vol III, monograph 58 MUṆḌĪTIKĀ (leaf of Sphaeranthus indicus Linn.) lists Gorakhmundi under Gujarati and Punjabi, with Hindi: Mundi.
verdicts.reason: FOI attests गोरखमुंडी as the Hindi name in Devanagari and it is the trade name the drug is sold under. Worth noting on the page that API records the Hindi name as मुंडी and places Gorakhmundi under Gujarati/Punjabi, so गोरखमुंडी is a widely shared north-Indian name rather than Hindi-exclusive.

verdicts.name: கொண்டைக் கரந்தை
verdicts.reason: Misspelling of an attested name. DSAL/Madras Tamil Lexicon has 'koṭṭai-k-karantai, n. கொட்டை+. Indian globe-thistle. See விஷ்ணுக்கரந்தை. (M. M. 910.)' — i.e. கொட்டைக்கரந்தை with கொட்டை (seed/kernel). Flowers of India gives Tamil 'கொட்டை கரந்தை (Kottai Karantai), சிவகரந்தை (Sivakarantai)' and API Vol III gives 'Kotook, Karandai, Kottakarthai'. There is no dictionary entry at all for கொண்டைக்கரந்தை; கொண்டை means a hair-knot, a different word. Publish கொட்டைக்கரந்தை instead.

verdicts.name: गुड़मार
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol V, monograph 52 MEṢAŚṚṄGĪ (root of Gymnema sylvestre R. Br.) — Hindi: Gudmaar, Medhaasingee; Sanskrit: Madhunāśinī, Ajaśṛṅgī.
verdicts.reason: API's official Hindi name for Gymnema sylvestre is Gudmaar = गुड़मार ('sugar destroyer'), which is also the commercial name. Nuqta on ड़ is correct here (गुड़ = jaggery).

verdicts.name: சிறுகுறிஞ்சா
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Madras Tamil Lexicon s.v. குறிஞ்சா: 'a medicinal creeper of two kinds with bitter leaves, periploca sylvestris, சிறுகுறிஞ்சா and asclepias vomitoria, பெருங்குறிஞ்சா'; Winslow gives the same two-kinds entry. Periploca sylvestris Retz. is the basionym of Gymnema sylvestre (Retz.) R.Br. ex Sm., and API Vol V gives the English name of the Meṣaśṛṅgī drug as 'Periploca of the woods'.
verdicts.reason: The lexicon ties சிறுகுறிஞ்சா to Periploca sylvestris, which is this species under its older name, and API's own English gloss confirms that equation. Not marked preferred because API Vol V lists the Tamil names as Shakkaraikkolli (சர்க்கரைக்கொல்லி) first, with 'Shirukurumkaay' second.

verdicts.name: गुड़मार
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol V, monograph 52 MEṢAŚṚṄGĪ (Gymnema sylvestre R. Br.) — Hindi: Gudmaar.
verdicts.reason: Same retrieval as the gudmar page: API gives Gudmaar = गुड़मार as the Hindi name for Gymnema sylvestre.

verdicts.name: சிறுகுறிஞ்சா
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Madras Tamil Lexicon / Winslow s.v. குறிஞ்சா: 'periploca sylvestris, சிறுகுறிஞ்சா' — Periploca sylvestris Retz. being the basionym of Gymnema sylvestre; API Vol V calls the drug's English name 'Periploca of the woods'.
verdicts.reason: Attested via the lexicon's Periploca sylvestris identification. API's first Tamil name for the species is சர்க்கரைக்கொல்லி, so சிறுகுறிஞ்சா is not marked preferred.

verdicts.name: गिलोय
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 27 GUḌŪCĪ (Tinospora cordifolia) — Hindi: Giloe, Gurcha; 'Names of Plants in India' list gives Hindi गिलोय, गुलांचा, गुलबेल.
verdicts.reason: API's Hindi name for this exact species, with the Devanagari spelling attested in the Names of Plants in India compilation.

verdicts.name: गुडुची
verdicts.reason: Short-u spelling is wrong. API Part I Vol I titles the monograph GUḌŪCĪ (गुडूची) for Tinospora cordifolia, and the Sanskrit synonym lists in API and the Names of Plants in India compilation give गुडूची. Correct the vowel length rather than publishing गुडुची.

verdicts.name: अमृतलता
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Rāja Nighaṇṭu via wisdomlib s.v. Amṛtalatā: 'Amṛtalatā is another name for Guḍūcī, a medicinal plant identified with Tinospora cordifolia'; Monier-Williams: a nectar-giving creeper, Cocculus cordifolius (= Tinospora cordifolia).
verdicts.reason: Nighantu-attested synonym for this species. Not the primary Sanskrit form, which is गुडूची (API's monograph name) with अमृता and अमृतवल्ली as the leading synonyms.

verdicts.name: சீந்திற்கொடி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Winslow s.v. சீந்திற்கொடி: 'The சீந்தில் creeper, heart-leaved moon-seed'; Madras Tamil Lexicon / Fabricius / DSAL s.v. சீந்தில்: 'gulanch, Tinospora cordifolia'; API Part I Vol I gives Tamil: Seendal, Seendil kodi.
verdicts.reason: Directly attested in Winslow for this species and matched by API's 'Seendil kodi'. The ல் → ற் sandhi in the compound is standard Tamil.

verdicts.name: हल्दी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 30 HARIDRĀ (cured rhizomes of Curcuma longa Linn.) — Hindi: Haldi, Hardi; Flowers of India (Turmeric) in Devanagari: 'Hindi: हल्दी (Haldi)'.
verdicts.reason: API and FOI agree; हल्दी is the universal Hindi name for Curcuma longa.

verdicts.name: हरिद्रा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 30 is titled HARIDRĀ and defined as the rhizome of Curcuma longa Linn.; wisdomlib s.v. Haridrā quotes Monier-Williams ('Turmeric, either the plant or the powdered root') and identifies Curcuma longa L.
verdicts.reason: The pharmacopoeial drug name for this species is हरिद्रा itself, the strongest Sanskrit attestation available. API's further Sanskrit synonyms are Rajanī, Niśā, Niśī, Rātri, Kṣaṇadā, Doṣā.

verdicts.name: மஞ்சள்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 30 HARIDRĀ — Tamil: Manjal; Flowers of India (Turmeric) in Tamil script: 'Tamil: மஞ்சள் (Manjal)'.
verdicts.reason: API and FOI agree on மஞ்சள் for Curcuma longa; it is the ordinary Tamil word for turmeric.

verdicts.name: हरड़
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 31 HARĪTAKĪ (pericarp of mature fruits of Terminalia chebula Retz.) — Hindi: Harre, Harad, Harar; Flowers of India gives Hindi 'हर्रा (Harra), हरड़ (Harad)'.
verdicts.reason: API lists Harad among the Hindi names and FOI attests the Devanagari हरड़. This is the trade name the fruit is sold under in north India and the form a Hindi speaker would search.

verdicts.name: हरीतकी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'जड़ीबूटियों द्वारा चिकित्सा' (AWGP Hindi herbal literature, chapter on हरड़) uses हरीतकी as the Hindi headword for Terminalia chebula and states that in Hindi it is also called हरड़ and हर्रे; API Part I Vol I titles the monograph HARĪTAKĪ for the same species.
verdicts.reason: A Sanskrit loanword in general Hindi medical usage, attested as such in Hindi-language herbal literature for this species. Not the preferred Hindi form — API lists Hindi as Harre/Harad/Harar and places Haritaki under Bengali and Marathi.

verdicts.name: हर्रे
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 31 HARĪTAKĪ — Hindi: Harre, Harad, Harar; 'जड़ीबूटियों द्वारा चिकित्सा' (AWGP) likewise: 'हिन्दी में इसे हरड़ और हर्रे भी कहा जाता है'.
verdicts.reason: API's first listed Hindi name is Harre = हर्रे, corroborated in a Hindi herbal text. A genuine regional variant alongside हरड़/हर्रा, but not the leading form; Flowers of India spells the variant हर्रा.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa (the pipal / bo-tree)
verdicts.reason: This is the planted error and it is a real botanical error, not merely an unattested string. wisdomlib s.v. Aśvattha, citing Sanskrit lexicons, Dharmaśāstra, Śaivism and Ayurveda/Rasaśāstra sources, identifies अश्वत्थ unanimously as Ficus religiosa L. (Moraceae), another name for Pippala. API Part I Vol I's Sanskrit synonyms for HARĪTAKĪ are Abhayā, Kāyasthā, Śivā, Pathyā, Vijayā — अश्वत्थः is absent, as it is from every nighantu synonym list for Terminalia chebula I retrieved. The same bogus alias is attached to Adhatoda vasica and Aegle marmelos in this dataset, confirming it is a Wikidata alias contamination. It must be removed, and it would mislead a reader badly if left: Ficus religiosa is a different family and a different drug.

verdicts.name: हरीतकी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 31 is titled HARĪTAKĪ and defined as the pericarp of mature fruits of Terminalia chebula Retz.; wisdomlib s.v. Haritaki cites the Sanskrit dictionary gloss 'the yellow myrobalan tree, Terminalia chebula'.
verdicts.reason: The official pharmacopoeial Sanskrit drug name for this species. API's additional Sanskrit synonyms are Abhayā, Kāyasthā, Śivā, Pathyā and Vijayā (with the explicit caution 'Not Bhaṅgā' against confusing Vijayā with cannabis).

verdicts.name: கடுக்காய்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol I, monograph 31 HARĪTAKĪ — Tamil: Kadukkai; Madras Tamil Lexicon and DSAL s.v. கடுக்காய்: 'Gall-nut, one of the tiri-palai' and 'Chebulic myrobalan, m. tr., Terminalia chebula'.
verdicts.reason: API and the Madras Tamil Lexicon both give கடுக்காய் for Terminalia chebula, the lexicon naming the species outright and noting it as one of the three fruits of திரிபலை (triphala). Standard Tamil and Siddha name.

verdicts.name: செங்கரும்பு
verdicts.denotesInstead: the red-caned cultivar of sugarcane specifically ('செந்நிறமுள்ள கரும்புவகை'), not Saccharum officinarum as a species
verdicts.reason: Madras Tamil Lexicon, Fabricius, Winslow and DSAL all gloss செங்கரும்பு narrowly as 'Red sugar-cane; செந்நிறமுள்ள கரும்புவகை' — a colour variety, செம் (red) + கரும்பு. The species-level Tamil name is கரும்பு: API Part I Vol II, monograph 22 IKṢU (dried stem of Saccharum officinarum Linn.) gives Tamil: Karumbu, and Flowers of India gives 'Tamil: கரும்பு (Karumbu), புண்டறம் (Pundaram)'. Publishing செங்கரும்பு as the Tamil name of the Ikshu drug would misstate it as a cultivar name.

verdicts.name: इंद्रायन
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I Vol III, monograph 30 INDRAVĀRUṆĪ (fruit of Citrullus colocynthis Schrad.) — Hindi: Indrayan; Gujarati: Indrayan; Punjabi: Indrayana. Flowers of India (Bitter Apple) gives Hindi 'बड़ी इन्द्रायन Badi Indrayan, इन्द्रायन Indarayan'.
verdicts.reason: API's official Hindi name for Citrullus colocynthis is Indrayan, and FOI attests the Devanagari. The candidate uses anusvāra (इंद्रायन) where FOI uses the conjunct (इन्द्रायन) — the same word in two standard spellings, so it stands. For Devanagari consistency across the site, इन्द्रायन is the form the printed sources use.

verdicts.name: குமட்டிக்காய்
verdicts.denotesInstead: the unqualified கொம்மட்டி / குமட்டி denotes a small watermelon (Citrullus, i.e. C. lanatus) and Cucumis trigonus per DSAL; Citrullus colocynthis is distinguished in Tamil by the பேய்- prefix (பேய்த்தும்மட்டி / பேய்க்கொம்மட்டி)
verdicts.reason: Not attested for this species. API Part I Vol III, monograph 30 INDRAVĀRUṆĪ gives Tamil: Peitummatti (and Telugu Peikummatti); Flowers of India gives Tamil 'kumatti, pey-komatti'. The Tamil dictionaries make the distinction explicit: DSAL s.v. கொம்மட்டி = 'A small water-melon, climber, Citrullus' and 'Country cucumber, climber, Cucumis trigonus; தும்மட்டி', while குமட்டிக்காய் appears only in Na Kadirvelu Pillai's dictionary glossed as 'ஆற்றுத்தும்முட்டிக்காய்' with no species. Published as the Tamil name of the colocynth drug it would point a reader at watermelon or Cucumis trigonus.

verdicts.name: गुग्गुल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Guggal' page (Commiphora wightii): "Hindi: गुग्गुल (Guggul), गुग्गल (Guggal)"; independently MMPND (Univ. of Melbourne Multilingual Multiscript Plant Name Database), Commiphora page: Hindi "Guggul (as C. mukul)".
verdicts.reason: Two independent non-Wikidata sources list this exact Devanagari form under Hindi for C. wightii. Flowers of India prints it in Devanagari verbatim, so no reconstruction was needed. It is also the trade name of the oleo-gum-resin, so it is the form a Hindi speaker would search.

verdicts.name: गुग्गुलुसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: No source I retrieved attests this. Flowers of India gives Sanskrit "गुग्गुलु (Guggulu), Ahavabhishtha, Bhutahara"; MMPND gives Sanskrit "Guggulu". The candidate is गुग्गुलु plus -सस्यम् ('the guggulu crop/plant'), a descriptive compound of the kind Sanskrit Wikipedia uses for article titles, not a lexical name from any nighantu or pharmacopoeia. Same -सस्यम्/-वृक्षः pattern recurs across this batch (apamarga, agastya, amra, ananta-mool), which points to Sanskrit Wikipedia titles being harvested as aliases. Correct Sanskrit name is गुग्गुलु.

verdicts.name: अरहर
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Arhar' page (Cajanus cajan): "Hindi: अरहर (Arhar), तुवर (Tuvar)"; MMPND Cajanus page: Hindi "Arahara (Arhar)" with Devanagari image.
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in Flowers of India under Hindi, corroborated by MMPND. This is the ordinary Hindi name of the plant and crop, so it is the preferred Hindi form.

verdicts.name: अरहर की दाल
verdicts.reason: Neither Flowers of India nor MMPND lists this. It is not a plant name: it denotes the split dehusked pulse (the food commodity) made from the seed, literally 'the dal of arhar'. Harvested almost certainly from the Hindi Wikipedia article on the pulse rather than the plant. A botanical monograph on Cajanus cajan should not carry a commodity phrase as a vernacular plant name.

verdicts.name: अरहर दाल
verdicts.reason: Same defect as अरहर की दाल: unattested in any per-species source I retrieved, and denotes the split pulse rather than the plant. A bare noun-noun commodity compound, not a vernacular name.

verdicts.name: तुअर दाल
verdicts.reason: Unattested in Flowers of India or MMPND. Denotes the split pulse ('tuar dal'), not the plant. 'तुअर' itself is a colloquial variant of तुवर but no source I read gives it for the species, and the दाल compound is a commodity term.

verdicts.name: तुवर दाल
verdicts.reason: Unattested; commodity term for the split pulse. The plant name underneath it, तुवर, IS attested (Flowers of India, Hindi) but the दाल compound is not a plant name.

verdicts.name: तूवर
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Cajanus page lists Hindi "Toor, Tuur, Tur, Tuvar, Tuver" (the Tuur/Toor forms carry the long vowel); Flowers of India 'Arhar' page prints the Hindi form as तुवर (Tuvar).
verdicts.reason: The name is genuine for Cajanus cajan, but the attested Devanagari spelling in Flowers of India is तुवर with short उ; the long-ऊ form तूवर matches only MMPND's romanisation 'Tuur/Toor'. Right species, variant spelling, so not the preferred Hindi form. अरहर is preferred.

verdicts.name: तुवरी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Arhar' page: "Sanskrit: आढकी (Adhaki), काक्षी (Kakshi), तुवरी (Tuvari)" — printed in Devanagari, exact match.
verdicts.reason: I expected this to be the batch's wrong-plant error, because तुवरी/तुवरिका also denotes alum (sphaṭikā) in Sanskrit; retrieval overturned that. Flowers of India attests तुवरी in Devanagari as a Sanskrit name of Cajanus cajan. Confirmed, but preferred=false: the name is polysemous with alum, and the pharmacopoeial Sanskrit name for this drug is आढकी, which is missing from the candidate set even though the page is named after it.

verdicts.name: துவரை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Arhar' page: "Tamil: ஆடகி (Adhaki), இருப்புலி (Iruppuli), காய்ச்சி (Kaycci), துவரை (Tuvarai)" — printed in Tamil script, exact match.
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match in an independent source. துவரை is the everyday Tamil name for pigeonpea, so it is the preferred Tamil form.

verdicts.name: अगस्ति
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sesbania page: Hindi "अगस्ति Agasti (Aagasti), अगासती Agasati, बसना Basna, गाछ मूंगा Gaach-munga" — Devanagari printed, exact match.
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match under Hindi in MMPND, which cites print floras rather than Wikidata. It is the leading Hindi form listed, so preferred.

verdicts.name: अगस्त्यवृक्षः
