verdicts.reason: Unattested. MMPND gives Sanskrit "अगस्ति Agasti, Agati, Agastya, Drigapalaka, Munipriya, Varnari" for Sesbania grandiflora. The bare stem अगस्त्य is attested; the compound अगस्त्यवृक्षः ('the Agastya tree') with the nominative -ः ending is a Sanskrit Wikipedia article-title construction, not a nighantu name. Right species, fabricated lexeme. Use अगस्ति.

verdicts.name: அகத்தி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sesbania page: Tamil "Agathi, Agatti, Akatti, அகத்தி Akatthi, அகத்திக் கீரை Agathi keeray, Peragathi" — printed in Tamil script, exact match.
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match. அகத்தி is the standard Tamil name (the leaves are sold as அகத்திக் கீரை), so preferred.

verdicts.name: कलिहारी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Gloriosa page: Hindi "बचनाग Bachnag, Kadyanag, Kalihari, करी हरी Kari hari, Kathari, Kulhari, Languli, उलट चन्दल Ulatchandal".
verdicts.reason: MMPND attests Kalihari under Hindi for Gloriosa superba. Flowers of India's Hindi list for the species (बचनाग, करी हरी, उलट चन्दल, kadyanag, languli) does not include it, but MMPND is an independent named source and कलिहारी is the standard Hindi/trade name for the drug, so preferred. Note MMPND prints this one in roman only; the Devanagari spelling कलिहारी is the conventional rendering.

verdicts.name: காந்தள்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Gloriosa page: Tamil "Anaravan, Iradi, Kaandhal, Kallappai kilangu, Kalappai kizhangu, Kannoru, Kannovu, Tonri"; Flowers of India (Glory Lily) prints Tamil "செங்காந்தள் (Chenkantal), கலப்பை கிழங்கு (Kallappai kilangu)".
verdicts.reason: MMPND attests the base form Kaandhal = காந்தள் for Gloriosa superba, and Flowers of India independently prints the compound செங்காந்தள் ('red kāntaḷ') in Tamil script for the same species, which presupposes காந்தள். Preferred Tamil form; செங்காந்தள் is the more specific variant.

verdicts.name: अफ़ीम पोस्ता
verdicts.reason: Not attested as a unit. Flowers of India (Opium Poppy) gives Hindi "अफ़ीम (Aphim), ख़शख़ाश (Khash-khash)"; MMPND gives Hindi "Aphim (Afim), Khashkhash (Kaskas), Post". Both components exist separately — अफ़ीम is the opium latex, पोस्ता the poppy — but no source lists the juxtaposed phrase as a name. It is the Hindi Wikipedia article title, which stacks two names to disambiguate. Right species, synthetic form. Use अफ़ीम or ख़शख़ाश.

verdicts.name: கசகசா
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Opium Poppy' page (Papaver somniferum): "Tamil: abini, gashagasha, kasakasa, postaka".
verdicts.reason: Flowers of India lists kasakasa = கசகசா under Tamil for P. somniferum; the same item appears in its Kannada list in Kannada script (ಕಸಕಸೆ) and Malayalam list, confirming the lexeme rather than a one-off. Preferred Tamil form. Worth noting on the page: in ordinary Tamil usage கசகசா names the poppy SEED specifically, not the whole plant.

verdicts.name: अजवाईन
verdicts.reason: Misspelling. Flowers of India (Ajwain) prints Hindi "अजवाइन, अजवायन Ajwain"; MMPND gives "अजवान Ajawan, अजवाइन Ajawain, अजवायन Ajavayan". Every attested Devanagari form has इ or या in the third syllable; the candidate has ई (अजवा-ई-न), which no source I retrieved uses. Right plant, wrong orthography — exactly the kind of defect that would sit on a reference page unchallenged. Use अजवाइन.

verdicts.name: यवाग्रजः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdomlib's Sanskrit/Ayurveda entry for Yavāgraja, citing the 13th-c. Rāja Nighaṇṭu, lists Yavāgraja among the Sanskrit synonyms of Yavānī, identified with Trachyspermum ammi Linn. (Apiaceae).
verdicts.reason: I flagged this for checking because neither Flowers of India nor MMPND lists it, and the etymology ('born from the tip of barley') suggested a mineral. Retrieval found genuine nighantu attestation for the species, so confirmed. preferred=false for two reasons: the citation form is यवाग्रज (the -ः is the inflected nominative), and the same word also denotes यवक्षार / saltpetre (potassium nitrate) in Sanskrit lexicography, so it is polysemous and a poor headline name. यवानी is the safe Sanskrit name.

verdicts.name: यवानी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Ajwain' page: "Sanskrit: अजमोद Ajamoda, अजमोदिका Ajamodika, dipyaka, यवानी yavani, yamanika" — Devanagari printed, exact match; MMPND Trachyspermum page: Sanskrit "यवानी Yavani, Yawani (NCL)".
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in two independent sources, and it is the pharmacopoeial Sanskrit name for the drug, so preferred. Caution for whoever builds this page: both sources also list अजमोद / अजमोदिका under Sanskrit for T. ammi. That is a well-known conflation — Ajamodā properly denotes Trachyspermum roxburghianum / Apium graveolens, a different drug. Do not carry those two across from these lists.

verdicts.name: ஓமம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Ajwain' page: "Tamil: ஓமம் Omam"; MMPND Trachyspermum page: Tamil "Asamtavomam, Asampadam, Amam, ஓமம் Omam (Katz)" — both print the Tamil script form.
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match in two independent sources. ஓமம் is the ordinary Tamil name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: अकरकरा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Anacyclus page: Hindi "Akarkara"; Shri Dharmasthala Ayurveda College Dravyaguna Vigyan monograph 'Akarakarabha' (Anacyclus pyrethrum): Hindi "akarkara".
verdicts.reason: Two independent sources attest Akarkara under Hindi for A. pyrethrum; अकरकरा is the conventional Devanagari rendering and the trade name of the root. Both sources print it in roman only, so the script form is the standard rendering rather than a direct read. Separate caveat for the page: 'Akarkara' in Indian trade very often means Acmella oleracea / Spilanthes, so the Hindi name alone does not pin the species.

verdicts.name: அக்கராகாரம்
verdicts.reason: Not attested in this spelling. The Dravyaguna department monograph at sdach.ac.in gives Tamil "Akkiraakaaram" (அக்கிராகாரம்) and MMPND gives Tamil "Akkirakkaram, Akkalkara" — both have -கிர- in the second syllable. The candidate has -கரா-, an extra long ā where the attested forms have i. Right species, wrong vowel. Use அக்கிராகாரம்.

verdicts.name: अख़रोट
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Walnut' page (Juglans regia): "Hindi: अखरोट Akhrot"; also Urdu ﺍﺧﺮﻭﭦ Akhrot.
verdicts.reason: Flowers of India prints अखरोट in Devanagari for J. regia. The candidate differs only by the optional nuqta on ख़, which is a standard orthographic option for this Persian-derived word, not a different word — so confirmed, and preferred as the universal Hindi name. Flowers of India spells it without the nuqta.

verdicts.name: அக்ரூட்
verdicts.reason: Unattested. Flowers of India gives Tamil "Akarottu" for Juglans regia (and Telugu Akarottu, Kannada ಅಕ್ರೋಡು Akrodu); MMPND lists no Tamil name at all for the species. அக்ரூட் is a direct transliteration of Hindi/English 'akhrot/walnut' rather than the Tamil name any per-species source gives. Right species, but a loan spelling with no authority behind it. Use அகரோட்டு.

verdicts.name: लौकी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Bottle Gourd' page (Lagenaria siceraria): "Hindi: लौकी Lauki, घिया Ghiya" — Devanagari, exact match; SDACH Dravyaguna 'Alabu' monograph: Hindi "Lauki, Ghiya".
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in Flowers of India, corroborated by an Ayurveda-college Dravyaguna monograph. लौकी is the dominant Hindi name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: अलाबु
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Shri Dharmasthala Ayurveda College Dravyaguna Vigyan monograph 'Alabu' (Lagenaria siceraria), quoting Bhāvaprakāśa Nighaṇṭu in Devanagari: "अलाबूः कथिता तुम्बी" ('alābu is also called tumbī').
verdicts.reason: Attested in Devanagari in a classical nighantu verse quoted by a Dravyaguna department for this species, which is exactly the kind of corroboration Wikidata cannot supply. Confirmed and preferred. Note for the page: the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India Part I Vol. III carries this drug under the title Tumbinī (fresh fruit), so तुम्बी/तुम्बिनी is the official pharmacopoeial name alongside अलाबु.

verdicts.name: சுரைக்காய்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Bottle Gourd' page: "Tamil: சுரைக்காய் Surakkai" — printed in Tamil script, exact match; SDACH Dravyaguna 'Alabu' monograph: Tamil "Suraikkai".
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match in Flowers of India plus independent agreement from the Dravyaguna monograph. சுரைக்காய் is the ordinary Tamil name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: आँवला
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Amla' page (Emblica officinalis / Phyllanthus emblica): "Hindi: आँवला Aonla" — Devanagari, exact match including the candrabindu; MMPND Phyllanthus page: Hindi "आमला Amla, आंवला Amvalaa, आंवला Anwla, Aonla".
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in Flowers of India, corroborated by MMPND. Dominant Hindi name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: धात्री
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Amla' page: "Sanskrit: Dhatri, amalaka"; MMPND Phyllanthus page: Sanskrit "धात्रिका Dhatrika, Dhatriphala" alongside आमलकः Amalakah.
verdicts.reason: Dhātrī ('the nurse') is attested as a Sanskrit name of P. emblica by Flowers of India, and MMPND independently attests the cognates धात्रिका and Dhatriphala for the same species, so the lexeme is sound. preferred=false because the standard pharmacopoeial Sanskrit name is आमलकी / आमलकः, which MMPND prints in Devanagari and which is absent from the candidate set.

verdicts.name: நெல்லி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Amla' page: "Tamil: Nelli" (and Malayalam Nelli, Nellikka; Kannada Betta nelli); MMPND Phyllanthus page prints Tamil "நெல்லி Nelli" in Tamil script along with காட்டுநெல்லி Kattu-nelli and தோப்புநெல்லி Toppu nelli.
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match in MMPND and roman agreement in Flowers of India. நெல்லி is the ordinary Tamil name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: चांगेरी
verdicts.denotesInstead: Correct species (Oxalis corniculata) but wrong language: चांगेरी is the SANSKRIT name, not Hindi.
verdicts.reason: This is the batch's real error. Two independent sources agree on the language assignment and both contradict the candidate. Flowers of India ('Creeping Wood Sorrel', Oxalis corniculata) lists "Sanskrit: चांगेरी Changeri, अम्लः Amla, अम्ली Amli" and separately "Hindi: Amrul अम्रुल" — चांगेरी appears under Sanskrit, Marathi and Kannada, never Hindi. The Kerala State Medicinal Plants Board herbal database (smpbkerala.in) independently gives Sanskrit "Changeri", Hindi "Amrul", Tamil "Puliyarai". So the name is genuine and the species is right, but filed in the wrong language slot, which on a published monograph would misinform every Hindi reader. The Hindi name is अम्रुल.

verdicts.name: புளியாரை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Kerala State Medicinal Plants Board herbal database (smpbkerala.in), Oxalis corniculata: Tamil "Puliyarai", Malayalam പുളിയാറില Puliyarila; Flowers of India gives Tamil "Paliakiri" for the same species.
verdicts.reason: SMPB Kerala, a state medicinal-plants-board database organised per species, attests Puliyarai = புளியாரை for O. corniculata, and the Malayalam cognate പുളിയാറില on the same page supports the stem (puḷi- 'tamarind/sour'). Preferred Tamil form. SMPB prints it in roman; the Tamil-script spelling is the standard rendering.

verdicts.name: आम
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Mango' page (Mangifera indica): "Hindi: Am (आम)" — Devanagari, exact match; MMPND Mangifera page: Hindi "आम Āma (aam)".
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in two independent sources. Dominant Hindi name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: आम्रवृक्षः
verdicts.reason: Unattested. MMPND gives Sanskrit "आम्र Aamra, Ambrah, Amra chuta, Madhuula..." for M. indica; wisdomlib's Amarakośa citation gives Āmra and Rasāla. The bare stem आम्र is the name; आम्रवृक्षः ('the mango tree') is a descriptive compound with a nominative ending, the Sanskrit Wikipedia title pattern seen throughout this batch. Right species, fabricated lexeme. Use आम्र.

verdicts.name: चूतम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdomlib's Sanskrit-dictionary and Ayurveda entry for Cūta (चूत): "the mango tree", glossed botanically as Mangifera indica (Anacardiaceae), with Rāmāyaṇa and Śākuntala attestations and Amarakośa synonyms Āmra and Rasāla; MMPND Mangifera page independently lists Sanskrit "Amra chuta".
verdicts.reason: The lexeme is genuine classical Sanskrit for mango, attested in dictionary and kāvya sources, so confirmed. preferred=false on two counts: the citation form is चूत (the candidate's -म् is an inflected neuter ending that no lexicon uses as the headword), and आम्र is the standard name. Also note चूत carries an unrelated anatomical sense in Sanskrit medical texts, so it reads awkwardly as a headline name.

verdicts.name: இந்திய மா
verdicts.reason: Unattested as a name. Flowers of India gives Tamil "Ma (மா)" for M. indica; MMPND prints Tamil "ஆம்பிரம் Āmpiram, மா Mā, மாங்காய் Māṅkāy, மாம்பழம் Māmpaḻam". No source lists இந்திய மா. It is literally 'Indian mango' — a Tamil Wikipedia descriptive article title built by prefixing the species epithet to the real name, not something a Tamil speaker would say or search. Right species, constructed phrase. Use மா.

verdicts.name: आम
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Mango' page: "Hindi: Am (आम)"; MMPND Mangifera page: Hindi "आम Āma".
verdicts.reason: Attested for Mangifera indica, so the name-species link is sound. But preferred=false and flagged: this page is Amra Beeja, the SEED/kernel drug, and आम names the fruit or tree. Presenting it as the Hindi name of the page's subject would mislabel the drug. The candidate sets for amra and amra-beeja are byte-identical, which means the harvest keyed on the botanical name and ignored the plant part — every name on this page inherits that scope error.

verdicts.name: आम्रवृक्षः
verdicts.reason: Unattested, for the same reason as on the amra page: MMPND gives Sanskrit आम्र for M. indica and the -वृक्षः compound is a Sanskrit Wikipedia title. Doubly wrong here — it names the tree, while this page is the seed kernel.

verdicts.name: चूतम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdomlib entry for Cūta (चूत) = the mango tree, Mangifera indica, with Amarakośa synonyms Āmra and Rasāla; MMPND lists Sanskrit "Amra chuta".
verdicts.reason: Genuine Sanskrit for mango, so species-correct. preferred=false: the citation form is चूत not चूतम्, and it names the tree rather than this page's drug (the kernel), for which the Sanskrit would be a bīja/majjā compound.

verdicts.name: இந்திய மா
verdicts.reason: Unattested construction, same as on the amra page: Flowers of India gives Tamil மா, MMPND gives மா / மாங்காய் / மாம்பழம் / ஆம்பிரம், and no source gives இந்திய மா. A Tamil Wikipedia descriptive title. Also out of scope for a seed monograph.

verdicts.name: மாங்கா இஞ்சி
verdicts.reason: Misspelling. Flowers of India, 'Mango Ginger' page (Curcuma amada), gives Tamil "Arukamlaka, Mankayyinchi" — that is மாங்காய் இஞ்சி, with the final ய் of மாங்காய் ('unripe mango'). The candidate drops it, giving மாங்கா, which is not the Tamil word. Right species and right compound, defective form. Use மாங்காய் இஞ்சி.

verdicts.name: अनंतमूल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Indian Sarsaparilla' page (Hemidesmus indicus): "Hindi: अनंतमूल Anantamul, दूधली Dudhli" — Devanagari, exact match; MMPND Hemidesmus page: Hindi "Anantamool".
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in Flowers of India, corroborated by MMPND. It is the name under which the root is traded and searched, so preferred.

verdicts.name: क्षीरिणीसस्यम्
verdicts.denotesInstead: Manilkara hexandra (syn. Mimusops hexandra); and as Satyanāśī, Argemone mexicana — both given for क्षीरिणी in nighantu literature
verdicts.reason: Two separate problems. First, the form: no source attests क्षीरिणीसस्यम्. Flowers of India gives Sanskrit "अनंतमूल Anantamul, Sariva" for H. indicus and MMPND gives "Anantamoola, Sariva" — neither mentions Kṣīriṇī, and the -सस्यम् suffix is the Sanskrit Wikipedia pattern. Second, and worse, the base word is not species-specific: wisdomlib's Kṣīriṇī entry records it as a name of Manilkara hexandra (Sapotaceae) and, as Satyanāśī, of Argemone mexicana / Euphorbia spp., and the Rāja Nighaṇṭu lists Kṣīriṇī as an unidentified plant. It does carry a secondary modern application to Hemidesmus, so it is ambiguous rather than flatly wrong — but ambiguous is disqualifying for a headline Sanskrit name on a botanical reference. Use सारिवा or अनन्तमूला.

verdicts.name: நன்னாரி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Indian Sarsaparilla' page: "Tamil: Nannari, Sugandipala", with the Kannada list printing the cognate ನನ್ನಾರಿ Nannaari in Kannada script; MMPND Hemidesmus page: Tamil "Nannari".
verdicts.reason: Two independent sources attest Nannari under Tamil for H. indicus (it is the root used in nannari sarbath). Preferred Tamil form. Both print it in roman; நன்னாரி is the standard Tamil-script rendering.

verdicts.name: अकोल
verdicts.reason: Not attested in this form. Three independent per-species sources agree on the nasal: Kerala State Medicinal Plants Board (smpbkerala.in) gives Hindi "Dhera, Ankol"; ayushvedah.com's drug entry gives Hindi "Dhera, Ankol"; the SDACH Dravyaguna 'Ankola' monograph gives Hindi "Ankol". The candidate अकोल drops the anusvāra. 'Akola' appears only in MMPND's SANSKRIT list for A. salviifolium, not under Hindi. Right species, wrong form and arguably wrong language. Use अंकोल or ढेरा.

verdicts.name: அழிஞ்சில்
verdicts.reason: Cannot corroborate from an authority. All three per-species sources I retrieved give different Tamil names: SMPB Kerala "Elangi, Alandi", ayushvedah.com "Elangi, Alandi", SDACH Dravyaguna "Alangi"; MMPND lists no Tamil name for the species. அழிஞ்சில் turns up only in Tamil Wiktionary, Tamil Wikipedia and personal blogs — and a language wiki is a weak corroborator here precisely because it may mirror Wikidata, so by the brief I cannot set confirmed. It is probably a genuine Tamil name: the attested Malayalam ഇരിഞ്ഞിൽ Irinjil (SMPB Kerala) and Kannada Arinjil (ayushvedah) are clear cognates. It needs the Tamil Lexicon or the API Tamil name before it goes on a page.

verdicts.name: अपामार्ग
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Prickly Chaff Flower' page (Achyranthes aspera): "Hindi: अघाड़ा (Aghara), अपामार्ग (Apamarga), चिरचिरा (Chirchira)" — Devanagari, exact match, listed under Hindi as well as Sanskrit.
verdicts.reason: Flowers of India prints अपामार्ग in Devanagari under Hindi for this species (the Sanskrit name has been fully naturalised into Hindi, and the same page lists it for Bengali, Gujarati, Nepali and Odia too). It is also the name under which the Ayurvedic drug is searched, so preferred among the Hindi forms.

verdicts.name: लटजीरा
verdicts.reason: Could not corroborate from a per-species authority. Flowers of India's Hindi list for A. aspera is अघाड़ा, अपामार्ग, चिरचिरा; SMPB Kerala gives Hindi "Apang"; MMPND gives Hindi "Latkana" — close but not the same word. 'Latjira/Latjeera' is widely repeated in pharmacognosy review articles, but review-paper name lists are exactly the uncorroborated chain this check exists to break, and none of the three species-organised sources I retrieved carries it. Likely genuine regional Hindi, but it needs the API Hindi name to confirm.

verdicts.name: अपामार्गसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: Unattested. Flowers of India gives Sanskrit अपामार्ग for A. aspera and MMPND gives "Apamarga". The candidate is that name plus -सस्यम् ('the apāmārga crop'), the Sanskrit Wikipedia title pattern. Right species, fabricated lexeme, and it sits on the same page as the correct अपामार्ग, so it adds nothing but error. Use अपामार्ग.

verdicts.name: நாயுருவி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Achyranthes page: Tamil "Naayuruvi, Naayuruvi vaer"; Kerala State Medicinal Plants Board (smpbkerala.in), Achyranthes aspera: Tamil "Nayurivi, Naagarkaai".
verdicts.reason: Two independent species-organised sources attest Nāyuruvi under Tamil for A. aspera (MMPND also gives the root, 'Naayuruvi vaer', which is the Siddha drug). Preferred Tamil form. Both print roman; நாயுருவி is the standard Tamil-script rendering. Flowers of India instead lists ஆகாடம் and அபாமார்க்கம், which are Tamil renderings of the Sanskrit name, not the native one.

verdicts.name: अपराजिता
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, 'Butterfly Pea' page (Clitoria ternatea): "Hindi: अपराजिता (Aparajita)" — Devanagari, exact match (also Assamese অপৰাজিতা, Manipuri, Nepali).
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match under Hindi in an independent source. Standard Hindi name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: अपराजिता
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Shri Dharmasthala Ayurveda College Dravyaguna Vigyan monograph 'Aparajita' (Clitoria ternatea), which gives the Sanskrit synonyms Aparajita, Girikarnu, Asphota and Vishnukranta.
verdicts.reason: The Dravyaguna monograph for this species heads its Sanskrit synonym list with Aparājitā, and the name is the title of the drug in Ayurvedic usage, so confirmed and preferred. One caution for the page: Clitoria ternatea is frequently sold and written up as Śaṅkhapuṣpī, which properly denotes Convolvulus pluricaulis — do not let that synonym migrate onto this monograph.

verdicts.name: கருவிளை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: India Biodiversity Portal species page for Clitoria ternatea (species/show/32124), whose Tamil common-name list includes karuvilai alongside kakkanam, kakkattan, kannikkodi and uyvai; independently attested in Sangam literature, Kuṟuntokai 110, where karuvilai flowers are compared to the eyes on peacock feathers.
verdicts.reason: Species-correct and genuinely Tamil, with a literary attestation independent of any modern database. Two caveats I should be straight about: the India Biodiversity Portal page itself returned 403 to direct fetch, so I read its common-name list through the search index rather than the page, and Flowers of India gives a different Tamil name (சங்கு கன்னிக்கொடி). preferred=false because the name a Tamil speaker would actually use or search is சங்குப்பூ or நீலக்காக்கணம்; கருவிளை is the classical/literary form.

verdicts.name: கருஞ்சீரகம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, UPAKUNCIKA monograph (seeds of Nigella sativa Linn., Fam. Ranunculaceae) — Tamil slot reads "Karunjeerakam, Karunjiragam". Local full text: /Users/jairajsharma/Projects/ayurveda-atlas/sources-private/api-all.txt line 15250.
verdicts.reason: API's own Nigella sativa monograph gives Karunjeerakam/Karunjiragam as the Tamil name, which is கருஞ்சீரகம் (karu + sīrakam, 'black cumin'). Independent of Wikidata. Only Tamil candidate on the page, and the standard form.

verdicts.name: कालमेघ
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Names of Plants in India :: Andrographis paniculata (Burm.f.) Nees (Dave's Botanary compilation, indiantreepix/efloraofindia) — Hindi list reads "हरा चिरायता hara chirayata, कालमेघ kalmegh, कल्पनाथ kalpanath, किरयित् kirayit, महातीता mahatita".
verdicts.reason: Retrieved the Hindi list for Andrographis paniculata and कालमेघ is in it verbatim in Devanagari. It is also the name the drug trades under in Hindi, so it is the form a Hindi speaker would search. Note my local API copy contains no Kalamegha monograph, so API could not be used here.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa Linn. (the pipal/bodhi tree)
verdicts.reason: This is the planted error and it is a genuine Sanskrit plant name for a completely different tree. The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India carries its own separate monograph headed ASVATTHA (Bark), defined as 'dried bark of Ficus religiosa Linn. (Fam. Moraceae)' — api-all.txt lines 126-128 and 3132-3135 — and its Bengali/Kannada synonym slots there repeat Asvattha/Ashvattha for Ficus religiosa. Meanwhile the retrieved Sanskrit list for Andrographis paniculata (Names of Plants in India) is 'भूनिम्ब bhunimba, कालमेघ kalamegha, महातिक्ता mahatikta, यवतिक्ता yavatikta' and contains no अश्वत्थ at all. Must be dropped from this page; it is the same bad Wikidata alias that also contaminates Adhatoda vasica and Aegle marmelos.

verdicts.name: कालमेघः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Names of Plants in India :: Andrographis paniculata (Burm.f.) Nees — Sanskrit list reads "भूनिम्ब bhunimba, कालमेघ kalamegha, महातिक्ता mahatikta, यवतिक्ता yavatikta"; corroborated by efloraofindia's Andrographis paniculata page giving the Sanskrit synonyms bhunimba, kalamegha, mahatikta, yavatikta.
verdicts.reason: कालमेघ is attested as Sanskrit for this species by two compilations that list names per botanical species and agree. The candidate's nominative-singular form कालमेघः is the dictionary form of the same name. This is the Ayurvedic drug name the monograph is built on, so it is the preferred Sanskrit form; भूनिम्ब is the other major one and is reported in `discovered`.

verdicts.name: நிலவேம்பு
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Names of Plants in India :: Andrographis paniculata (Burm.f.) Nees — Tamil list reads "நிலவேம்பு nilavempu".
verdicts.reason: Attested in Tamil script for this species. One caveat worth carrying onto the page: the API attaches Tamil 'Nilavembu' to its KIRATATIKTA monograph, i.e. Swertia chirata (api-all.txt line 9997), reflecting the long-standing chirata/kalmegh substitution. So the name is shared with Swertia chirata, but its primary Siddha referent is Andrographis paniculata (Nilavembu Kudineer), which is why I confirm rather than flag it as denoting another species.

verdicts.name: கருஞ்சீரகம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, UPAKUNCIKA monograph (seeds of Nigella sativa Linn.) — Tamil slot "Karunjeerakam, Karunjiragam" (api-all.txt line 15250).
verdicts.reason: Same species as the kalajaji page and the same API attestation. கருஞ்சீரகம் is the standard Tamil name for Nigella sativa seed.

verdicts.name: कमल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KAMALA monograph (dried flowers of Nelumbo nucifera Gaertn., Fam. Nymphaeaceae) — Hindi slot "Kamal, Kanwal" (api-all.txt line 23951 ff.); independently, Names of Plants in India :: Nelumbo nucifera gives Hindi "कमल Kamal".
verdicts.reason: Both an official per-monograph source and an independent per-species compilation give कमल as the Hindi name. This is unambiguously the form a Hindi speaker uses.

verdicts.name: कमलम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India — the monograph itself is headed KAMALA and defined as the flowers of Nelumbo nucifera Gaertn.; its Sanskrit synonym slot adds "Abja, Aravinda, Padma, Kalhara, Sitopala, Pankaja". Names of Plants in India :: Nelumbo nucifera gives Sanskrit "कमलम् Kamalam".
verdicts.reason: API monograph titles are the official Sanskrit drug names, and this one is Kamala for Nelumbo nucifera; the neuter nominative कमलम् is its dictionary form and is attested in Devanagari by Names of Plants in India. Correct and preferred.

verdicts.name: தாமரை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KAMALA (flowers of Nelumbo nucifera) — Tamil slot "Tamarai, Thamaraipoo, Aravindan, Paduman, Kamalam, Sarojam"; Names of Plants in India :: Nelumbo nucifera gives Tamil "தாமரை Tamarai".
verdicts.reason: Attested by API in romanisation and by Names of Plants in India in Tamil script, for this exact species. தாமரை is the ordinary Tamil word for lotus.

verdicts.name: कमल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KAMALA monograph (flowers of Nelumbo nucifera Gaertn.) — Hindi slot "Kamal, Kanwal"; Names of Plants in India :: Nelumbo nucifera, Hindi "कमल Kamal".
verdicts.reason: Correct Hindi name for the species. Flagging a scope mismatch rather than a name error: this page is the stamen/filament drug (kesara), and कमल names the plant and its flower, not the stamens specifically. The name is right for the species but a reader should not take it as the Hindi term for the stamen drug.

verdicts.name: कमलम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India — monograph headed KAMALA, flowers of Nelumbo nucifera Gaertn.; Names of Plants in India :: Nelumbo nucifera, Sanskrit "कमलम् Kamalam".
verdicts.reason: Attested Sanskrit name for the species. Same scope caveat as the Hindi entry: the stamen drug would be a kamala-kesara compound, and the plain कमलम् names the plant. I found no organ-specific Sanskrit synonym for the stamens in the sources I retrieved, so I am not inventing one.

verdicts.name: தாமரை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KAMALA (flowers of Nelumbo nucifera) — Tamil slot "Tamarai, Thamaraipoo, ..."; Names of Plants in India :: Nelumbo nucifera, Tamil "தாமரை Tamarai".
verdicts.reason: Correct Tamil name for the species; names the plant rather than the stamens, same scope caveat as above.

verdicts.name: कमल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KAMALA monograph (dried rhizome with roots of Nelumbo nucifera Gaertn.) — Hindi slot "Kamal Kand, Kamal Kakdi" (api-all.txt line 42286 ff.).
verdicts.reason: कमल is the correct Hindi name for the species. Scope note: this page is the rhizome drug, and API's rhizome monograph gives the organ-specific Hindi names कमल कंद / कमल ककड़ी, which are more precise than bare कमल; both are in `discovered`.

verdicts.name: कमलम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India — monograph headed KAMALA for Nelumbo nucifera; Names of Plants in India :: Nelumbo nucifera, Sanskrit "कमलम् Kamalam".
verdicts.reason: Correct Sanskrit species name. Scope note: API's rhizome monograph lists its own Sanskrit synonyms 'Padmakanda, Saluka, Ambhoruha' for this organ, which are the names that actually denote kamala-kanda; they are in `discovered`.

verdicts.name: தாமரை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KAMALA (rhizome of Nelumbo nucifera) — Tamil slot "Tamardi Kizangu"; KAMALA (flowers) — Tamil "Tamarai".
verdicts.reason: Correct Tamil name for the species. API's rhizome monograph gives the organ-specific Tamil form தாமரைக் கிழங்கு ('Tamardi Kizangu'), reported in `discovered`.

verdicts.name: कचनार
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KANCANARA monograph (dried stem bark of Bauhinia variegata Blume, Fam. Leguminosae) — Hindi slot "Kachanar, Kanchanar, Kachnar" (api-all.txt line 7815 ff.); Names of Plants in India :: Bauhinia variegata L. gives Hindi "कचनाल kachnal, कचनार kachnar".
verdicts.reason: Attested for this exact species by the official per-monograph source and by an independent per-species compilation, in Devanagari. This is the name Hindi speakers use and search.

verdicts.name: मन्दारः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Primarily Erythrina variegata / E. suberosa (the coral tree); also Calotropis gigantea and C. procera (arka), Piliostigma malabaricum, Ficus benjamina and Bauhinia tomentosa
verdicts.reason: This is a real Sanskrit plant name but a badly ambiguous one that would mislead on a Bauhinia variegata page. API's KANCANARA monograph (Bauhinia variegata) gives Sanskrit 'Kancanaraka' only, with no Mandara anywhere. Within the genus, API attaches the mandara word-family to a different species: its PITA-KANCANARA monograph (Bauhinia racemosa Lamk., api-all.txt line 101405 ff.) lists Kannada 'Kadu manthara, ... Mandara', Malayalam 'Mandarum' and Tamil 'Malai-mandarai'. The lexicon compilation at wisdomlib.org/definition/mandara resolves mandāra chiefly to Erythrina suberosa, Erythrina variegata, Calotropis procera and C. gigantea, with Bauhinia variegata appearing only as a secondary identification. The Sanskrit name for this species is काञ्चनारः (API monograph title), which I report in `discovered`. Drop मन्दारः.

verdicts.name: மலையாத்தி
verdicts.denotesInstead: Bauhinia racemosa Lamk. per the Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India; Bauhinia malabarica Roxb. per MMPND
verdicts.reason: Species-level error. API's PITA-KANCANARA monograph, which is explicitly Bauhinia racemosa Lamk., lists Tamil 'Atthi, Malai-atti, Malai-mandarai' — so the official source assigns Malai-atti (மலையாத்தி) to B. racemosa, not B. variegata. The Multilingual Multiscript Plant Name Database (Univ. of Melbourne, plantnames.unimelb.edu.au/Sorting/Bauhinia.html) assigns 'மலையாத்தி Malaiyatti' to Bauhinia malabarica Roxb. and gives no Tamil name at all for B. variegata. API's Tamil for B. variegata is 'Sigappu mandarai, Sihappu mantarai' (செம்மந்தாரை). Names of Plants in India does list மலையாத்தி under B. variegata, but it is outvoted by two sources that place it on other Bauhinia species, and on a reference page it would send a reader to the wrong tree.

verdicts.name: कंकोल
verdicts.reason: Right species, wrong language tier. API's KANKOLA monograph (mature dried fruits of Piper cubeba Linn.f., api-all.txt line 7974 ff.) lists 'Kankolaka, Cinosana, Cinatiksna, Kakkola, Kankolika' as the SANSKRIT synonyms and places the bare 'Kankol' in the Marathi slot; its Hindi slot is 'Seetalchini, Kababchini'. MMPND's Piper page gives Hindi as 'Cubab-chinee, कबाब चीनी Kabab chini, शीतल चीनी Sheetal chini' and does not list कंकोल as Hindi. So कंकोल is attested for this species but as the Sanskrit drug name (and as Marathi), not as Hindi. Reassign it to Sanskrit rather than publish it as Hindi.

verdicts.name: कबाबचीनी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KANKOLA monograph (Piper cubeba Linn.f.) — Hindi slot "Seetalchini, Kababchini"; MMPND (plantnames.unimelb.edu.au/Sorting/Piper.html) gives Hindi "कबाब चीनी Kabab chini" for Piper cubeba.
verdicts.reason: Attested as Hindi for this exact species by both the official monograph and MMPND, the latter in Devanagari. This is the name cubeb trades under in Hindi, so it is the preferred Hindi form.

verdicts.name: क्यूबेब
verdicts.reason: Not a vernacular name — a Devanagari respelling of the English/trade word 'cubeb'. API's Hindi slot for the Kankola monograph is 'Seetalchini, Kababchini'; MMPND's Hindi entry is 'Cubab-chinee, कबाब चीनी, शीतल चीनी'. Neither attests क्यूबेब as a Hindi plant name. Harvest artifact of an English label; drop it.

verdicts.name: शीतलचीनी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KANKOLA monograph (Piper cubeba Linn.f.) — Hindi slot "Seetalchini, Kababchini"; MMPND Piper page, Hindi "शीतल चीनी Sheetal chini".
verdicts.reason: Genuinely attested as Hindi for Piper cubeba by both sources, MMPND in Devanagari. Not marked preferred because कबाबचीनी is the commoner trade and search form; both belong on the page.

verdicts.name: सुगंधमरिच
verdicts.reason: Language mis-assignment, not a species error. API's KANKOLA monograph places 'Sugandhamaricha' in the BENGALI slot ('Kahabchini, Sugandhamaricha'), not the Hindi slot. MMPND's Piper cubeba entry does not list it at all. The name does belong to this species, but as Bengali; publishing it as Hindi would be wrong. Reassign to Bengali or drop.

verdicts.name: வால்மிளகு
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KANKOLA monograph (Piper cubeba Linn.f.) — Tamil slot "Vaali milaku, Valmilagu"; MMPND Piper page lists Tamil "Vaalmilagu" for Piper cubeba.
verdicts.reason: Attested for this exact species by both sources (both in romanisation; வால்மிளகு is the transparent Tamil form, 'tailed pepper', matching the English common name). Only Tamil candidate and the standard one.

verdicts.name: गुंजा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND (plantnames.unimelb.edu.au/Sorting/Abrus.html) lists under HINDI for Abrus precatorius: "Ganchi, Guncai, गुंच Gunch, Gunche, गुंची Gunchi, गुञ्जा Gunja, कूंच Kunch, माषा Masha, पाटहिका Patahika, करजनी, रत्ती Ratti".
verdicts.reason: MMPND attests गुञ्जा/गुंजा under Hindi for Abrus precatorius in Devanagari, so it is not merely the Sanskrit form bleeding across. Not marked preferred: API's GUNJA monographs (seeds, api-all.txt line 6424; root, line 21658) give the Hindi slot as 'Ratti, Ghungchi', and गुंजा is primarily the Sanskrit drug name that titles the monograph. रत्ती and घुंघची are what a Hindi speaker would say; both are in `discovered`.

verdicts.name: குன்றி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, GUNJA monographs (seeds and root of Abrus precatorius Linn.) — Tamil slots "Kuntri, Kunrimani, Kundamani" and "Kunrimani, Kundumani"; MMPND Abrus page lists Tamil "குன்றி" and "குன்றிமணி".
verdicts.reason: Attested for this exact species by the official monograph and by MMPND in Tamil script. குன்றி is the base form (குன்றிமணி being the seed); the standard Tamil name.

verdicts.name: किवांच
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Names of Plants in India :: Mucuna pruriens — Hindi names include "किवांच (Kivanch), कवांच (Kavanch), केवांच (Kevanch)"; Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, ATMAGUPTA monographs (seed, api-all.txt line 37197; root, line 56834) give Hindi "Kewanch, Kaunch" and "Kevanch, Kaunch, Khujanee".
verdicts.reason: किवांच is attested in Devanagari for this species by Names of Plants in India, and API's romanised Kewanch/Kevanch is the same name. Not marked preferred because API lists कौंच (Kaunch) alongside it and that is the commoner Hindi form; कौंच is in `discovered`. Note API uses the synonym Mucuna prurita Hook. for the same taxon.

verdicts.name: பூனைக்காலி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, ATMAGUPTA monographs (Mucuna prurita Hook. syn. M. pruriens) — Tamil slots "Poonaikkali" and "Punaik-Kalee, Punaikkalee, Punaippidukkam"; Names of Plants in India :: Mucuna pruriens gives Tamil "Poonaikaali (பூனைக்காலி)".
verdicts.reason: Attested for this exact species by the official monograph (twice, in two organ monographs) and in Tamil script by Names of Plants in India. The standard Tamil name.

verdicts.name: कठबेल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND (plantnames.unimelb.edu.au/Sorting/Limonia.html) lists under HINDI for Limonia acidissima: "... कैट Kait, कैथ Kait, कैथा Kaitha, कपित्थ Kapitth, कठबेल Katabel, कत्बेल Katbel".
verdicts.reason: कठबेल is attested as Hindi for this species in Devanagari by MMPND. Not marked preferred because API's KAPITTHA monograph (dried pulp of Feronia limonia (Linn.) Swingle, api-all.txt line 24166 ff.) gives the Hindi slot as 'Kaitha', and कैथ/कैथा is the name a Hindi speaker actually uses; it is in `discovered`.

verdicts.name: कपित्थ
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Limonia page lists "कपित्थ Kapitth" under HINDI and "कपित्थं Kapittha" under SANSKRIT for Limonia acidissima; API's monograph is itself titled KAPITTHA for Feronia limonia (= Limonia acidissima).
verdicts.reason: Attested as Hindi by MMPND as well as being the Sanskrit drug name. It is a Sanskrit loan in Hindi rather than the colloquial term, so not preferred; कैथ is the everyday Hindi form.

verdicts.name: कबिट
verdicts.reason: Not attested as standard Hindi. MMPND's Limonia acidissima entry lists the comparable forms 'Kabeet' and 'Kabut' explicitly tagged to the Fiji Islands, i.e. Fiji Hindi, not Indian Hindi; its Indian Hindi list is कैट/कैथ/कैथा/कपित्थ/कठबेल/कत्बेल. API's Kapittha monograph puts the cognate forms elsewhere: Bengali 'Kayet Bael, Kavataleal, Kavita' and Marathi 'Kavatha'. Right species, but the language label is wrong and the spelling is not corroborated; drop or reassign.

verdicts.name: விளா
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Limonia page lists under TAMIL: "கபித்தம் Kapittam, கவித்தம் Kavittam, தந்தசடம் Tantacatam, Velam, Velan, விளா Vila (viḷā), விளா மரம் Vilamaram, விளாம்பழம் Vilam palam, ..."; API's KAPITTHA monograph gives Tamil "Vilamaram, Vilangai".
verdicts.reason: Attested in Tamil script by MMPND and in romanisation by the official monograph, for this exact species (API uses the synonym Feronia limonia; POWO's accepted name is Limonia acidissima L.). விளா is the base form and the one a Tamil speaker would use or search.

verdicts.name: करंज
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KARANJA monographs (seeds of Pongamia pinnata (Linn.) Merr., api-all.txt line 8646; dried root bark, line 24555) — Hindi slots "Dithouri, Karuaini" / "Karanj", with 'Karanj' also in the Punjabi slot of the seed monograph.
verdicts.reason: API's root-bark monograph gives Hindi 'Karanj' for this species, which is करंज. Note the taxonomy: POWO's accepted name is Millettia pinnata (L.) Panigrahi and API uses the synonym Pongamia pinnata, so the monograph is the same taxon as the page. करंज is the ordinary Hindi name and the preferred form.

verdicts.name: पोंगैमिया
verdicts.reason: Not a vernacular name at all — a Devanagari transliteration of the Latin genus 'Pongamia'. API's Hindi slots for the two Karanja monographs are 'Dithouri, Karuaini' and 'Karanj'; nothing resembling पोंगैमिया appears in any Indian-language slot. This is a harvest artifact of a scientific-name label being treated as a Hindi alias. Drop it.

verdicts.name: Karanja(ಕರಂಜ)
verdicts.reason: Malformed string, not a name: Latin 'Karanja' concatenated with a Kannada-script parenthetical and filed under Sanskrit. It is not Sanskrit (no Devanagari), and ಕರಂಜ is not even the Kannada name for this species — API gives Kannada as 'Honge, Hulagilu' / 'Honge Beru' in the two Karanja monographs. Drop outright; it cannot be fixed by relabelling.

verdicts.name: करञ्जवृक्षः
verdicts.reason: Unattested compound. API's Sanskrit synonym slot for both Karanja monographs reads 'Karanjaka, Naktamala, Naktahva, Ghrtakaranja' — karañja-vṛkṣaḥ ('karanja tree') is a descriptive phrase built on the drug name, not a lexical synonym any source I retrieved gives. The attested Sanskrit forms करञ्जकः, नक्तमालः and घृतकरञ्जः are in `discovered`; use those instead.

verdicts.name: புங்கை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KARANJA (dried root bark of Pongamia pinnata (Linn.) Merr.) — Tamil slot "Pungai" (api-all.txt line 24555 ff.); the seed monograph gives Tamil "Pungan, Pongana".
verdicts.reason: The official monograph gives Pungai as the Tamil name for this exact species, which is புங்கை. Attested twice across the two organ monographs in cognate forms. The standard Tamil name.

verdicts.name: करेला
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KARAVALLAKA monograph (fresh fruit of Momordica charantia Linn., Fam. Cucurbitaceae, api-all.txt line 25354 ff.) — Hindi slot "Karela"; efloraofindia / Names of Plants in India :: Momordica charantia gives Hindi "करेला karela, कठिल्ल kathilla, परारु poraru".
verdicts.reason: Attested for this exact species by the official monograph and in Devanagari by an independent per-species compilation. करेला is the universal Hindi name and clearly the preferred form.

verdicts.name: कारवेल्लम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KARAVALLAKA monograph (Momordica charantia Linn.) — Sanskrit slot "Karavella, Kathilla, Varivalli, Karavalli"; efloraofindia / Names of Plants in India :: Momordica charantia gives Sanskrit "कारवेल्लकः kaarvellakah, कटिल्लः kathillah, सुषवी sushavi, ऊर्ध्वासितः urdhvaasitah".
verdicts.reason: The Sanskrit name is attested by both sources; the candidate कारवेल्लम् is the neuter-nominative form of API's 'Karavella', and efloraofindia gives the -ka extension कारवेल्लकः. Same name, standard form variation, right species. Preferred Sanskrit form on the page.

verdicts.name: பாகல்
verdicts.reason: Almost certainly a correct Tamil form, but I could not corroborate the bare stem in an authoritative source, so by the brief's rule it does not pass. What I actually retrieved: API's KARAVALLAKA monograph gives Tamil 'Paharkai' (பாகற்காய்); efloraofindia / Names of Plants in India gives Tamil 'இராசவள்ளி iraca-valli, பாகற்காய் pagakkai'; MMPND's Momordica page gives Tamil 'Pava aki' (Pavakkai) for M. charantia and places 'Pakal' under Sinhalese names for Momordica balsamina; the Kerala State Medicinal Plants Board page gives 'Pavakai Paaharkaai'. The bare form பாகல் is attested only by Tamil Wikipedia and Tamil Wiktionary, which the brief treats as weak corroborators, plus a Tamil Virtual Academy Siddha materia medica entry slugged 'paagal' that I could not open (HTTP 526). No species error here — it is the right plant — so the safe fix is to publish the attested பாகற்காய் (in `discovered`) rather than the unverified stem.

verdicts.name: कैर
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Names of Plants in India :: Capparis decidua (Forssk.) Edgew. (groups.google.com/g/indiantreepix/c/JYIwKvz8KUo) — Hindi list reads "कैर kair, कैरिया kairiya, करीर karir, करील karil, करीं kareen, पीचू pichu, टींट teent, टेंटी tenti".
verdicts.reason: Attested in Devanagari for this exact species, heading the Hindi list. My local API copy has no Capparis decidua monograph (it covers C. spinosa as Himsra and C. sepiaria as Vyaghranakha), so this rests on one independent per-species compilation rather than on API. कैर is the name used across the Rajasthan/Haryana range of the plant, so preferred.

verdicts.name: कमरख
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Names of Plants in India / efloraofindia :: Averrhoa carambola — Hindi list reads "कमरख (kamarakha), कमरक (kamaraka), दन्तसठ (dantasatha), पर्णमाचाल (parnamachal), पीतफल (pitaphala), शिराल (shiral)".
verdicts.reason: Attested in Devanagari as Hindi for this exact species. One honest qualification: flowersofindia.net's Star Fruit page gives Hindi as 'Karmal करमल' and places 'ﻛﻤﺮﺥ Kamrakh' under Urdu, so the two compilations differ on the language label. Since Names of Plants in India attests कमरख as Hindi and it is the form in common Hindi use for star fruit, I confirm it and mark it preferred, with करमल reported in `discovered`. No API monograph exists for Averrhoa carambola in my local copy.

verdicts.name: பாரம் (மலர்)
verdicts.reason: Malformed harvest artifact plus a weakly sourced archaism. The '(மலர்)' is a Tamil Wikipedia disambiguator meaning '(flower)' and is no part of any plant name — it is article-title cruft from the Wikidata label. The bare word பாரம் is given as a Sangam-literary word for cotton by the Tamil Wikipedia article ta.wikipedia.org/wiki/பாரம்_(மலர்) ('பாரம் என்பது பருத்தி', citing the ninety-nine flowers of Kuriñcippāṭṭu), which is a language Wikipedia mirroring Wikidata and so a weak corroborator on its own. The attested Tamil names for this species are different: API's KARPASA monograph (seeds of Gossypium herbaceum Linn., Fam. Malvaceae, api-all.txt line 9215 ff.) gives Tamil 'Parutti kkoottam', and MMPND (plantnames.unimelb.edu.au/Sorting/Gossypium.html) gives Tamil 'Karbasam, Karpasam, Nattupparutti, Talipparutti, Venparutti' with Parutti/Parutthi across the genus and expressly no 'Param'. Drop the string; publish பருத்தி / கற்பாசம் from `discovered`.

verdicts.name: பாரம் (மலர்)
verdicts.reason: Same malformed string on the root-drug page, rejected for the same reasons. '(மலர்)' is a Tamil Wikipedia disambiguator, not part of a name, and is doubly wrong here since this page is the root (moola), not the flower. The bare பாரம் rests only on Tamil Wikipedia; API's KARPASA monograph gives Tamil 'Parutti kkoottam' and MMPND gives Karpasam/Nattupparutti/Parutti for Gossypium herbaceum. Drop it.

verdicts.name: करेला
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, KARAVALLAKA monograph (fresh fruit of Momordica charantia Linn.) — Hindi slot "Karela"; efloraofindia / Names of Plants in India :: Momordica charantia, Hindi "करेला karela".
verdicts.reason: Same species as the karela page, same two attestations. करेला is the standard Hindi name and the preferred form; note the page slug Karvellaka is itself API's Sanskrit drug name for this monograph.

verdicts.name: कारवेल्लम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India — monograph headed KARAVALLAKA for Momordica charantia Linn., Sanskrit slot "Karavella, Kathilla, Varivalli, Karavalli"; efloraofindia / Names of Plants in India, Sanskrit "कारवेल्लकः kaarvellakah".
verdicts.reason: Attested by the official monograph (whose own title is this name) and by an independent compilation in Devanagari. कारवेल्लम् is the neuter-nominative form of the same name. Preferred Sanskrit form.

verdicts.name: பாகல்
verdicts.reason: Rejected for the same reason as on the karela page: the authoritative sources give the fuller form, not the bare stem. API's KARAVALLAKA monograph gives Tamil 'Paharkai'; efloraofindia gives பாகற்காய்; MMPND gives 'Pava aki' (Pavakkai) for M. charantia and attaches 'Pakal' to Momordica balsamina under Sinhalese; the Kerala SMPB page gives 'Pavakai Paaharkaai'. பாகல் alone is attested only on Tamil Wikipedia/Wiktionary, a weak corroborator. Right species, so no denotesInstead — but publish the attested பாகற்காய் instead.

verdicts.name: गाँजे का पौधा
verdicts.reason: Retrieved the Hindi list for Cannabis sativa from 'Names of Plants in India' (Wayback capture of the classic site, 2020-11-04): भांग, बिजया, चरस, गांझा, मातुलानी, सन, सिद्धि. Flowers of India (Marijuana page) gives the same core set. 'गाँजे का पौधा' appears in neither; it is a descriptive genitive phrase ('the ganja plant'), the shape of a Wikidata display label rather than a plant name. Not a different species, just not a name.

verdicts.name: भृंगराज
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib Ayurveda glossary entry for Bhṛṅgarāja: 'a Sanskrit word referring to false daisy… The official botanical name is Eclipta alba (synonym: Eclipta prostrata)', used throughout the Caraka-saṃhitā and Suśruta-saṃhitā; the same entry records the Hindi forms of the name.
verdicts.reason: The species identification is solid from classical Ayurvedic sources via wisdomlib. भृंगराज (anusvāra orthography) is the form current in Hindi for this plant and the form a Hindi speaker searches. Note the same source gives भांगरा/भंगरा as the indigenous Hindi name, which I return under discovered.

verdicts.name: भृङ्गराज
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib Ayurveda glossary, Bhṛṅgarāja (भृङ्गराज) = Eclipta alba / Eclipta prostrata, Caraka-saṃhitā and Suśruta-saṃhitā.
verdicts.reason: Same word as the entry above in Sanskrit conjunct orthography (ङ्ग). Correct for the species, but it is the Sanskrit spelling carried into a Hindi field, so not the preferred Hindi form.

verdicts.name: भृङ्गराजसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: Searched the Sanskrit lexica aggregated on wisdomlib (Apte, Monier-Williams, Śabda-Sāgara) and the Sanskrit list in 'Names of Plants in India'. The attested Sanskrit names are भृङ्गराजः, मार्कवः and केशराजः. No source gives भृङ्गराजसस्यम्. The '-सस्यम्' (crop/plant) suffix is a coined descriptive compound of the kind Wikidata labels generate, not a lexicon name.

verdicts.name: கரிசலாங்கண்ணி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon, Karicalāṅkaṇṇi (கரிசலாங்கண்ணி), glossed கையாந்தகரை (Vaittiya Malai Akarāti); CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names (via wisdomlib) identifies Karisalankanni with Eclipta alba and Eclipta prostrata.
verdicts.reason: Two independent naming authorities attest this Tamil name for this species. It is also the form in everyday Tamil use for bhringraj hair preparations.

verdicts.name: கீழா நெல்லி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': 'Kila-nelli [கீழாநெல்லி] in the Tamil language is the name of a plant identified with Phyllanthus fraternus G.L.Webster'; the same entry also maps it to Phyllanthus amarus. DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon gives Kīḻānelli = Phyllanthus niruri.
verdicts.reason: Attested for Phyllanthus fraternus by name, which is the one candidate here that matches the page's species exactly. The canonical spelling is கீழாநெல்லி as a single word; the space in the harvested form is an artifact. Worth noting the Tamil Lexicon's P. niruri gloss reflects the long-standing P. niruri / amarus / fraternus conflation rather than a different plant.

verdicts.name: भोजपत्र
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': 'Bhojapatra [भोजपत्र] … identified with Betula utilis D. Don … synonym Betula bhojpattra'; DDSA A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary: भोजपत्र = the bark of the birch tree (used to write on).
verdicts.reason: The species is right and the name is the one Hindi speakers use. The Betula utilis synonym 'Betula bhojpattra' is itself derived from this name. Strictly the word denotes the bark/leaf as much as the tree, which is how the Hindi dictionary glosses it; that is a nuance, not an error. Note the Wisdom Library biology entry tags the form as Nepali as well as Hindi.

verdicts.name: लेमन ग्रास
verdicts.reason: Retrieved the Hindi name for Cymbopogon citratus from Flowers of India: गंधत्रिण (Gandhatrina); Sanskrit भूस्तृण. 'लेमन ग्रास' is a Devanagari transliteration of the English 'lemon grass' and appears in no naming authority I checked (Flowers of India, wisdomlib lexica). It is real commercial usage, so a reader would recognise it, but nothing attests it as an Indic name for the species.

verdicts.name: நரந்தம் புல்
verdicts.reason: DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon gives நரந்தம் (Narantam) as (1) musk deer, (2) 'bitter orange, see நாரத்தை', (3) crow, with a fragrant-grass sense in the Pattuppāṭṭu that is not tied to any species. Flowers of India gives the Tamil for Cymbopogon citratus as கர்ப்பூரப்புல். The only places I found 'narandham' attached to lemongrass were nursery and trade listings, which are not naming authorities. The name is too ambiguous to confirm, and its clearest lexical sense (via நாரத்தை) points at Citrus aurantium rather than a grass, so leaving it on the page would be actively misleading.

verdicts.name: बहेड़ा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'Names of Plants in India' list for Terminalia bellirica (indiantreepix mirror): Hindi बहेड़ा (bahera), बहुवीर्य, भूतवास, कल्क, कर्षफल.
verdicts.reason: Standard, well-attested Hindi name for this species and the form a Hindi speaker would use or search. Corroborated indirectly by the Bengali বহেড়া and Gujarati બહેડા in the same list.

verdicts.name: बिभीतकीवृक्षः
verdicts.reason: The Sanskrit names attested for Terminalia bellirica are बिभीतकः, विभीतकः, अक्षः, कर्षः, कासघ्नः and बहुवीर्य ('Names of Plants in India'; wisdomlib: Bibhītaka = Terminalia bellirica per the 7th-century Mādhavacikitsā Jvaracikitsā and 'Essentials of Ayurveda'). बिभीतकीवृक्षः ('the bibhītakī tree') is a coined descriptive compound with वृक्षः appended and is in no lexicon. The stem is right, the name as given is not attested.

verdicts.name: தான்றி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'Names of Plants in India' list for Terminalia bellirica: Tamil தான்றி (tanri); corroborated by Malayalam താന്നി (thaanni) in the same list and by the Kerala State Medicinal Plants Board page 'Terminalia bellirica, Thanni'.
verdicts.reason: Attested Tamil name for this species, the base of the common market form தான்றிக்காய்.

verdicts.name: नागरङ्गफलम्
verdicts.denotesInstead: Citrus aurantium (bitter/Seville orange)
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte (DDSA Practical Sanskrit-English): 'Nāgaraṅga (नागरङ्ग).—the orange'; Śabda-Sāgara: 'The orange; in India usually applied to the Sylhet orange, (Citrus aurantium)'; Monier-Williams: 'an orange-tree'; Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': Nagaranga [नागरंगा] Sanskrit = Citrus aurantium L.
verdicts.reason: This is a genuine Sanskrit plant name, but for the wrong species. Every lexicon I retrieved assigns नागरङ्ग to the orange (Citrus aurantium / C. sinensis), not to the citron. The Sanskrit for Citrus medica is बीजपूर (Apte: 'the citron tree'; Bhojanakutūhala, 17th c.) and मातुलुङ्ग (Apte: 'a kind of citron tree'). Leaving नागरङ्गफलम् on a Citrus medica monograph would put the orange's name on the citron.

verdicts.name: நாரத்தம்பழம்
verdicts.denotesInstead: Citrus aurantium (orange / Seville orange) in the University of Madras Tamil Lexicon
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon, Nārattai (நாரத்தை): '1. Orange, Citrus aurantium; 2. Seville orange; 3. Loose-skinned orange, Citrus Aurantium-nobilis; 4. Indian wild-lime'. 'Names of Plants in India' gives the Tamil for Citrus medica as கொம்மட்டிமாதுளை, மாதுலங்கம், பீதபூரம், பேரெலுமிச்சை.
verdicts.reason: The நாரத்தை family of names is a floating Citrus label: CRC World Dictionary (via wisdomlib) attaches 'Narattai' to Atalantia monophylla, Citrus aurantifolia, Citrus aurantium AND Citrus medica, while the Tamil Lexicon, the stronger authority, lists only oranges and wild lime. Modern Tamil Nadu pickle usage (நார்த்தங்காய்) does sometimes mean citron, which is exactly why this name cannot be presented as the Tamil for Citrus medica without misleading. Not confirmed; the lexicon's primary referent is a different species.

verdicts.name: बिल्व
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary (via wisdomlib): 'Bilva (बिल्व):—(nm) the wood-apple— Aegle marmelos'; also 'Vilva (विल्व) … wood-apple tree and its fruit — Aegle marmelos'.
verdicts.reason: A Hindi dictionary attests the form for this species directly. It is the learned/Sanskritic form in Hindi rather than the everyday one, so not marked preferred.

verdicts.name: बेल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary (via wisdomlib): 'Bela (बेल) [Also spelled bel]:—(nm) wood-apple— Aegle marmelos; -[patra] leaves of wood-apple'.
verdicts.reason: The everyday Hindi name for this species, attested in a Hindi dictionary, and the form a speaker would use or search. Caution noted: बेला (with the final vowel) is a jasmine (Jasminum sambac) in the same dictionary, and Kannada ಬೇಲ is Limonia acidissima — but बेल itself is correct here.

verdicts.name: बेल फल
verdicts.reason: No naming authority lists 'बेल फल' as a name; it is the Hindi word for the fruit assembled from बेल + फल, and the space is a harvest artifact. The attested Sanskrit for the fruit is बिल्वफल (wisdomlib, from the 17th-century Bhojanakutūhala). Correct species, but a descriptive phrase rather than a name.

verdicts.name: श्री फल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte (DDSA Practical Sanskrit-English): 'Śrīphala (श्रीफल).—the Bilva tree. (-lam) the Bilva fruit'; Śabda-Sāgara: 'A fruit tree, (Ægle marmelos)'; Wisdom Library biology entry: 'Shriphala in India is the name of a plant defined with Aegle marmelos'.
verdicts.reason: A genuine attested name for this species, but with two caveats a reader needs: the correct orthography is श्रीफल as one word (the space is a harvest artifact), and Apte also glosses श्रीफल as 'a cocoanut', which is the dominant everyday Hindi sense. Confirmed for the species, not preferred.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa (peepal / bodhi tree)
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for Aśvattha: Monier-Williams and the Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries give 'the holy fig tree, Ficus religiosa'; the Caraka-saṃhitā and the 15th-century Yogasārasaṅgraha identify अश्वत्थ as Ficus religiosa Linn. (Moraceae); Rāja Nighaṇṭu associates it with the Puṣya nakṣatra.
verdicts.reason: This is the seeded Wikidata error. अश्वत्थ is unambiguously Ficus religiosa in every Sanskrit lexicon and classical Ayurvedic source I retrieved, and Ficus religiosa is in a different family (Moraceae) from Aegle marmelos (Rutaceae). It must be dropped from this page.

verdicts.name: बिल्वः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte (DDSA Practical Sanskrit-English) s.v. Vilva/Bilva: 'A species of tree, Aegle Marmelos or wood-apple; its leaves are used in the worship of Śiva… Derivable forms: bilvaḥ (बिल्वः)'; wisdomlib Ayurveda glossary: 'Bilva (बिल्व) is a Sanskrit word referring Aegle marmelos', part of the Śākavarga in Caraka-saṃhitā sūtrasthāna 27.
verdicts.reason: The core Sanskrit name for this species, attested in both lexicon and classical Ayurvedic text, in exactly the masculine nominative form given.

verdicts.name: बिल्वम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte s.v. Vilva/Bilva: '-lvam 1 The fruit of this tree', quoting Bhāvaprakāśa: बिल्वं बालं कषायोष्णं पाचनं वह्निदीपनम् । संग्राहि तिक्तकटुकं तीक्ष्णं वातकफापहम् ॥
verdicts.reason: Attested neuter form denoting the bael fruit, quoted in the Bhāvaprakāśa dravya verse. Correct for this species; the tree name proper is बिल्वः, so not preferred.

verdicts.name: வில்வம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon, Vilvam (வில்வம்): '1. Bael, medium tree Aegle marmelos' (Patārtta Kuṇa Cintāmaṇi 448); Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': 'Vilvam in the Tamil language is the name of a plant identified with Aegle marmelos (L.) Correa'.
verdicts.reason: Two independent authorities attest it for this species, and it is the form a Tamil speaker would use. The Lexicon's second sense (a garlic-pear species, பெரியமாவிலிங்கம்) is secondary and does not displace the primary bael reading.

verdicts.name: बिल्व
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary: 'Bilva (बिल्व):—(nm) the wood-apple— Aegle marmelos'.
verdicts.reason: Attested Hindi form for this species. Learned/Sanskritic rather than the everyday Hindi form, so not preferred.

verdicts.name: बेल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary: 'Bela (बेल) [Also spelled bel]:—(nm) wood-apple— Aegle marmelos'.
verdicts.reason: Everyday Hindi name for this species, dictionary-attested, and the search form. Relevant to this page since bilva majja is the fruit pulp (बेल का गूदा).

verdicts.name: बेल फल
verdicts.reason: Not listed as a name in any authority; a descriptive phrase (बेल + फल) with a harvest-artifact space. The attested Sanskrit name for the fruit is बिल्वफल (Bhojanakutūhala, 17th c., via wisdomlib). Correct species, not a name.

verdicts.name: श्री फल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte: 'Śrīphala (श्रीफल).—the Bilva tree. (-lam) the Bilva fruit'; Śabda-Sāgara: 'A fruit tree, (Ægle marmelos)'.
verdicts.reason: Genuine attested name for this species; Apte's neuter gloss 'the Bilva fruit' is directly apt for a majja (fruit-pulp) page. Two caveats: correct orthography is श्रीफल as one word, and Apte also glosses श्रीफल as 'a cocoanut', which is the dominant everyday Hindi sense.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa (peepal / bodhi tree)
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for Aśvattha: Monier-Williams / Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries 'the holy fig tree, Ficus religiosa'; Caraka-saṃhitā and the 15th-century Yogasārasaṅgraha identify अश्वत्थ as Ficus religiosa Linn.
verdicts.reason: The seeded Wikidata error, repeated on this page. अश्वत्थ is Ficus religiosa (Moraceae), not Aegle marmelos (Rutaceae). Drop it.

verdicts.name: बिल्वः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte s.v. Vilva/Bilva: 'A species of tree, Aegle Marmelos or wood-apple… Derivable forms: bilvaḥ (बिल्वः)'; wisdomlib Ayurveda glossary, Bilva = Aegle marmelos, Śākavarga of Caraka-saṃhitā sūtrasthāna 27.
verdicts.reason: Core Sanskrit name for this species in exactly this form, attested in lexicon and classical text.

verdicts.name: बिल्वम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte s.v. Vilva/Bilva: '-lvam 1 The fruit of this tree', quoting Bhāvaprakāśa बिल्वं बालं कषायोष्णं पाचनं वह्निदीपनम्…
verdicts.reason: Attested neuter form for the bael fruit, which is precisely what this page's drug (bilva majja, the pulp) is taken from. Not preferred only because बिल्वः is the tree name proper.

verdicts.name: வில்வம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon, Vilvam (வில்வம்) = 'Bael, medium tree Aegle marmelos'; Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs', Vilvam (Tamil) = Aegle marmelos (L.) Correa.
verdicts.reason: Attested for this species by two independent authorities and the ordinary Tamil form.

verdicts.name: बिल्व
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary: 'Bilva (बिल्व):—(nm) the wood-apple— Aegle marmelos'; same entry under Vilva: '~[patra] leaves of the wood apple tree'.
verdicts.reason: Attested Hindi form for this species, and the dictionary explicitly records the leaf compound विल्वपत्र/बिल्वपत्र, which is this page's drug. Learned form, so not preferred over बेल.

verdicts.name: बेल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary: 'Bela (बेल) [Also spelled bel]:—(nm) wood-apple— Aegle marmelos; -[patra] leaves of wood-apple'.
verdicts.reason: Everyday Hindi name for this species, dictionary-attested, with the leaf compound बेलपत्र recorded in the same entry. The form a Hindi speaker would use or search.

verdicts.name: बेल फल
verdicts.reason: Not a name in any authority; a descriptive phrase for the fruit, with a harvest-artifact space. It is also the wrong plant part for a patra (leaf) page. The attested Hindi leaf compound is बेलपत्र (DDSA A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary).

verdicts.name: श्री फल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte: 'Śrīphala (श्रीफल).—the Bilva tree. (-lam) the Bilva fruit'; Śabda-Sāgara: 'A fruit tree, (Ægle marmelos)'.
verdicts.reason: Genuine attested name for the species. Caveats: the correct orthography is श्रीफल as one word, Apte also glosses it as 'a cocoanut' (the dominant everyday Hindi sense), and it names the fruit, not the leaf this page covers.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa (peepal / bodhi tree)
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for Aśvattha: Monier-Williams / Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries 'the holy fig tree, Ficus religiosa'; Caraka-saṃhitā and Yogasārasaṅgraha (15th c.) identify अश्वत्थ as Ficus religiosa Linn.
verdicts.reason: The seeded Wikidata error, third occurrence on an Aegle marmelos page. Especially dangerous here: both Ficus religiosa leaves and bilva leaves are ritual offerings, so an aśvattha gloss on a bilva-patra page would read plausibly and still be wrong. Drop it.

verdicts.name: बिल्वः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte s.v. Vilva/Bilva: 'A species of tree, Aegle Marmelos or wood-apple; its leaves are used in the worship of Śiva… Derivable forms: bilvaḥ (बिल्वः)'; wisdomlib Ayurveda glossary, Bilva = Aegle marmelos (Caraka-saṃhitā sūtrasthāna 27).
verdicts.reason: Core Sanskrit name for the species, and Apte's gloss explicitly mentions the leaves used in Śiva worship, which is this page's subject.

verdicts.name: बिल्वम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte s.v. Vilva/Bilva: '-lvam 1 The fruit of this tree', quoting Bhāvaprakāśa बिल्वं बालं कषायोष्णं…
verdicts.reason: Attested neuter form for this species, though it denotes the fruit rather than the leaf. Correct name, secondary to बिल्वः, and the attested leaf compound is बिल्वपत्र.

verdicts.name: வில்வம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon, Vilvam (வில்வம்) = 'Bael, medium tree Aegle marmelos'; Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs', Vilvam (Tamil) = Aegle marmelos (L.) Correa.
verdicts.reason: Attested for this species by two independent authorities; the ordinary Tamil form, familiar from வில்வ இலை in Śaiva ritual.

verdicts.name: कुंदुरी
verdicts.reason: The attested Hindi name is कुन्द्रू / कुंदरू, not कुंदुरी: Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs' gives 'Kundru [कुन्द्रू] in the Hindi language … identified with Coccinia grandis (L.) Voigt'; Flowers of India gives Hindi कुन्द्रू; and the 13th-century Rāja Nighaṇṭu entry for Tiktatuṇḍī (verse 3.64-65, via wisdomlib) says it is 'commonly known in Hindi as Kundarū'. No source attests the spelling कुंदुरी. Flagging a real hazard rather than a verdict: the near-homograph कुन्दुरु is, per Monier-Williams and Śabda-Sāgara, Boswellia thurifera / Boswellia serrata and its resin (olibanum, frankincense; cited to Varāhamihira's Bṛhat-saṃhitā lvii.5), so a reader meeting कुंदुरी on this page can easily land on the wrong plant. I have not set denotesInstead because the spellings differ and the intended referent here is plausibly Coccinia.

verdicts.name: बिम्बफलम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Apte and Monier-Williams (via wisdomlib): 'Bimbaphala (बिम्बफल) — the Bimba fruit' (Kumārasambhava 3, Bhartṛhari); Monier-Williams: 'Bimbī … Momordica Monadelpha, [Suśruta]' (Momordica monadelpha is a synonym of Coccinia grandis); Rāja Nighaṇṭu 3.64-65 gives बिम्बी as a synonym of तिक्ततुण्डी = Coccinia indica; Alar Kannada-English corpus: ಬಿಂಬಫಲ = 'the edible fruit of the vine Coccinia cordifolia (= C. indica, = Bryonia grandis, = Momordica monadelpha)'.
verdicts.reason: The बिम्ब / बिम्बी name group is securely attested for this species in both Sanskrit lexica and the Rāja Nighaṇṭu, and the Kannada entry attaches बिंबफल specifically to the Coccinia fruit. Confirmed, but not marked preferred: the plant name proper in Sanskrit is बिम्बी, which I return under discovered, and बिम्बफलम् names the fruit.

verdicts.name: கொவ்வை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon, Kovvai (கொவ்வை): 'A common creeper of the hedges, Coccinia indica; கொவ்வைக்கொடி'; CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names (via wisdomlib): 'Kovvai in India is the name of a plant defined with Coccinia cordifolia'.
verdicts.reason: Attested for this species by the Tamil Lexicon and a second independent dictionary. Coccinia indica and C. cordifolia are both synonyms of Coccinia grandis. The variant கோவை appears in Flowers of India; கொவ்வை is the Lexicon headword and the form a Tamil speaker would use.

verdicts.name: करेला
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Bitter Gourd page (Momordica charantia): 'Hindi: करेला Karela, कठिल्ल kathilla, परारु poraru', alongside Gujarati કારેલું, Bengali করলা, Urdu کريلا.
verdicts.reason: Universally attested Hindi name for this species and the obvious search form.

verdicts.name: कारवेल्लम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Śabda-Sāgara (via wisdomlib): 'Kāravella (कारवेल्ल).—m. A kind of gourd, (Momordica charantia)'; Apte: 'Kāravella — Name of a bitter vegetable… See also kāravellaka'; wisdomlib Ayurveda: 'Kāravellaka (कारवेल्लक) or Kareli — Momordica charantia', from the 17th-century Vaidyavallabha of Hastiruci; Flowers of India gives Sanskrit कारवेल्लकः.
verdicts.reason: The name कारवेल्ल / कारवेल्लक is attested for this exact species in two Sanskrit lexica and a 17th-century Ayurvedic work. The harvested form कारवेल्लम् is the neuter of that attested name (the lexica cite कारवेल्लः and कारवेल्लकः), an inflectional variant rather than a coinage, so I confirm it. This is unlike बिभीतकीवृक्षः on the bibhitaki page, where a whole extra word was appended.

verdicts.name: பாகல்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon, Pākal (பாகல்): 'balsam-pear, a climber, Momordica charantia' (cf. Kannada hāgal, Malayalam pāval); Flowers of India gives Tamil பாகற்காய் for the fruit.
verdicts.reason: The Tamil Lexicon attests பாகல் for this species as the plant name, with பாகற்காய் the fruit form used in markets. Correct and the natural base form.

verdicts.name: करेला
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Bitter Gourd page (Momordica charantia): 'Hindi: करेला Karela, कठिल्ल kathilla, परारु poraru'.
verdicts.reason: Universally attested Hindi name for this species and the obvious search form. Same species as the bitter-gourd page, so the same verdict holds.

verdicts.name: कारवेल्लम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Śabda-Sāgara: 'Kāravella (कारवेल्ल).—m. A kind of gourd, (Momordica charantia)'; wisdomlib Ayurveda: 'Kāravellaka (कारवेल्लक) or Kareli — Momordica charantia', 17th-century Vaidyavallabha; Flowers of India: Sanskrit कारवेल्लकः.
verdicts.reason: Attested for this species in Sanskrit lexica and a 17th-century Ayurvedic text; the harvested कारवेल्लम् is the neuter inflection of that attested name, not a coinage.

verdicts.name: பாகல்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: DDSA: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon, Pākal (பாகல்): 'balsam-pear, a climber, Momordica charantia'.
verdicts.reason: Tamil Lexicon attests பாகல் for this species as the plant (rather than fruit) name, which suits a page about the herb.

verdicts.name: ब्रम्हमाण्डुकी
verdicts.denotesInstead: Centella asiatica (mandukaparni / gotu kola)
verdicts.corroboratingSource: SDM Ayurveda College (Hassan) Dravyaguna Vigyan monograph on Mandukaparni (sdach.ac.in): Sanskrit synonyms 'Manduukaparni, Manduukaparnikaa, Maanduuki, Saraswati, Brahma-manduuk', Hindi 'Bramhmamnduki, bemgsag', Tamil 'Vallarai', botanical name Centella asiatica.
verdicts.reason: A second genuine misidentification in this batch. ब्रह्ममण्डूकी / ब्रह्ममण्डूक belongs to the मण्डूकपर्णी group, which is Centella asiatica (Apiaceae), not Bacopa monnieri (Plantaginaceae). The confusion is old and well documented: 'brahmi' was conflated with mandukaparni from about the 16th century, which is exactly why a mandukaparni-derived name must not sit on a Bacopa page. None of the Hindi lists I retrieved for Bacopa ('Names of Plants in India': बाम, ब्राह्मी, जलबूटी, जलनीम, नीरब्राह्मी, सफेद चमनी) contains it.

verdicts.name: ब्राम्हीभेद
verdicts.reason: 'brāhmī-bheda' means 'a variety/kind of brahmi'. It is a disambiguating description, not a name, and it appears in none of the Hindi lists I retrieved for Bacopa monnieri ('Names of Plants in India' and Flowers of India: बाम, ब्राह्मी, जलबूटी, जलनीम, नीरब्राह्मी, सफेद चमनी) nor in the DDSA Hindi dictionary. Unattested, and the '-भेद' suffix is characteristic of label-generation rather than vernacular naming.

verdicts.name: ब्राह्मी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs': 'Brahmi [ब्राह्यी] in the Hindi [language] … identified with Bacopa monnieri (L.) Wettst.'; 'Names of Plants in India' Hindi list for Bacopa monnieri includes ब्राह्मी; DDSA A Practical Hindi-English Dictionary: 'Brāhmī (ब्राह्मी):—(nf) a medicinal plant'.
verdicts.reason: Attested in Hindi for this species and the form a Hindi speaker would use or search. One caveat to carry on the page: in north and west India ब्राह्मी is frequently applied to Centella asiatica instead, which is why the species-specific qualifiers जलब्राह्मी / नीरब्राह्मी exist. Correct here, but genuinely polysemous.

verdicts.name: ब्राह्मी जड़ी बूटी
verdicts.reason: Literally 'brahmi, the herb'. A description with a category word appended, not a name; absent from every Hindi list I retrieved ('Names of Plants in India', Flowers of India) and from the DDSA Hindi dictionary. The same label-generation pattern as 'गाँजे का पौधा' on the bhanga page.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa (peepal / bodhi tree)
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for Aśvattha: Monier-Williams / Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries 'the holy fig tree, Ficus religiosa'; Caraka-saṃhitā and Yogasārasaṅgraha identify अश्वत्थ as Ficus religiosa Linn. (Moraceae); Bhagavad-Gītā 15.1.
verdicts.reason: The seeded Wikidata error again, here on a Bacopa page. अश्वत्थ is a large fig tree; Bacopa monnieri is a creeping aquatic herb. Nothing connects them. Drop it.

verdicts.name: ब्राह्मी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'Names of Plants in India' Sanskrit list for Bacopa monnieri (Wayback capture 2020-11-04): ब्राह्मी brahmi, तिक्तलोणिका tiktalonika; corroborated by Flowers of India's Brahmi page (same Sanskrit pair) and Apte: 'Brahmī (ब्रह्मी) — Name of a medicinal plant'.
verdicts.reason: The standard Sanskrit drug name for this species, attested by two independent compilations. Caveat as above: in parts of India ब्राह्मी is applied to Centella asiatica, so the identification is traditionally contested even though it is correct for this page.

verdicts.name: நீர்ப்பிரமி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'Names of Plants in India' Tamil list for Bacopa monnieri: நீர்ப்பிரமி nir-p-pirami, பிரமி pirami, பிரமியம் piramiyam, தராய் taray; Flowers of India's Brahmi page gives the same Tamil set.
verdicts.reason: Attested for this species by two independent compilations. The நீர்- ('water') qualifier is precisely what distinguishes Bacopa from the Centella sense of brahmi, which makes this the most useful and least ambiguous Tamil form.

verdicts.name: चंदन
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'Names of Plants in India' Hindi list for Santalum album (Wayback capture 2021-11-06): चन्दन chandan, संदल sandal; Flowers of India's Sandalwood page carries the same vernacular set.
verdicts.reason: Attested Hindi name for this species; चंदन is the ordinary anusvāra orthography and the form a Hindi speaker would type, so it takes preferred over the conjunct spelling.

verdicts.name: चन्दन
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'Names of Plants in India' Hindi list for Santalum album: चन्दन chandan (exact form), संदल sandal.
verdicts.reason: The same word in conjunct orthography, and the exact string the source prints. Correct for the species; not preferred only because चंदन is the commoner Hindi spelling.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa (peepal / bodhi tree)
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for Aśvattha: Monier-Williams / Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries 'the holy fig tree, Ficus religiosa'; Caraka-saṃhitā and the 15th-century Yogasārasaṅgraha identify अश्वत्थ as Ficus religiosa Linn.
verdicts.reason: The seeded Wikidata error, fourth occurrence in this batch. अश्वत्थ is Ficus religiosa (Moraceae); Santalum album is Santalaceae. The extensive Sanskrit synonym list for sandalwood in 'Names of Plants in India' (चन्दनम्, श्रीखण्ड, गन्धसार, मलयज, पटीर, हरिगन्ध and many more) contains nothing of the sort. Drop it.

verdicts.name: चन्दनम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'Names of Plants in India' Sanskrit entry for Santalum album: चन्दनम् chandanam, with a further synonym list including श्रीखण्ड, गन्धसार, मलयज, पटीर, हरिगन्ध, चन्द्रद्युति, पीतसार.
verdicts.reason: The primary Sanskrit name for this species, in exactly the neuter form given, and the etymon of the Hindi, Tamil, Malayalam and Odia names in the same list. The page slug itself derives from it.

verdicts.name: श्रीगन्धः
verdicts.reason: Not a species error but a language error, which would still mislead a reader. श्रीगंध / ಶ್ರೀಗಂಧ is Kannada (also Konkani and Tulu): 'Names of Plants in India' lists Kannada ಶ್ರೀಗಂಧ srigandha, Konkani श्रीगंध shrigandh, Tulu ಶ್ರೀಗ೦ಧ, Telugu శ్రీగంధం under Santalum album, while its Sanskrit entry is चन्दनम् plus a long synonym list that does not include श्रीगन्ध. Wisdom Library 'Local Names of Plants and Drugs' likewise files 'Srigandha [ಶ್ರೀಗಂಧ]' as Kannada for Santalum album. The Sanskrit counterpart is श्रीखण्ड (Śabda-Sāgara and Benfey, via wisdomlib: 'Śrīkhaṇḍa — sandal-wood or the sandal-tree'). Right plant, wrong language label.

verdicts.name: சந்தனம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: 'Names of Plants in India' Tamil entry for Santalum album: சந்தனம் chandanam; Flowers of India's Sandalwood page gives the same.
verdicts.reason: Attested for this species by two independent compilations and the only Tamil form in ordinary use.

verdicts.name: ஆளி விரை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry 'Ali-virai, Āḷivirai (ஆளிவிரை)' identifies it with Lepidium sativum, citing CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names (regional names) and the DDSA University of Madras Tamil Lexicon; Flowers of India and 'Names of Plants in India' give Tamil ஆளி (Ali) for Lepidium sativum, with Sanskrit चन्द्रशूर and रक्तराजी.
verdicts.reason: Attested for this species, and the ஆளி stem is independently confirmed as the Tamil for garden cress. Two cautions for the page: the canonical spelling is ஆளிவிரை as one word (the space is a harvest artifact), and the near-homograph ஆளிவிதை (āḷi vidhai) is flax/linseed, Linum usitatissimum, a different family. The names are separated only by விரை vs விதை, so the entry is worth spelling carefully.

verdicts.name: चांगेरी
