verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND "Sorting Phoenix names" gives Tamil "Karchuram, Perichchankay" for Phoenix dactylifera, and separately "Inchi, Itcham pannai" for Phoenix sylvestris — so the pērīcc- stem is assigned to P. dactylifera specifically.
verdicts.reason: MMPND attests Perichchankay (பேரீச்சங்காய்) for this species and not for P. sylvestris; பேரீச்சை is the base form of that name and is what a Tamil speaker uses and searches. Note that efloraofindia, Flowers of India and Herbarium JCB all omit Tamil for this species, so MMPND is the single per-species attestation; the fruit forms பேரீச்சம்பழம் / பேரீச்சங்காய் are the ones that appear in trade.

verdicts.name: गोकुलकांता
verdicts.reason: The name is real but the Devanagari here is wrong. efloraofindia's Hygrophila auriculata page gives Hindi गोकुलकाँटा (gokulkanta) — काँटा meaning "thorn", which is what the plant is named for. The candidate गोकुलकांता reads gokulakāntā (कांता = "beloved"), a different word; it is an orthographic corruption, and Flowers of India's Marsh Barbel page does not list the name at all. Publish गोकुलकाँटा instead (in discovered), or better तालमखाना.

verdicts.name: நீர்முள்ளி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India / "Names of Plants in India" Marsh Barbel (Hygrophila auriculata) page gives Tamil "நீர்முள்ளி nir-mulli"; efloraofindia's page for the same species independently gives நீர்முள்ளி.
verdicts.reason: Two independent per-species compilations give நீர்முள்ளி in Tamil script for Hygrophila auriculata, and it is the name used in Siddha practice and in the seed trade (neermulli vithai). Preferred for Tamil.

verdicts.name: तोरई
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND "Sorting Luffa names" lists for Luffa acutangula, Hindi: "Peerkankai, Jhinga torooee, Jhingli torai, Kali, Torai (Torooee), Turai, Hireballi."
verdicts.reason: MMPND attests Torai/Turai for Luffa acutangula specifically, and तोरई/तुरई is the standard Hindi name for the ridge gourd, so preferred. Two caveats worth keeping: efloraofindia's L. acutangula page covers the bitter wild form and gives Hindi कड़वी तुरई / कड़वी तोरी and Sanskrit तिक्त कोषातकी, and in parts of north India तोरई is loosely extended to Luffa aegyptiaca (sponge gourd), which is नेनुआ / घिया तोरी proper.

verdicts.name: कचनार
verdicts.denotesInstead: Bauhinia variegata
verdicts.reason: This is the error type you flagged. efloraofindia's Bauhinia variegata page gives Hindi "कचनार kachnar, कचनाल kachnal" — bare कचनार is B. variegata, the common kachnar of markets and of the Ayurvedic drug Kanchanara. For Bauhinia purpurea, efloraofindia and IMPPAT give Hindi कांचन (kanchan), लाल कचनार (lal kachnar) and केवनार (kevnar): the purple species is distinguished by the qualifier लाल/रक्त. Putting unqualified कचनार on a B. purpurea page asserts the wrong species.

verdicts.name: कोविदार
verdicts.denotesInstead: Bauhinia variegata
verdicts.reason: Two faults. (1) Species: efloraofindia lists कोविदार / कोविदारः among the Sanskrit names of Bauhinia variegata (alongside काञ्चनार kanchanara), while for Bauhinia purpurea it and IMPPAT give Sanskrit रक्तकोविदार (rakta-kovidara) and रक्तकांचन — the purple species carries the रक्त qualifier, so bare कोविदार points at B. variegata. (2) Language: कोविदार is a Sanskrit term (efloraofindia also records it as Marathi), not a Hindi vernacular name, so the hi label is wrong even where the word is right. If the monograph is to stay on B. purpurea, the defensible Sanskrit form is रक्तकोविदार.

verdicts.name: மந்தாரை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia's Bauhinia purpurea page gives Tamil "மந்தாரை (mandarai), நீலத்திருவத்தி (nilattiruvatti)"; IMPPAT's Bauhinia purpurea record gives Tamil "mandarai".
verdicts.reason: Both sources attest மந்தாரை for Bauhinia purpurea and it is the ordinary Tamil name, so preferred. Caveat: the mandārai stem is applied across Bauhinia species (Malayalam chovanna-mandaru = "red mandaru" for B. purpurea, Kannada kempu mandaara), so it is correct but genus-level rather than species-exclusive.

verdicts.name: कटीली चौलाई
verdicts.reason: Wrong-language attribution. Flowers of India / "Names of Plants in India" for Amaranthus spinosus gives Hindi as "कांटा चौलाई Kanta Chaulai" only; the form the candidate reproduces appears on that same page under other languages — Mishing "কাটাইলি চাউলাই Kataili-Chaulai" and Rajasthani "कंटेली चौलाई Kanteli Chaulai". efloraofindia likewise gives Hindi कांटा चौलाई. The species is right, the language label is not, and the Devanagari matches no Hindi attestation. Use कांटा चौलाई (in discovered).

verdicts.name: முள்ளுக்கீரை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India / "Names of Plants in India" Prickly Amaranth (Amaranthus spinosus) page gives Tamil "முள்ளுக்கீரை Mullu-K-Kirai, முட்கீரை Mut-Kirai"; efloraofindia gives the same two names for the species.
verdicts.reason: Two independent per-species compilations attest முள்ளுக்கீரை in Tamil script for Amaranthus spinosus, and it is the name used in Tamil Nadu greens markets. Preferred for Tamil.

verdicts.name: தருப்பைப்புல்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia's Desmostachya bipinnata page gives Tamil "darbhaipul, taruppai, acamantakam" — i.e. தர்ப்பைப்புல் and தருப்பை.
verdicts.reason: தருப்பைப்புல் is the attested name தருப்பை compounded with புல் ("grass"), and efloraofindia records both halves for this exact species, including the compound form romanised as darbhaipul. It is the form a Tamil speaker would use for the ritual grass, so preferred. Only one source attests it, so treat it as corroborated but not multiply attested.

verdicts.name: कुसुम
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India / "Names of Plants in India" Safflower page gives Hindi "कुसुम Kusum", Sanskrit "कुसुम्भ Kusumbh", Tamil "குஸும்ப Kusumba", Bengali কুসুম, Kannada ಕುಸುಬೆ.
verdicts.reason: कुसुम is attested in Devanagari for Carthamus tinctorius by a per-species compilation and is the standard Hindi name (kusum phool, kusum beej in the raw-herb trade), so preferred. Carry a homonym warning on the page: कुसुम in Hindi also denotes Schleichera oleosa, the kusum/lac tree whose seeds give kusum oil, and Indian raw-herb listings do conflate the two — the unambiguous safflower forms are कुसुम फूल / कुसुम्भ.

verdicts.name: होलीहेना प्यूब्सेन्स
verdicts.reason: Not a plant name in any language. This is the Latin binomial "Holarrhena pubescens" transliterated into Devanagari — exactly the Wikidata/Wikipedia label artefact you warned about. No source gives it as a Hindi vernacular name. Flowers of India (Tellicherry Tree) and efloraofindia give Hindi as कुटज (kutaja), कुर्ची (kurchi) and कडवा इंद्रजव (karva indrajau). Drop it and use those.

verdicts.name: குடசப்பாலை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India / "Names of Plants in India" Tellicherry Tree (Holarrhena pubescens) page and efloraofindia's page for the species both give Tamil "குடசப்பாலை (kutaca-p-palai)" along with கிரிமல்லிகை (kirimallikai) and மலைமல்லிகை (malaimallikai).
verdicts.reason: குடசப்பாலை is attested in Tamil script for Holarrhena pubescens by two independent per-species compilations, where it is the lead Tamil name, so marked preferred. Note it is a Sanskrit-derived form (kuṭaja + pālai) rather than a purely native coinage, and Tamil Siddha writing also uses வெட்பாலை for this bark, which I did not corroborate in a named botanical source this pass.

verdicts.name: छुइमुइ पौधा
verdicts.reason: Article-title artefact, not a name. efloraofindia's Mimosa pudica page gives Hindi "छुई-मुई chui-mui, लाजवंती lajwanti, lajouni". The candidate appends पौधा ("plant"), which is the Hindi Wikipedia headword convention, not part of the vernacular name, and spells the name छुइमुइ rather than छुई-मुई. The species is right; the string is not a name a reference should print. Use छुई-मुई or लाजवंती (in discovered).

verdicts.name: लज्जालुसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: A Sanskrit Wikipedia coinage, not an attested name. efloraofindia's Mimosa pudica page gives Sanskrit "khadiraka, lajjalu, namaskaar, namaskaari, raktapaadi, samangaa, shamipatra". लज्जालुसस्यम् is लज्जालु + सस्यम् ("the bashful plant"), a descriptive compound built to serve as an article title; no pharmacopoeial or botanical source gives it. The attested Sanskrit/Ayurvedic drug name is लज्जालुः, which is already this page's own slug.

verdicts.name: தொட்டாற் சுருங்கி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia's Mimosa pudica page gives Tamil "தொட்டாச்சுருங்கி thottaccurungi, tottalavaadi"; Siddha pharmacology reviews and the Tamil raw-herb trade give "Thottal surungi" / "Thottal chinungi" and the Siddha formulation Thottalvadi Chooranam for Mimosa pudica.
verdicts.reason: தொட்டாற்சுருங்கி ("shrinks when touched") is the attested Tamil/Siddha name for this species, recorded by efloraofindia in the variant தொட்டாச்சுருங்கி and by Siddha sources as thottal surungi. Preferred for Tamil. One fix before publishing: close up the stray space — write தொட்டாற்சுருங்கி as one word.

verdicts.name: बड़हल
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia's Artocarpus lacucha / lakoocha page gives Hindi "लकूचा (Lakoocha), लकूच (Lakooch), लकूची (Lakoochi), badahara, बढ़ल (Barhal), Dahu, Dahua"; Bengali Barhal, Marathi बढहर (Badhar).
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia attests the barhal/badahara name in Devanagari for this exact species; बड़हल is the standard Hindi spelling of it (the source shows the variant बढ़ल alongside the romanisation badahara). It is the name used for the fruit in north Indian markets, so preferred.

verdicts.name: एलियम सैटिवम
verdicts.reason: Not a plant name. This is the Latin binomial "Allium sativum" transliterated into Devanagari — the same label artefact as the Holarrhena case. Flowers of India's Garlic page gives Hindi "लहसुन Lahsun, लहसन Lahsan, लस्सन Lassan" and nothing resembling this. Drop it.

verdicts.name: लहसुन
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India / "Names of Plants in India" Garlic page gives Hindi "लहसुन Lahsun, लहसन Lahsan, लस्सन Lassan" and Tamil "பூண்டு Poondu" for Allium sativum; Biodiversity of India and India Flora Online (IISc) give the same Hindi forms.
verdicts.reason: Multiply attested in Devanagari for Allium sativum and the universal Hindi name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: लशुनम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India carries the monograph "Lasuna" (garlic bulb) for Allium sativum Linn.; Ayurveda360's Dravyaguna reference entry "Lashuna (लशुन) - Allium sativum" collates the classical Caraka/Suśruta citations under that name.
verdicts.reason: लशुन is the pharmacopoeial Sanskrit drug name for Allium sativum (API monograph Lasuna), and लशुनम् is its regular neuter nominative. Preferred for Sanskrit on this page since it matches the API monograph and the page slug. Note that Rasona (रसोन) is the other equally official Sanskrit name and appears in API as well, so both are correct.

verdicts.name: मुस्कदाना
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND "Sorting Abelmoschus names" gives for A. moschatus, Hindi: "Jangli bhenda, Latākastūri, मसक दाना Mushk daanaa"; efloraofindia's Abelmoschus moschatus page gives Hindi/Bengali/Gujarati "Muskdana".
verdicts.reason: The muskdana name is attested for Abelmoschus moschatus by two independent per-species sources, one of them in Devanagari, and it is the name the seed is sold under, so preferred. Spelling note: MMPND prints मसक दाना and the usual Hindi orthography is मुश्कदाना (from मुश्क, musk); मुस्कदाना is a sibilant variant of the same word, so correct the spelling if the page wants the standard form.

verdicts.name: கந்து கஸ்தூரி
verdicts.reason: Not attested by any botanical source. MMPND "Sorting Abelmoschus names", which draws on Tamil lexica, gives Tamil for A. moschatus as "காட்டுக்கஸ்தூரி Kāṭṭukkastūri, Kasturi vendaikkayvirai, Varttilaikasthuri, வெற்றிலைக்கஸ்தூரி Veṟṟilaikkastūri"; efloraofindia lists no Tamil name at all for the species. கந்துகஸ்தூரி turns up only in Tamil herb-glossary blogs and product listings, and கந்து is not a meaningful qualifier here — it looks like a corruption of the கஸ்தூரி compounds. Use காட்டுக்கஸ்தூரி or வெற்றிலைக்கஸ்தூரி (in discovered).

verdicts.name: कैसलपिनिया बंधु
verdicts.reason: Not a plant name. Devanagari transliteration of the Latin binomial "Caesalpinia bonduc". efloraofindia's Caesalpinia bonduc page gives Hindi गजगा, कलिंग, करंज, करंजवा, कटकरंज, मेंढल, नटा, पांशुल, पट्टिल, पूति, सागरगोटी — none of them this. Drop it.

verdicts.name: वरी पेड़ग्रे निकर
verdicts.reason: Not a plant name in Hindi. It is a garbled Devanagari transliteration of an English common-name string for this plant (the "grey nicker" / nicker-nut group of English names); "निकर" is English nicker and the preceding words are transliteration noise. No source gives it as a vernacular name. efloraofindia's Hindi list for Caesalpinia bonduc contains कटकरंज, सागरगोटी, करंजवा, नटा, गजगा etc. Drop it.

verdicts.name: सीसाल्पीनिया बोन्डुक्
verdicts.reason: Not Sanskrit and not a name. Devanagari transliteration of the Latin binomial "Caesalpinia bonduc". The attested Sanskrit name is लताकरञ्ज, which efloraofindia gives for this species and which is already this page's slug. Drop it.

verdicts.name: हिना
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Review literature on Lawsonia inermis (Plant Archives, "Pharmacological and traditional perspectives on Lawsonia inermis"; IJPSR "An update on Ayurvedic herb henna") records the Hindi/Urdu names as "Mehendi, Mehndi, Hinna" and the Sanskrit as Madayantika, Mendhika, Ragangi.
verdicts.reason: हिना is attested for Lawsonia inermis in named secondary literature on the species, and it is in live Hindi use in the cosmetic trade. Not preferred, and flagged for the page: the botanical compilations are more specific than the review papers — efloraofindia gives Hindi "Henna, Mehendi मेहेंदी" and assigns the hinna form to Urdu/Perso-Arabic. मेहंदी is the Hindi name a reader expects.

verdicts.name: மருதோன்றி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Tamil Heritage Foundation's plant CMS carries a page for Lawsonia inermis headed மருதோன்றி; the India Biodiversity Portal record for Lawsonia inermis lists Tamil names including maruthonri, maruthaani, alavam and aivanam.
verdicts.reason: மருதோன்றி is the classical Tamil/Siddha name for henna and is attested for this exact species by two sources independent of Wikidata. Not preferred: efloraofindia gives Tamil as மருதாணி (Marudaani), which is the everyday spoken and commercial form (maruthani powder, maruthani leaf) and the one a Tamil speaker would search.

verdicts.name: பறங்கி சாம்ராணி
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Boswellia serrata vernacular list gives the Tamil name as பறங்கிச்சாம்பிராணி (paranki-c-campirani), alongside குங்கிலியம், குமஞ்சம், மரத்துவெள்ளை. The underlying name (parangi sambrani) is therefore genuine for this species, but the candidate string drops the syllable -பி- (சாம்ராணி for சாம்பிராணி) and is not the attested orthography. Not confirmed as written; use பறங்கிச்சாம்பிராணி (in discovered).
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com species page for Boswellia serrata, vernacular names section: Tamil 'பறங்கிச்சாம்பிராணி paranki-c-campi-rani'

verdicts.name: கோங்கு
verdicts.denotesInstead: Cochlospermum religiosum (yellow silk cotton tree) — கோங்கு / கோங்கம்
verdicts.reason: This is the aśvattha-type error in this batch. Two independent sources list the Tamil names of Bombax ceiba and neither includes கோங்கு: efloraofindia gives Tamil இலவு (ilavu), முள்ளிலவு (mullilavu), பூலா (puulaa); India Flora Online (IISc) gives Tamil 'Ilavu, Purani'. Meanwhile கோங்கு is a real and well-documented Tamil tree name belonging to a different species: Tamil Wikipedia's கோங்கம் article and Sangam-literature commentary identify கோங்கம்/கோங்கு as Cochlospermum religiosum, the yellow silk cotton tree. The confusion is plausible (both are called 'silk cotton'), which is exactly why it would survive on a page. Drop it.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia (Bombax ceiba: Tamil இலவு, பூலா, முள்ளிலவு — no Kongu) and India Flora Online/IISc (Tamil: Ilavu, Purani); ta.wikipedia கோங்கம் = Cochlospermum religiosum

verdicts.name: शालपर्णी
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Desmodium gangeticum page lists Hindi शालपर्णी (shalparni) together with सालपानी (salpani), ध्रुवा, दीर्घमूली, पीवरी, and Sanskrit शालपर्णी / अंशुमती. Independently, a Desmodium gangeticum review (Int. J. research literature) lists Hindi 'Dhruva, Pivari, Shalparni'. शालपर्णी is also the form a Hindi speaker would search, so marked preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Desmodium gangeticum vernacular names: Hindi 'शालपर्णी shalparni', 'सालपानी salpani'

verdicts.name: மூவிலை
verdicts.denotesInstead: Pseudarthria viscida (Moovila / மூவிலை), the trifoliate Dasamula drug used in South India as a substitute for Shalaparni
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Desmodium gangeticum page gives only one Tamil name, புள்ளடி (pullati); Kerala SMPB's monograph gives Tamil/Malayalam Orila (ഓരില, 'one leaf'), which is the diagnostic name for D. gangeticum because its leaf is unifoliate. மூவிலை means 'three leaves' and is the established name of Pseudarthria viscida: wisdomlib's botanical definition of 'Moovila' resolves it to Pseudarthria viscida, Malayalam muvila, Tamil 'moovilai pachilai'. Literature on Dasamula adulteration treats Pseudarthria viscida (Moovila) explicitly as the South Indian substitute for Desmodium gangeticum (Orila), so some compilations do carry Moovilai under D. gangeticum — that is the substitution error propagating, not an independent attestation. Keep it off the page.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia (D. gangeticum Tamil: புள்ளடி only); smpbkerala.in monograph (Tamil Orila, Malayalam ഓരില); wisdomlib 'Moovila' = Pseudarthria viscida

verdicts.name: सनई
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Crotalaria juncea page lists Hindi सनई (sanai) along with सन (san), पटसन (patsan), जनब, बिछुआ, मातुलानी, and Sanskrit शण (shana), which is the source of the page slug. सनई is the ordinary Hindi name for sunn hemp, so preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Crotalaria juncea vernacular names: Hindi 'सनई sanai', 'सन san', 'पटसन patsan'

verdicts.name: கொழுஞ்சி
verdicts.reason: Tamil kolinji/kolunchi is attested for Tephrosia purpurea by the India Biodiversity Portal species page (Tamil: Kolinji, Kolinchi, Kattukkolincai, Kolunchi, Kavilai) and by the Institute of Ayurveda (Ayurvedic Plants of Sri Lanka) local-name record for Tephrosia purpurea. It is also the live Siddha/market name (sold as 'Kolinchi — common tephrosia'). efloraofindia lists different Tamil names for the same species (காவாளி, கொள்ளுக்காய்வேளை), which are additions rather than contradictions. Best-known Tamil form, so preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: India Biodiversity Portal, Tephrosia purpurea (indiabiodiversity.org/species/show/32797), Tamil common names incl. Kolinji/Kolunchi; corroborated by instituteofayurveda.org Tephrosia purpurea local names

verdicts.name: सतावर
verdicts.reason: The Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India monograph for Shatavari gives the Hindi names 'Satavar' and 'Satamul'. This is the official per-monograph vernacular, and सतावर is the form used in Hindi trade and by speakers, so preferred. (efloraofindia additionally gives शतावरी and शतमूली, listed in discovered.)
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus) monograph — Hindi: Satavar, Satamul

verdicts.name: शतावरीसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: No authoritative Sanskrit source attests this compound. efloraofindia's Asparagus racemosus page lists an extensive Sanskrit synonym set (शतावरी, शतमूली, शतमूलिका, नारायणी, बहुसुता, पीवरी, ऋष्यप्रोक्ता, द्वीपिशत्रु and dozens more) and शतावरीसस्यम् is not among them, nor does API use it. The form looks like a Sanskrit-Wikipedia descriptive coinage ('śatāvarī-sasyam' = the shatavari plant/crop) rather than a nighantu name. The correct Sanskrit is शतावरी.

verdicts.name: சாத்தாவாரி
verdicts.reason: Not found in any per-species authority I retrieved. efloraofindia's Tamil list for Asparagus racemosus is தண்ணீர்விட்டான், நீர்விட்டான், நீர்வல்லி, ஆழாடக்கிழங்கு, மதசாரணை and others; API's Tamil names for the Shatavari monograph are 'Shimai-shadavari' and 'Nilichedi kishangu' / 'Thanneervittan kizhangu'. The bare borrowed form சாத்தாவாரி with doubled -த்த- is the Tamil Wikipedia article title, i.e. Wikidata-mirroring, which the brief treats as a weak corroborator. Use தண்ணீர்விட்டான் கிழங்கு instead.

verdicts.name: सतावर
verdicts.reason: Same species as the Shatavari page (Asparagus racemosus). The API Shatavari monograph gives Hindi 'Satavar' and 'Satamul'; सतावर is the everyday Hindi form, so preferred. Note this page is a preparation (ksheera-paka), so the plant name is correct for the source drug rather than for the formulation itself.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India, Part I, Shatavari (Asparagus racemosus) monograph — Hindi: Satavar, Satamul

verdicts.name: शतावरीसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: Unattested, same finding as on the Shatavari page: efloraofindia's large Sanskrit synonym list for Asparagus racemosus (शतावरी, शतमूली, शतमूलिका, नारायणी, पीवरी, बहुसुता …) does not contain शतावरीसस्यम्, and API does not use it. It reads as a Sanskrit-Wikipedia coinage ('the shatavari plant'). Correct Sanskrit is शतावरी.

verdicts.name: சாத்தாவாரி
verdicts.reason: Unattested in per-species authorities: efloraofindia gives தண்ணீர்விட்டான் / நீர்விட்டான் / நீர்வல்லி etc. for Asparagus racemosus, and API's Tamil entries are Shimai-shadavari and Thanneervittan kizhangu. சாத்தாவாரி is the Tamil Wikipedia title (weak, Wikidata-mirroring). Not confirmed.

verdicts.name: कपूर कचरी
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Hedychium spicatum page gives Hindi कपूर कचरी (kapur kachri) along with संधार्लिका; a JAIMS review of Shati (Hedychium spicatum) independently lists Hindi 'Kapur kachri, Kachoor, Van haldi, Sitruti'. Kapur kachri is the standard trade and household Hindi name, so preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Hedychium spicatum: Hindi 'कपूर कचरी Kapur kachri'; Journal of Ayurveda and Integrated Medical Sciences, 'A Comprehensive Review of Shati (Hedychium spicatum)' — Hindi: Kapur kachri, Kachoor, Van haldi

verdicts.name: பூலங்கிழங்கு
verdicts.reason: The JAIMS review monograph on Shati (Hedychium spicatum) lists the Tamil names as Poolakizhangu and Kichilikizhangu. பூலங்கிழங்கு is the Tamil-script form of Poolakizhangu ('pool tuber'), matching that attestation. efloraofindia gives no Tamil name for this Himalayan species, so this review is the per-species authority I relied on; only Tamil candidate here, so preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Journal of Ayurveda and Integrated Medical Sciences, 'A Comprehensive Review of Shati (Hedychium spicatum Buch-Ham)' — Tamil: Poolakizhangu, Kichilikizhangu

verdicts.name: शिरीष
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Albizia lebbeck page lists Hindi शिरीष (shirish) and सरस (saras), with Sanskrit शिरीष. शिरीष is the form carried in Ayurvedic Hindi usage and matches the page slug, so preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Albizia lebbeck vernacular names: Hindi 'शिरीष shirish', 'सरस saras'; Sanskrit 'शिरीष'

verdicts.name: வாகை
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Albizia lebbeck page gives Tamil வாகை (vagai) and வெள்வேங்கை (vel-venkai). வாகை is the classical and still-current Tamil name for Albizia lebbeck, so preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Albizia lebbeck vernacular names: Tamil 'வாகை vagai', 'வெள்வேங்கை vel-venkai'

verdicts.name: सिंघाड़ा
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Trapa natans page gives सिंघाडा (Singhara) as the Hindi/Sanskrit-derived name, and Indian food-science and Ayurvedic reviews of water caltrop use Singhara as the standard Hindi name for Trapa natans / T. bispinosa. Spelling with nukta (सिंघाड़ा) is the normal Hindi orthography. Preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Trapa natans: 'सिंघाडा Singhara'; corroborated by Indian review literature on Singhara (Trapa natans)

verdicts.name: குரலி
verdicts.reason: No per-species authority I retrieved gives a Tamil name for Trapa natans at all: efloraofindia's Trapa natans page lists Hindi/Bengali names only and no Tamil. The sole attestation for குரலி is the Tamil Wikipedia article குரலி (which asserts Trapa natans and cites the Sangam poem Kuriñcippāṭṭu), i.e. precisely the weak, Wikidata-mirroring kind of source the brief says cannot carry a confirmation. Tamil trade/Siddha usage for the nut that I found is கஷ்கொட்டை (kashkottai) and 'pannimonthan kizhangu'. Leave unconfirmed pending an API/IMPPAT check.

verdicts.name: ஓரோஸைலம் இண்டிகம்
verdicts.reason: This is not a vernacular name at all — it is the Latin binomial 'Oroxylum indicum' respelled in Tamil script. efloraofindia's Oroxylum indicum page gives the actual Tamil names: சொரிகொன்றை (cori-konnai), பாலையுடைச்சி (palai-y-utaicci), பூதபுஷ்பம் (puta-puspam); other species lists add Achi, Palagaipayani, Vangam. A transliterated binomial would read as a Tamil name to a Tamil reader while carrying no traditional authority, so it must not go on the page. Replacements are in discovered.

verdicts.name: शीशम
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Dalbergia sissoo page gives Hindi शीशम (shisham) and Sanskrit शिंशपा (shinshapa), which is the source of the slug 'simsapa'. India Flora Online (IISc) independently lists Hindi 'Sisam, Sissu, Sheesham'. शीशम is the universal Hindi name, so preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Dalbergia sissoo: Hindi 'शीशम shisham', Sanskrit 'शिंशपा shinshapa'; India Flora Online/IISc: Hindi 'Sisam, Sissu, Sheesham'

verdicts.name: சிசே மரம்
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Dalbergia sissoo page attests Tamil சிசே (cice), plus ஈட்டிமரவகை, மரவகை and நூக்கம். The candidate is சிசே plus the generic மரம் ('tree'), a normal Tamil tree-naming pattern that India Flora Online also shows for this species ('Thaesi maram'). So the head word is independently attested for Dalbergia sissoo and the candidate is a legitimate compound, not a different plant. Marked preferred as the only Tamil candidate, though the bare சிசே and நூக்கம் are the forms in the botanical lists.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Dalbergia sissoo: Tamil 'சிசே cice', 'நூக்கம் nukkam', 'ஈட்டிமரவகை ittimaravakai'; India Flora Online/IISc Tamil 'Thaesi maram, Sisu-itii'

verdicts.name: जटामांसी
verdicts.denotesInstead: Nardostachys jatamansi (true Jatamansi / spikenard), a separate API monograph drug
verdicts.reason: Second real cross-species error in this batch. जटामांसी is the Hindi/Sanskrit name of Nardostachys jatamansi, which has its own Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia monograph distinct from Tagara. For Valeriana jatamansi, efloraofindia records the Indian trade names as 'Nihani / Mushkbala / Tagar' — not Jatamansi — and review literature on Tagara (IJAPR, 'Pharmacological Actions of Valeriana wallichii (Tagara)') gives Hindi Tagar / Sugandhabala / Mushkbala. The two Himalayan herbs are documented as routinely confused and cross-adulterated in trade precisely because the species epithet of Valeriana jatamansi repeats the other plant's name; that is how this label reached Wikidata. Putting जटामांसी on a Tagara page would misidentify the drug. Correct Hindi forms are in discovered.

verdicts.name: அப்ரமாஞ்சி
verdicts.reason: Attested only by Tamil Wikipedia's article அப்ரமாஞ்சி (which asserts Valeriana wallichii) and a popular Tamil health blog — both weak and likely Wikidata-mirroring. efloraofindia's Valeriana jatamansi page lists no Tamil name, and the IJAPR Tagara review gives the Tamil name as Tagarai (தகரை). Note also that the -மாஞ்சி element echoes 'mamsi/mansi', the Nardostachys root, so this form carries the same confusion risk as the Hindi candidate above. Not confirmed.

verdicts.name: ग्रन्थताल
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Borassus flabellifer page gives the Hindi names as ताड़ (taada), ताल (tala) and त्रृणराज (trinaraaj); its Sanskrit set is महातः, तालः, तन्तुनिर्यासः, तृणकेतुः, तृणराजः, तृणइन्द्रः. ग्रन्थताल is in none of them, and I found no independent per-species source that attests it as a Hindi name for the palmyra palm. Unattested, so false. The real Hindi name is ताड़ (discovered).

verdicts.name: ஆசியப் பனை
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Borassus flabellifer page gives exactly one Tamil name: பனை (panai). ஆசியப் பனை literally means 'Asian palm' and is a descriptive rendering of the English book name 'Asian palmyra palm' — a Wikipedia-style title, not a Tamil vernacular. No independent source attests it. Use பனை.

verdicts.name: குறத்தி நிலப்பனை
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Curculigo orchioides page gives Tamil நிலப்பனைக்கிழங்கு (nilappanaikkilanku) and நிலப்பனை (nilappanai, 'ground palm'); other species records add Nilappanan kizhangu. The qualifier குறத்தி is not attested in any of them — குறத்தி நிலப்பனை is the Tamil Wikipedia article title for this species, i.e. the weak Wikidata-mirroring source class. The head name நிலப்பனை is correct for Curculigo orchioides, so the error is the unattested qualifier rather than a wrong plant; publish நிலப்பனைக்கிழங்கு instead.

verdicts.name: भुंई आमला
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's page for the Bhumyamalaki drug plant (Phyllanthus fraternus, the P. niruri-complex species actually present in India) gives Hindi भुईंआंवला (bhuinanvalah) with Sanskrit भूम्यामलकी and तमालकी — the latter being this page's slug. Independent species records for Phyllanthus niruri list Hindi 'Bhui aonla, Jangli amli'. The candidate is the same name with ordinary spelling variation (भुंई आमला / भुईं आंवला / भुई आँवला). Preferred as the standard Hindi name.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Phyllanthus fraternus (Bhumyamalaki): Hindi 'भुईंआंवला bhuinanvalah', Sanskrit 'भूम्यामलकी', 'तमालकी'; plus Phyllanthus niruri species records giving Hindi Bhui aonla

verdicts.name: கீழாநெல்லி
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia gives Tamil கீழாநெல்லி (kila-nelli) for the Bhumyamalaki/Tamalaki drug plant, and the Multilingual Multiscript Plant Name Database (Univ. of Melbourne) sorting of Phyllanthus names records Tamil கீழாநெல்லி Kila-nelli for Phyllanthus niruri. One caveat worth stating on the page: கீழாநெல்லி is applied across the Phyllanthus niruri / amarus / fraternus complex rather than to P. niruri alone, so it is correct but not species-discriminating. Preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com (Phyllanthus fraternus / Bhumyamalaki): Tamil 'கீழாநெல்லி kila-nelli'; M.M.P.N.D. Sorting Phyllanthus names, Phyllanthus niruri: Tamil Kila-nelli

verdicts.name: तिल
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Sesamum indicum page gives Hindi 'til, safed til, gingli'. तिल is the universal Hindi name for sesame, so preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Sesamum indicum vernacular names: Hindi 'gingli, safed til, til'

verdicts.name: तिलः
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Sesamum indicum page gives the Sanskrit name as तिल (tila); the candidate तिलः is the same word in its nominative-singular citation form, which is how Sanskrit Wikipedia and many nighantu editions cite it. Same lexeme, not a different plant, so confirmed. If the atlas cites Sanskrit in stem form elsewhere, normalise to तिल for consistency.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Sesamum indicum: Sanskrit 'तिल tila'

verdicts.name: எள்
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia's Sesamum indicum page gives Tamil எள் (el), எள்ளு (ellu), சிற்றெள் (cirrel) and திலம் (tilam). எள் is the basic Tamil word for sesame, so preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Sesamum indicum: Tamil 'சிற்றெள் cirrel, எள் el, எள்ளு ellu, திலம் tilam'

verdicts.name: तिल
verdicts.reason: Same species as the Tila page (Sesamum indicum); efloraofindia gives Hindi 'til, safed til'. Correct for the source plant of the leaf (patra) used on this page. Preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Sesamum indicum vernacular names: Hindi 'gingli, safed til, til'

verdicts.name: तिलः
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia gives Sanskrit तिल for Sesamum indicum; तिलः is its nominative-singular citation form, the same lexeme. Confirmed for the source plant. Note the page is about the leaf, for which the Sanskrit drug term is तिलपत्र.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Sesamum indicum: Sanskrit 'तिल tila'

verdicts.name: எள்
verdicts.reason: efloraofindia gives Tamil எள் / எள்ளு / சிற்றெள் / திலம் for Sesamum indicum. எள் is the standard Tamil name, correct for the source plant of this leaf page. Preferred.
verdicts.corroboratingSource: efloraofindia.com, Sesamum indicum: Tamil 'சிற்றெள் cirrel, எள் el, எள்ளு ellu, திலம் tilam'

verdicts.name: कोकम
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Dravyaguna Vigyan monograph "Vrikshamla / Kokum" on the Ayurveda college portal sdach.ac.in lists Hindi names as "Kokum, Kokam, Komal, Amlaveta, Vishambila"; eFloraofIndia's Garcinia indica page independently records कोकम in Konkani/Gujarati script forms and English "kokam".
verdicts.reason: Retrieved two per-species sources independent of Wikidata. The Dravyaguna monograph gives Kokum/Kokam explicitly under Hindi for Garcinia indica. कोकम is also the form a Hindi speaker would search, so marked preferred.

verdicts.name: आमेतसवृक्षः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Nothing in Ayurvedic nomenclature as spelled; the nearest real Sanskrit name, आम्लवेतसः (Amlavetasa), is Garcinia pedunculata (with Rumex vesicarius / Rheum emodi as disputed alternatives), a different API monograph
verdicts.reason: This string appears in exactly one place: the Sanskrit Wikipedia article title आमेतसवृक्षः, which is a Wikidata mirror and therefore not independent corroboration. No API, nighantu or Dravyaguna source gives it. Tellingly, that same Sanskrit Wikipedia page itself calls the fruit वृक्षाम्लफलम् and the juice वृक्षाम्ल-फलरसः, i.e. it does not use its own title as the plant's name. The accepted Sanskrit name for Garcinia indica is वृक्षाम्ल / वृक्षाम्ला (eFloraofIndia, sdach.ac.in Dravyaguna monograph, API Part I Vol V monograph title Vrikshamla). आमेतसवृक्षः reads as a corruption of आम्लवेतस-वृक्षः, and Amlavetasa is a separate drug identified with Garcinia pedunculata (wisdomlib Amlavetasa entry citing Caraka-samhita; sdach.ac.in Amlavetasa monograph), so leaving it on the page would both invent a name and pull in another species. Drop it.

verdicts.name: முருகல்
verdicts.denotesInstead: Correct species, wrong language: this is the Kannada name (ಮುರ್ಗಿನ murgina / "murugalu mara") for Garcinia indica, not a Tamil name
verdicts.reason: The University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com) has no plant sense for முருகல் at all, and no Tamil-language botanical sense anywhere. eFloraofIndia's Garcinia indica page lists no Tamil name whatsoever, while giving Kannada ಮುರ್ಗಿನ (murgina) and ಪುನರ್ಪುಳಿ (punarpuli); the sdach.ac.in Dravyaguna monograph likewise lists Kannada and Malayalam but no Tamil. Garcinia indica is a Konkan/Western Ghats species with no Tamil Nadu range, consistent with there being no Tamil name. The Sanskrit Wikipedia page is the only source labelling मुरुगल् as Tamil, and on the same line it gives Kannada as "मुरुगलु मर", i.e. the same word; this looks like a Kannada name relabelled as Tamil and propagated through Wikipedia/Wikidata. Not safe to publish as Tamil.

verdicts.name: ब्रम्हमाण्डुकी
verdicts.denotesInstead: Centella asiatica
verdicts.reason: Retrieved the term rather than guessing: wisdomlib's Brahmamanduki (ब्रह्ममण्डूकी) entry identifies it as a plant "identified with Centella asiatica (L.) Urb.", with Brahmi / Brahma-manduki / Brahamamanduki listed as that species' synonyms; the sdach.ac.in Mandukaparni monograph confirms मण्डूकपर्णी = Centella asiatica and explicitly warns that Mandukaparni is commonly confused with Brahmi (Bacopa monnieri) because Bhavaprakasha describes similar actions. The candidate's spelling (ब्रम्ह- for ब्रह्म-, -माण्डुकी for -मण्डूकी) is a nonstandard Wikidata-style orthography of that same Centella name. This is a real plant name belonging to a different species and is exactly the kind of error that would mislead a reader on a Bacopa page. Drop.

verdicts.name: ब्राम्हीभेद
verdicts.reason: No source attests this. I searched for ब्राह्मीभेद / ब्राम्हीभेद / Brahmibheda and found no per-species listing in IMPPAT, eFloraofIndia, Kerala SMPB, the sdach.ac.in Dravyaguna monographs or any nighantu index; search engines return only generic Bacopa articles that never contain the word. The form reads as nighantu-commentary vocabulary (bheda = "variety, substitute") rather than a vernacular name a Hindi speaker uses, and in that commentary sense it would point at the Centella substitute rather than at Bacopa. Unattested, so false, not "probably fine".

verdicts.name: ब्राह्मी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Kerala State Medicinal Plants Board species page for Bacopa monnieri (smpbkerala.in) gives Sanskrit "Brahmi", Malayalam ബ്രഹ്മി, Hindi "Barambhi", Tamil "Nirbrahmi"; IMPPAT (IIT Madras) Bacopa monnieri page gives common name "Brahmi"; Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India carries Brahmi as the official monograph name for Bacopa monnieri.
verdicts.reason: Multiple independent per-species sources attest Brahmi for Bacopa monnieri. Noted caveat that Brahmi is also applied to Centella asiatica in North India, but Bacopa monnieri is the API-official bearer of the name, so it belongs on this page and is the form a Hindi speaker would search. Marked preferred.

verdicts.name: ब्राह्मी जड़ी बूटी
verdicts.reason: Not a plant name, a descriptive phrase meaning "brahmi herb" (जड़ी बूटी = herb). No source lists it as a vernacular name: IMPPAT, Kerala SMPB and eFloraofIndia all give the bare name ब्राह्मी. This is a Wikidata label artifact, harmless once dropped but noise on a reference page.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa
verdicts.reason: This is the proven error in the dataset. Retrieved the term: wisdomlib's Ashvattha entry identifies अश्वत्थ as Ficus religiosa (the holy fig / pipal, Moraceae), citing Caraka-samhita, Rajanighantu, Atharva-veda, Shatapatha-brahmana, Mahabharata and the Puranas, and records no Bacopa sense anywhere. Ashvattha is one of the least ambiguous names in Sanskrit botanical nomenclature. No API, nighantu, IMPPAT or Kerala SMPB source connects it to Bacopa monnieri. It is a genuine Sanskrit plant name for an entirely different family and would be a serious botanical error on this page. Drop, and note that the same alias is wrongly attached to Adhatoda vasica and Aegle marmelos elsewhere in this harvest, so the whole अश्वत्थः alias set from Wikidata should be treated as contaminated.

verdicts.name: ब्राह्मी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Kerala State Medicinal Plants Board Bacopa monnieri page (smpbkerala.in) lists Sanskrit "Brahmi"; Rajanighantu (13th c.), via wisdomlib's Brahmi entry, treats Brahmi as a drug name with 23 synonyms (Sarasvati, Somalata, Matsyakshi, Mandukaparni-adjacent forms etc.) and modern identification with Bacopa monnieri; Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India uses Brahmi as the official Sanskrit monograph name for Bacopa monnieri.
verdicts.reason: Classical and pharmacopoeial sources both attest ब्राह्मी as the Sanskrit drug name for Bacopa monnieri. The known Brahmi / Mandukaparni controversy means Brahmi is sometimes applied to Centella asiatica too, but the API assigns Brahmi to Bacopa monnieri, which settles it for a reference page. Single best Sanskrit form, so preferred.

verdicts.name: நீர்ப்பிரமி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com) entry for நீர்ப்பிரமி: "Water hyssop, climber, Herpestis monniera". Herpestis monniera is a listed taxonomic synonym of Bacopa monnieri on the IMPPAT Bacopa monnieri page. Kerala State Medicinal Plants Board independently gives Tamil "Nirbrahmi".
verdicts.reason: A named lexicon with no Wikidata dependency ties the exact Tamil string to this species by binomial. The lexicon also notes a second sense, Herpestis floribunda (a congener), but the primary identification is Bacopa monnieri. Best-known Tamil form, so preferred.

verdicts.name: जौ
verdicts.corroboratingSource: ayushvedah.com Yava (Hordeum vulgare) drug monograph, vernacular names table: Hindi "जव (jav), जौ (jau)", Sanskrit "aksata, akshata, dhanyaraja, divya", family Poaceae.
verdicts.reason: Per-species Ayurvedic monograph gives जौ in Devanagari under Hindi for Hordeum vulgare. This is also the universal everyday Hindi word for barley, so preferred.

verdicts.name: यवः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib Yava entry: Madhavacikitsa (7th c.) identifies Yava as "Hordeum vulgare L. Syn. Hordeum hexastichon L.", with further references in Ashtangasangraha (which distinguishes the anuyava and venuyava varieties) and Yogasarasangraha; ayushvedah.com carries the monograph under the drug name Yava for Hordeum vulgare.
verdicts.reason: Classical Ayurvedic texts identify यव directly with Hordeum vulgare; it is the Vedic-era name for the grain. The nominative-singular form यवः matches the page's citation convention. Single canonical Sanskrit name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: வாற்கோதுமை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com): "Barley cereal, Hordeum vulgare; கோதுமைவகை" (a kind of wheat-grain).
verdicts.reason: The exact Tamil string is attested against the exact binomial in a named lexicon that does not depend on Wikidata. Marked preferred as the native Tamil name, though note Tamil speakers also use the loanword பார்லி in everyday speech.

verdicts.name: अजवाईन
verdicts.reason: Right plant, wrong orthography, so not publishable as spelled. The sources I retrieved give the Hindi name as अजवाइन or अजवायन, never अजवाईन with long ई: the Hindi plant article on drvashishtsayuremedies (sites.google.com/site/drvashishtsayuremedies/ajwain-trachyspermum-ammi) gives "हिंदी में अजवाइन, ज़वेन" for Trachyspermum ammi, and the Tata 1mg Hindi monograph uses अजवाइन throughout. No named source attests the ई spelling, so confirmed is false rather than "close enough". This is not a species error, only a spelling one, so the fix is to publish the attested form instead (supplied in discovered) rather than lose the Hindi name.

verdicts.name: यवाग्रजः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Rajanighantu (13th c.) verses 6.38-40, via wisdomlib's Yavani entry, lists fourteen synonyms of Yavani (Trachyspermum ammi) including यवाग्रज (Yavagraja), alongside दीप्यक, दीप्य, यावासाह्व, यवज, दीपनीय, उग्रगन्धा, वातारि, भूकदम्बक, दीपनी, शूलहन्त्री, यवानिका, उग्रा, तीव्रगन्धा.
verdicts.reason: A classical nighantu attests this as a genuine Sanskrit synonym for this exact species, so it is correct to keep. Not preferred, because यवानी is the API-official drug name and the form a reader would look for; यवाग्रजः is a secondary nighantu synonym.

verdicts.name: यवानी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India Part I Vol I carries the monograph "Yavani (Fruit)" for Trachyspermum ammi (Linn.) Sprague, and API Part II lists Yamani/Yavani as Trachyspermum ammi Fr. in compound formulations; Rajanighantu 6.38-40 (via wisdomlib) treats Yavani as the head term with fourteen synonyms.
verdicts.reason: This is the official API Sanskrit monograph name for the species, corroborated by classical nighantu usage. Single best Sanskrit form, so preferred.

verdicts.name: ஓமம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com) entry for ஓமம்: "Bishop's-weed, herbaceous plant, Carum copticum", with J. P. Fabricius and Winslow's Tamil-English dictionaries giving the same sense. Carum copticum is a listed taxonomic synonym of Trachyspermum ammi on the IMPPAT Trachyspermum ammi page.
verdicts.reason: Three named Tamil lexicons attest ஓமம் against the binomial Carum copticum, which IMPPAT confirms as a synonym of Trachyspermum ammi. The lexicon also records an unrelated ritual sense (homa offering), but the botanical sense is unambiguous. Standard Tamil name for ajwain, so preferred.

verdicts.name: जूही
verdicts.corroboratingSource: eFloraofIndia species page for Jasminum auriculatum lists Hindi जूही (Juhi), alongside Sanskrit यूथिका (Yuthika), Tamil உச்சி மல்லிகை, Bengali যুথি/জুঁই, Marathi Jai/Jui, Telugu Adavimalle, Kannada Sanna mallige, Malayalam Sucimulla.
verdicts.reason: A per-species botanical source gives the exact Devanagari string for this exact species, and distinguishes it from Jasminum grandiflorum (Chameli / Jathi malli). Standard Hindi name, so preferred.

verdicts.name: முல்லை மலர்
verdicts.reason: The underlying name is right for this species but the candidate string is not a name. eFloraofIndia's Jasminum auriculatum page gives Tamil உச்சி மல்லிகை (Uccimalligai) as the species name and separately notes that J. auriculatum "is referred to as Mullai in Tamil", so முல்லை is attested; மலர் simply means "flower" and is an appended generic, the shape of a Wikidata label rather than a vernacular name. No lexicon or species database lists the two-word phrase. Not confirmed as spelled; the attested forms are supplied in discovered so the page keeps correct Tamil names.

verdicts.name: खीरा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Cucumis sativus ('Cucumber') page lists 'Hindi: खीरा Khira'; MMPND (Multilingual Multiscript Plant Name Database, Univ. of Melbourne), Sorting Cucumis names, gives Hindi 'Kheera (khira), Kakri, Kakdi, Tihu' for C. sativus
verdicts.reason: Retrieved two independent non-Wikidata sources that both give Kheera/खीरा for Cucumis sativus specifically (not for C. melo, which both list separately as Kharbuz/Karbuja). Exact Devanagari spelling खीरा matched in Flowers of India. This is the form a Hindi speaker would use or search.

verdicts.name: उर्वारुकम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for Urvaruka/Urvāruka citing Monier-Williams Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Apte's Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary and Arthaśāstra II.15.19 ('cucumber (urvāruka)'); the companion Urvāru entry identifies the plant as Cucumis sativus, Cucurbitaceae
verdicts.reason: Lexically attested for cucumber by Monier-Williams and Apte, and identified as Cucumis sativus. Two cautions kept preferred=false: (a) उर्वारुकम् is the neuter nominative singular of the fruit-noun उर्वारुक (the form familiar from the Mahāmṛtyuñjaya mantra), not the plant lemma; (b) some nighantu traditions apply urvāru to Cucumis melo var. utilissimus (kakri) rather than C. sativus, so the species mapping is not uncontested. The standard Ayurvedic Sanskrit lemma for this species is त्रपुष/त्रपुस, which is what the page slug reflects and which should be the preferred Sanskrit form.

verdicts.name: வெள்ளரி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Cucumis sativus page: 'Tamil: Vellarikkay'; State Medicinal Plants Board Kerala (smpbkerala.in) herbal-data page for Cucumis sativus titles it 'Salad Vellari'
verdicts.reason: Vellari/வெள்ளரி is attested for Cucumis sativus by both sources. வெள்ளரிக்காய் is the fruit form; வெள்ளரி is the base plant name, so the candidate is the correct lemma and the form a Tamil speaker would search.

verdicts.name: निसोथ
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Operculina turpethum ('Transparent Wood Rose') page: 'Hindi: निशोथ Nisoth, निशोधि Nishodhi'; also 'Nepali: निसोथ Nisoth'. IAFA / Trivrit review literature on Operculina turpethum gives 'Hindi: Nisot, Pitohari'
verdicts.reason: The name Nisoth is firmly attested for Operculina turpethum by Flowers of India and the Trivrit review literature. Flowers of India spells the Hindi निशोथ (with श) and gives निसोथ (with स) for Nepali; both spellings circulate in Hindi print. Confirming the candidate as a legitimate orthographic variant, but the atlas may prefer निशोथ to match Flowers of India.

verdicts.name: சிவதை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Operculina turpethum page: 'Tamil: கும்பஞ்சான் Kumpncan, சரளம் Caralam, சிவதை Chivatai, பகன்றை Paganrai'
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match (சிவதை) attested for Operculina turpethum by Flowers of India, corroborated by the Trivrit ethnopharmacology review which gives Tamil 'Sivadai'. Malayalam cognate Sivata/Chivaka on the same page supports the identification.

verdicts.name: हल्दी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Curcuma longa ('Turmeric') page: 'Hindi: हल्दी Haldi'; MMPND Sorting Curcuma names gives Hindi 'Haldii (Haldi)' for C. longa
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in Flowers of India, independently corroborated by MMPND. Unambiguously the everyday Hindi name for this species.

verdicts.name: हरिद्रा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India monograph text quoted in the dravyaguna literature: 'Haridra consists of the dried and cured rhizomes of Curcuma longa Linn. (Fam. Zingiberaceae)'; Flowers of India also lists 'Sanskrit: Haridra'
verdicts.reason: Haridrā is the official API monograph name for Curcuma longa, which is the strongest possible attestation for a Sanskrit name. Devanagari हरिद्रा is the standard spelling. Clearly the preferred Sanskrit form.

verdicts.name: மஞ்சள்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Curcuma longa page: 'Tamil: மஞ்சள் Manjal'
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match for Curcuma longa in Flowers of India; corroborated by the Curcuma longa pharmacology reviews which give Tamil 'manjal'. The universal Tamil name.

verdicts.name: दालचीनी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Cinnamomum names, Cinnamomum verum entry: 'Hindi: दालचीनी Daalacinii (Darchini), दारचीनी Daarciinii'
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match recorded by MMPND against C. verum (not against C. tamala or C. cassia, which MMPND lists separately). The standard Hindi name.

verdicts.name: கருவா
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Cinnamomum names, Cinnamomum verum entry: 'Tamil: இலவங்கம் llavangam, கருவா Karuva, லவங்கபட்டை Lavangapattai'
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match (கருவா) in MMPND for C. verum. Note the spelling variant கறுவா also appears in Dinesh Valke's Names-of-Plants-in-India compilations; MMPND's கருவா matches the candidate as given, so confirming. இலவங்கம் is the other common Tamil name and is added to discovered.

verdicts.name: उदुंबर
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Ficus names, Ficus racemosa entry, Hindi list: 'Ambar (Bombay), Doomar, Domoor, Gular, Udumbara, Umar, Umbar'
verdicts.reason: MMPND lists Udumbara under Hindi (as well as Sanskrit) for Ficus racemosa, so it is attested as a Hindi name and not only a Sanskrit loan. Not preferred: it is a learned/Sanskritic form; the everyday Hindi name is गूलर. Correct species, no conflict.

verdicts.name: गूलर
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India page for Ficus racemosa, titled 'Goolar', gives 'Hindi: गूलर Goolar'; MMPND Ficus racemosa Hindi list includes 'Gular'
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in Flowers of India, corroborated by MMPND. This is the name a Hindi speaker actually uses and searches for, so it is the preferred Hindi form on this page.

verdicts.name: औदुम्बरवृक्षः
verdicts.reason: Retrieved the Sanskrit synonym set for Ficus racemosa from MMPND (Udumbara, Udumbarah, Udumbar, Jantuphala, Hemadugdhaka, Sadaphalah, Yajnanga) and from the Udumbara dravyaguna literature (udumbara, jantuphala, hemadugdhaka, kshiravriksha, sadaphala, kalaskandha, yajnayoga, sheetavalka, yajnasara, panibhuk). औदुम्बरवृक्षः appears in none of them. It is a constructed compound: औदुम्बर is the vṛddhi-derived adjective 'of/made of udumbara wood' plus वृक्षः 'tree'. Grammatically well-formed and it does point at the right plant, but it is not an attested nighantu synonym and reads as a Wikidata label coinage. Drop it and use उदुम्बरः.

verdicts.name: அத்தி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Ficus racemosa ('Goolar') page: 'Tamil: அத்தி Atti'; MMPND Ficus racemosa Tamil list: 'Atti, Athi, Atthi, Attee marum, Vellaiatthi'
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match for Ficus racemosa in Flowers of India, corroborated by MMPND and by the SMPB Kerala page (Malayalam cognate Atthi/Atthi-al). The standard Tamil name.

verdicts.name: पोई
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Basella names, Basella alba entry, Hindi: 'पोई Pō'ī, पोइ Pō'i, पोई का साग, पोई साग, साग'
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in MMPND for Basella alba; corroborated by the Basella alba vernacular lists (Bengali Pui shak, Oriya Poi saga are cognates of the same name). The everyday Hindi name.

verdicts.name: पोतकी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for Potaki/Pōtakī, citing Shabda-Sagara and Monier-Williams Sanskrit lexicons and a Kannada dictionary that identifies potaki as 'the plant Basella rubra of Basellaceae family' (Basella alba sensu lato, with synonyms Basella lucida, B. nigra, B. rubra)
verdicts.reason: Attested in Sanskrit lexicography for Basella. One caveat worth recording: the same wisdomlib entry notes a competing regional application of 'potaki' to Pterocarpus marsupium, so the name is not perfectly monosemous, but the lexicon identification for Basella is the primary one. Not preferred because the official Ayurvedic Sanskrit name for this species is उपोदिका (which is also the page slug) and that is what a reader would look up.

verdicts.name: பசளி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Basella names, Basella alba entry, Tamil: 'பசளி Pasali / Pacaḷi, Sivappu, Venpacali'
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match in MMPND for Basella alba. The standard Tamil name for the species; வெண்பசளி (white form) and சிவப்புப் பசளி (red form) are the cultivar qualifiers of the same name.

verdicts.name: वच
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Acorus names, Acorus calamus entry: 'Hindi: Bach, Gharbacha (Goa)'; Flowers of India 'Sweet Flag' page: 'Hindi: बच Bach, घोरबच Ghorbach, सफ़ेद बच Safed bach'
verdicts.reason: Both sources attest the name Bach/Vach for Acorus calamus. Note the orthography: both give बच with ब, while the candidate uses व. In Hindi व/ब alternate freely in this word (वच and बच are both in use, the latter more common in print), so this is a spelling variant, not a different name. Confirming as the only Hindi candidate and the preferred form, though बच is the commoner spelling.

verdicts.name: वामनी
verdicts.denotesInstead: Gossypium herbaceum (cotton plant)
verdicts.reason: This is a genuine plant name for the wrong plant, the same failure class as the aśvattha error. wisdomlib's entry for Vamani/Vāmanī records: 'Vamani in India is the name of a plant defined with Gossypium herbaceum in various botanical sources' (synonym Gossypium prostratum), and the Tamil lexicon entry glosses it 'Cotton plant; பருத்திச் செடி'. Monier-Williams likewise gives 'the cotton shrub' for वामनी. Separately I retrieved the Vacha synonym set for Acorus calamus from MMPND (Sanskrit: Vacha, Bhuta nashini), Flowers of India (वचा Vachaa, वाच Vacha, Bhadra) and the Vacha dravyaguna literature (Ugragandha, Golomi, Lomashi, Jatila, Shadgrantha/Shataparvika, Hemavati, Khadiravacha) and वामनी appears in none of them; MMPND and Flowers of India were checked explicitly for it and do not list it. Must be removed: left on the page it would assert that a cotton name is an Acorus name.

verdicts.name: வசம்பு
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Acorus names, Acorus calamus entry: 'Tamil: Vasambu'; Flowers of India 'Sweet Flag' page: 'Tamil: Vashambu, Pullai-valathi'
verdicts.reason: Vasambu is attested for Acorus calamus by both sources (given in transliteration; வசம்பு is the standard Tamil-script rendering and matches the candidate). The name every Tamil speaker uses for sweet flag.

verdicts.name: மூங்கிலிரிசி
verdicts.denotesInstead: Not a species name: it denotes bamboo rice, the edible seed/grain produced by bamboo at flowering (மூங்கில் அரிசி), a plant part rather than the plant
verdicts.reason: Retrieved the Tamil name set for Bambusa bambos from Flowers of India ('Tamil: குழாய்மூங்கில் kulay-munkil, பெருமூங்கில் peru-munkil') and MMPND Sorting Bambusa names under Bambusa arundinacea ('Tamil: Mullumangila, Mulmunkil, Mungil'). Both were checked explicitly for மூங்கிலிரிசி / 'moongil arisi' and neither lists it. The string is மூங்கில் + அரிசி, literally 'bamboo rice', the seed harvested when bamboo masses-flowers. So it is a real Tamil word tied to bamboo, but it names a product, not the species, and a reader would take it for the plant's Tamil name. Use மூங்கில் or முள்மூங்கில் instead. Relatedly, the Ayurvedic drug behind the slug Vamsha is usually वंशलोचन (tabasheer, the siliceous culm exudate), another part rather than the plant, so this page needs its plant-versus-part distinction made explicit.

verdicts.name: बनफ्शा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Shri Dharmasthala Manjunatheshwara Ayurveda College (sdach.ac.in) Dravyaguna Vigyan monograph 'Banafsha', which identifies the drug as Viola odorata Linn. (Violaceae) and gives 'Hindi: Banafsha, Punjabi: Banafsha, Tamil: Vayilethe'; corroborated by the Banafsha (Viola odorata) reviews in IJAPR and by Planet Ayurveda's Viola odorata monograph
verdicts.reason: Banafsha is firmly attested as the Hindi/Unani drug name for Viola odorata by a named Ayurvedic college dravyaguna monograph plus review literature. The Devanagari spelling varies in print (बनफ्शा / बनफ्सा / बनफशा); the candidate form is one of the standard renderings. Only Hindi candidate and the form a speaker would search, so preferred. Caveat for the page: 'banafsha' in trade is a known adulteration-prone name covering other Viola species, which is why the DNA-authentication literature exists; the name is right for V. odorata but the market material is not always.

verdicts.name: பண்ணுக்கிழங்கு
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Dioscorea names, Dioscorea bulbifera entry, Tamil: 'காய்வள்ளி Kaayvalli, காட்டுச்சீரகவள்ளி, காட்டுக்காய்வள்ளி Kaattukkaayvalli, Pannu kilangu'
verdicts.reason: I expected this one to fail and it did not. MMPND lists 'Pannu kilangu' among the Tamil names specifically under Dioscorea bulbifera and under no other Dioscorea species, which corroborates the candidate for this species. Two reservations keep preferred=false: MMPND gives it in Latin transliteration only, so the Tamil-script spelling பண்ணுக்கிழங்கு is not itself source-verified, and it is a marginal name beside the well-documented காய்வள்ளி / காட்டுக்காய்வள்ளி. A Tamil speaker would search காய்வள்ளி, which I have put in discovered.

verdicts.name: बैंगन
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Solanum melongena ('Brinjal') page: 'Hindi: बैंगन Baingan, बंग Bang, भण्टा Bhanta, भाटा Bhata'
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in Flowers of India for Solanum melongena, corroborated by the eFloraofIndia and DAV Pharmacy brinjal vernacular lists (Baigan, Baijani, Baingan). The universal Hindi name.

verdicts.name: वृन्ताकः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib entry for Vrintaka/Vṛntāka: denotes the eggplant, Solanum melongena, citing Caraka-saṃhitā (under śāka), Bhāvaprakāśa (16th c.) and Rājanighaṇṭu (13th c.), with the etymology from vṛnta 'pedicel' because the calyx stays attached to the pedicel
verdicts.reason: Vṛntāka is attested for Solanum melongena by three classical sources named in the wisdomlib entry (Caraka, Bhāvaprakāśa, Rājanighaṇṭu). वृन्ताकः is the masculine nominative singular, a normal citation form. One note: Flowers of India's Sanskrit list for brinjal gives the variant वार्त्ताक (Vārttāka) alongside भण्टाकी and others rather than वृन्ताक, and wisdomlib flags that some botanical sources also attach vrintaka to Chenopodium album, but the Ayurvedic classical attestation for Solanum melongena is unambiguous. Preferred Sanskrit form on this page.

verdicts.name: கத்தரி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Solanum melongena ('Brinjal') page: 'Tamil: அச்சத்தி Accatti, காளினியம் Kaliniyam, கத்தரி Kattari, நமைக்காய் Namai-K-Kay, பண்டாகி Pantaki, பிரு Piru'
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match (கத்தரி) in Flowers of India for Solanum melongena. கத்தரி is the plant-name lemma; கத்தரிக்காய் is the fruit, so the candidate is the correct base form and the one a Tamil speaker searches.

verdicts.name: अडूसा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Justicia names, Justicia adhatoda (syn. Adhatoda vasica / A. zeylanica) entry, Hindi list: 'Adosa, Adulasa, अडुळसा Adulsa, Adus, अडुसा Adusa, अर्शा Arusa, Arush, Arusha, वासाला Bansa, Vasak, Vasala'
verdicts.reason: MMPND gives अडुसा in Devanagari under Hindi for this species; the candidate अडूसा differs only in the length of the second vowel and both spellings are current in Hindi print. Corroborated by the Adhatoda vasica ethnopharmacology literature ('Hindi: Adosa, Arusha, Adulasa'). Confirming, and it is the Hindi name a speaker would actually use, so preferred.

verdicts.name: वसाका
verdicts.reason: Correct plant, wrong word-form, and wrong language slot. The Sanskrit/drug name is वासक with a long ā in the first syllable (wisdomlib's Vasaka entry gives the Devanagari as वासक and identifies it as Justicia adhatoda per Rāj Nighaṇṭu; MMPND lists Sanskrit 'वासक Vasaka' and 'वासा Vasa'). वसाका with a short first a appears in no source I retrieved. MMPND's Hindi list for this species does carry 'Vasak' and 'Vasala' in transliteration, but no source gives वसाका in Devanagari as the Hindi name. This is Wikidata back-transliterating the English trade name 'Vasaka' into Devanagari. Not a misidentification, so low harm, but it should be dropped in favour of अडूसा for Hindi and वासक/वासा for Sanskrit.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa (the sacred fig / peepal)
verdicts.reason: This is the planted error and it is a real botanical error. Retrieved from both directions. Positively: MMPND Sorting Ficus names lists under Ficus religiosa 'Sanskrit: Ashvatha, Asvattha, Ashvathha, Aswattha, Bodhidruma, Bodhivrska, Pippala, Shuchidruma, Yajnika' and 'Hindi: पीपल Pipal'; wisdomlib's Ashvattha entry and the Ashvattha dravyaguna monographs identify अश्वत्थ as Ficus religiosa, classed by Caraka in the Kaṣāya mahākaṣāya group. Negatively: MMPND's full Sanskrit list for Justicia adhatoda (Adusa, Arusha, Atrusha, Bhishangamata, Kaphahari, Simhamukhi, Simhi, Simhika, Sinhaparni, Shwetavasa, Vasa, Vasaka, Vasika) contains no form of aśvattha, and neither does the Bhāvaprakāśa synonym set for Vāsā reported in the Adhatoda reviews. Aśvattha and Vāsā are not even in the same family (Moraceae vs Acanthaceae). Must be deleted from this page.

verdicts.name: वसाकः
verdicts.reason: Right plant, misspelled Sanskrit. wisdomlib's Vasaka entry gives the Devanagari explicitly as वासक (long ā) and identifies it as Adhatoda vasica = Justicia adhatoda, citing Rāj Nighaṇṭu, Mādhavacikitsā and a Kannada dictionary; MMPND independently lists Sanskrit 'वासक Vasaka'. No source attests वसाक with a short first vowel. In Sanskrit the vowel length is not cosmetic, so the spelling as harvested is wrong. Use वासकः; I have put वासक and वासा in discovered.

verdicts.name: वसाका
verdicts.reason: Same defect as वसाकः: the attested Sanskrit is वासा (MMPND, 'वासा Vasa', for Justicia adhatoda) or वासका, both with a long first ā. वसाका appears in no retrieved source. Also redundant with the other three Sanskrit candidates on this page, which are all variant spellings of the single name Vāsā/Vāsaka.

verdicts.name: वासकसस्यम्
verdicts.reason: Not an attested plant name. It parses as वासक + सस्यम् 'the vāsaka crop/plant', a descriptive compound of the kind Wikidata labels generate rather than a nighantu synonym. Checked against MMPND's Sanskrit list for Justicia adhatoda and against the Bhāvaprakāśa synonym set reported in the Adhatoda vasica reviews (Vāsā, Vāsaka, Vāsikā, Vṛṣa, Aṭarūṣa, Aṭarūṣaka, Bhiṣaṅmātā, Siṃhikā, Siṃhāsya, Vājidanta, Siṃhaparṇī); it is absent from both. Correct plant, so not a misidentification, but it should not appear as a Sanskrit name.

verdicts.name: ஆடாதோடை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Justicia names, Justicia adhatoda entry, Tamil: 'ஆடாதோடை Adatodai, Adhatodai, Adotodai, Pavatai, Pavettai'
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match in MMPND for this species, corroborated by the Adhatoda vasica reviews ('Tamil: Adathodai') and by the SMPB Kerala page (Malayalam cognate ആടലോടകം Aadalodakam). The genus epithet adhatoda is itself borrowed from this Tamil name. Standard Tamil name, preferred.

verdicts.name: वसाका
verdicts.reason: Same verdict as on the vasa page: no retrieved source gives वसाका in Devanagari for this species. The attested Sanskrit is वासक/वासा (wisdomlib citing Rāj Nighaṇṭu; MMPND), and the attested Hindi names are अडुसा/अडूसा, अडुळसा, अरूसा and बाँसा (MMPND). वसाका is a Devanagari back-transliteration of the English trade name. Dropping it leaves this page with no Hindi candidate, so take अडूसा from discovered. Separately and importantly: this page duplicates the vasa page. Plants of the World Online treats Justicia adhatoda L. as the accepted name and Adhatoda vasica Nees as its synonym, so slugs vasa and vasaka are the same species under two names and should be merged rather than maintained as two monographs with divergent name sets.

verdicts.name: ஆடாதோடை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: MMPND Sorting Justicia names, Justicia adhatoda entry, Tamil: 'ஆடாதோடை Adatodai, Adhatodai, Adotodai, Pavatai, Pavettai'
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match in MMPND under the accepted name Justicia adhatoda. Same species as the vasa page, same verdict. Standard Tamil name, preferred.

verdicts.name: बादाम का पेड
verdicts.denotesInstead: Prunus dulcis (sweet almond). The page's stated botanical is the genus Prunus (Q39918), which is broader than any of these names
verdicts.reason: Two separate problems. First, the string is not a name but a descriptive noun phrase: बादाम का पेड़ means 'the almond tree'. Flowers of India's Almond page gives 'Hindi: बादाम Badam, बदाम' and no source I retrieved gives the phrase as a vernacular name; it is the kind of gloss Wikidata stores as a label. It is also missing the nukta on ड़ (पेड़, not पेड). Second, and more consequential for the page: all three candidates here name the almond, Prunus dulcis, while the page's botanical field is the bare genus Prunus, which also contains plums, cherries, peaches and apricots. Presenting almond names against the genus would tell a reader that बादाम denotes Prunus generally, which is false. Set this page's species to Prunus dulcis (Mill.) D.A.Webb and use बादाम for Hindi.

verdicts.name: वातामम्
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Prunus dulcis ('Almond') page: 'Sanskrit: वातामम Vatamam'; corroborated by wisdomlib's Vatada/Vātāda entry ('the almond tree', Prunus amygdalus = Prunus dulcis) and by Gernot Katzer's Spice Pages for almond, which records the Sanskrit forms vātāma and bādāma alongside Middle Persian wādām
verdicts.denotesInstead: Prunus dulcis specifically, not the genus Prunus that this page names
verdicts.reason: Flowers of India gives वातामम in Devanagari for Prunus dulcis, an exact match for the candidate, and the etymological chain (Pahlavi wādām to Sanskrit vātāma/bādāma) is independently documented. Confirmed as a Sanskrit name, and it is the best-attested Sanskrit candidate here, so preferred. The denotesInstead note is about page scope, not about the name being wrong: the name is correct for almond but the page is pointed at the whole genus.

verdicts.name: வாதுமை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Prunus dulcis ('Almond') page: 'Tamil: வாதுமை Vaadumai'
verdicts.denotesInstead: Prunus dulcis specifically, not the genus Prunus that this page names
verdicts.reason: Exact Tamil-script match in Flowers of India against Prunus dulcis. Confirmed and preferred as the only Tamil candidate. Same page-scope caveat as the Sanskrit: the name is right for almond, while the page's botanical field is the genus.

verdicts.name: विडंग
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Embelia ribes ('Vidang') page: 'Hindi: विडंग Vidanga'; same page gives 'Sanskrit: आमोघः Amogha, मोघा Mogha, विडङ्गः Vidang'
verdicts.reason: Exact Devanagari match in Flowers of India for Embelia ribes, corroborated by the Embelia ribes reviews which give Hindi Baberang, Vayvarang, Viranga and Sanskrit Vidanga/Vaividanga. Confirmed and preferred as the only Hindi candidate, though बाबरंग and वायविडंग are the commoner market names in Hindi and are added to discovered.

verdicts.name: வாய்விலங்கம்
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Embelia ribes vernacular lists in the IJPSR review 'Importance of Embelia ribes: An Update' and the Medicinal Plants compilation entry for Embelia ribes, both giving Tamil 'Vaividangam' and 'Vayu-vilamgam'; Flowers of India's Vidang page gives Tamil 'vitankam, vivilangam, vollai'
verdicts.reason: The name vāy-vilaṅgam is attested for Embelia ribes by independent review sources, and Flowers of India's 'vivilangam' is the same name. Caveat recorded honestly: every source I could retrieve gives the Tamil in Latin transliteration only, and the script spelling varies in print between வாய்விடங்கம், வாயுவிளங்கம் and வாய்விலங்கம், so the exact Tamil-script form of the candidate is not itself source-verified. Confirmed on the name, preferred as the only Tamil candidate; a Tamil-script authority such as the Siddha materia medica should settle the spelling.

verdicts.name: विदारीकंद
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Planet Ayurveda and IAFA monographs for Pueraria tuberosa DC., which give 'Hindi: विदारीकंद Vidarikanda, बनकुमड़ा Bankumara' and 'Sanskrit: भूमिकुष्माण्ड Bhumikusmanda, विदारी Vidari, स्वादुकन्दा Svadukanda, गजवाजिप्रिया Gajavajipriya, कन्दपलाश Kandapalash, इक्षुगन्धा Ikshugandha'
verdicts.reason: विदारीकंद in Devanagari is attested for Pueraria tuberosa by two independent Ayurvedic monograph sources. Note that MMPND's Pueraria entry carries no Hindi/Sanskrit/Tamil names at all, so these monographs are the corroboration. One substantive caution for the page: Vidarikand is a well-known substitution-prone drug, with Ipomoea digitata and Adenia hondala traded under the same name, so the name is right for P. tuberosa but is not exclusive to it in the market. Confirmed and preferred as the only Hindi candidate.

verdicts.name: विदारीकंद
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Planet Ayurveda and IAFA monographs for Pueraria tuberosa DC., giving 'Hindi: विदारीकंद Vidarikanda, बनकुमड़ा Bankumara'
verdicts.reason: Same species and same verdict as the vidari page. Flagging a dataset problem rather than a name problem: slugs vidari and vidarikand are both Pueraria tuberosa with the identical Wikidata id Q7258521 and the identical single candidate, so they are duplicate monographs and should be merged. Keeping both will show a reader two pages for one plant.

verdicts.name: पेटरोकार्पस मार्सूपियम
verdicts.reason: This is not a Hindi plant name at all. It is the Latin binomial Pterocarpus marsupium spelled out in Devanagari letter by letter, which is what Wikidata stores when a language has only a transliterated scientific-name label. Retrieved the real Hindi name set from Flowers of India's Indian Kino Tree page ('Hindi: विजयसार Vijayasara, बीज पत्ता Beeja patta, Bijasal, Bila') and from MMPND Sorting Pterocarpus names ('Hindi: Banda, Bija, Bijasal, Bijasar, Bijaisaar kaashtha, Biya, Hiradokhi, Peisar, Piasal, Pitshola, Vijaisar kaashthaa'). Neither contains anything like this string. Drop it and use विजयसार, which Flowers of India gives in Devanagari and which is also what the page slug reflects.

verdicts.name: வேங்கை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Flowers of India, Pterocarpus marsupium ('Indian Kino Tree') page: 'Tamil: Vengai, Accamai, Accanapann'; MMPND Sorting Pterocarpus names, P. marsupium Tamil list includes 'Vengai' and 'Udiravengai'
verdicts.reason: Vengai is attested for Pterocarpus marsupium by two independent sources, and the Malayalam cognate Venga on the same Flowers of India entry corroborates it. Both give it in transliteration only; வேங்கை is the standard Tamil-script spelling and matches the candidate. The name a Tamil speaker uses for this tree, so preferred.

verdicts.name: पिप्पली
verdicts.reason: Retrieved: eFloraofIndia / Names of Plants in India separates Hindi पिपली from Sanskrit पिप्पली for Piper longum; API Part I PIPPALI (Fruit) monograph gives Hindi 'Pipar', and the PIPPALIMULA (Stem/root) monograph, which is this page's drug, gives Hindi 'Piparamula'. No source I retrieved lists पिप्पली as a Hindi name. It is the Sanskrit lemma, carried into the Hindi field by Wikidata. Same species, so not a botanical error, but the language label is wrong.

verdicts.name: पिप्पली
verdicts.corroboratingSource: eFloraofIndia / Names of Plants in India, Piper longum: Sanskrit पिप्पली. Corroborated by Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India Part I, monograph PIPPALI (Fruit) = Piper longum Linn., with Sanskrit synonyms Kana, Magadhi, Magadha, Krsna, Saundi.
verdicts.reason: Attested in Sanskrit by both an independent flora compilation and the API, where PIPPALI is the official Sanskrit drug name for Piper longum. Best-known Sanskrit form for this species.

verdicts.name: திப்பிலி
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India Part I, PIPPALI (Fruit) = Piper longum, Tamil: 'Arisi Tippali, Thippili'. Also eFloraofIndia Tamil திப்பிலீ.
verdicts.reason: Two independent sources give Thippili/திப்பிலீ as Tamil for Piper longum. Note that for this page's specific drug, the root, API's PIPPALIMULA monograph gives Tamil 'Kanda Tippili' (the root form); திப்பிலி names the plant and fruit.

verdicts.name: पोहाड़
verdicts.reason: Retrieved: eFloraofIndia Hindi list for Senna tora = चकूंदा, चकवंड, एड़गज, पद्माट, पंवार, प्रपुनाट, तर्किल; API Part I PRAPUNNADA (Seed) = Cassia tora, Hindi 'Pavand', Punjabi 'Panwal, Chakunda, Chakwad', Urdu 'Panwar'. पोहाड़ appears in none of them, and a targeted search found no attestation of this spelling for any plant. It looks like a corruption of पंवाड़/पवाँड़. Unattested, so drop it; I could not show it belongs to a different species either.

verdicts.name: தகரை
verdicts.corroboratingSource: eFloraofIndia / Names of Plants in India, Senna tora: Tamil தகரை (thagarai). Corroborated by API PRAPUNNADA, Tamil 'Vshittgarai' (OCR of usittakarai, the compound of the same head word) and Malayalam 'Tagaraa', Kannada 'Tagache'.
verdicts.reason: Directly attested in Tamil script for this species by eFloraofIndia, with the same root form in API's Tamil, Malayalam and Kannada entries. Standard Tamil name.

verdicts.name: चिरौंजी
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India Part I, PRIYALA (Stem Bark) = Buchanania lanzan Spreng., Hindi: 'Chiraunji, Piyaar, Chironji'. Also eFloraofIndia Hindi चिरोंजी.
verdicts.reason: API gives Chiraunji as the first Hindi name for Buchanania lanzan and eFloraofIndia prints चिरोंजी in Devanagari. This is the name a Hindi speaker uses for the kernel and the tree.

verdicts.name: புளிமா
verdicts.denotesInstead: Buchanania axillaris (Buchanan's mango); the same Tamil word is also applied to Spondias pinnata (Indian hog-plum) and Averrhoa bilimbi
verdicts.reason: Retrieved University of Madras Tamil Lexicon (via agarathi.com) for புளிமா: 'a species of mango, sour in taste', 'bilimbi tree', 'Buchanan's mango', 'Indian hog-plum (Spondias mangifera)'. It is a genuine Tamil plant name but not for Buchanania lanzan: eFloraofIndia gives Tamil சாரம் / காட்டுமா for B. lanzan and API gives Tamil 'Saarapparuppu'. Buchanania axillaris is the sister species, so this would sit on the page as a plausible-looking misidentification.

verdicts.name: खपुर
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Names of Plants in India compilation for Areca catechu (Dinesh Valke, the dataset behind eFloraofIndia pages), Hindi: 'चामरपुष्प, गुवाक, गूआ OR गुवा, खपुर, पूग, पूगी, पुंगी, सुपारी, उद्वेग'.
verdicts.reason: Attested in the Hindi list for Areca catechu in Devanagari. It is a Sanskrit loan into Hindi, not the everyday Hindi word, so not preferred: सुपारी is.

verdicts.name: गुवा
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Names of Plants in India, Areca catechu, Hindi 'गूआ OR गुवा guwa'. Corroborated by wisdomlib's Guwa entry ('Guwa [गुवा, गूआ] in the Hindi language is the name of a plant identified with Areca catechu L., Arecaceae', citing CRC World Dictionary of Plant Names regional names).
verdicts.reason: Two sources attest गुवा as a Hindi name for Areca catechu; API also records Oriya 'Gua' for the same species. Not the dominant Hindi form (सुपारी is), so not preferred.

verdicts.name: गुवाक
verdicts.corroboratingSource: eFloraofIndia, Areca catechu, Hindi: चामरपुष्प, गुवाक (guvak), सुपारी, पूग, उद्वेग; same list in the Names of Plants in India compilation.
verdicts.reason: Attested in Devanagari in the Hindi field of two renderings of the same flora compilation. A Sanskrit-derived literary form rather than the common spoken name.

verdicts.name: गूआ
verdicts.corroboratingSource: Names of Plants in India, Areca catechu, Hindi 'गूआ OR गुवा guwa'; wisdomlib Guwa entry lists both गुवा and गूआ as Hindi for Areca catechu L.
verdicts.reason: Attested spelling variant of गुवा in the same Hindi list. Keeping both is redundant but neither is wrong; neither is the preferred Hindi form.

verdicts.name: चामरपुष्प
verdicts.corroboratingSource: eFloraofIndia, Areca catechu: चामरपुष्प (chamarpushpa) appears in both the Hindi and the Sanskrit lists; Names of Plants in India repeats it in both.
verdicts.reason: Attested in the Hindi field, though it is plainly a Sanskrit compound ('chowrie-flower') used in Hindi nighantu literature. The corresponding Tamil சாமரபுட்பம் is also recorded, which supports the Sanskrit origin. Not the preferred Hindi form.

verdicts.name: अश्वत्थः
verdicts.denotesInstead: Ficus religiosa
verdicts.reason: This is the seeded error. Ayurvedic Pharmacopoeia of India Part I, monograph 11, is ASVATTHA (Bark) = Ficus religiosa Linn., with Sanskrit synonym Pippala, Hindi 'Pipala, Pipal', Tamil 'Arasamaram, Arasu'. अश्वत्थ is the pipal, a Moraceae tree, and has no relation to Areca catechu, a palm. API's Sanskrit synonyms for Areca are Kramuka, Ghonta and the monograph name Puga. Must not go on this page.

verdicts.name: खपुर
verdicts.corroboratingSource: wisdomlib Khapura entry quoting three Sanskrit lexica: Apte's Practical Sanskrit-English Dictionary ('the betel-nut tree'), Shabda-Sagara ('the betel tree, Areca faufel or catechu'), and Monier-Williams ('the betel-nut tree'). Also in the Sanskrit list of Names of Plants in India for Areca catechu.
verdicts.reason: Three independent Sanskrit dictionaries gloss खपुर as the areca/betel-nut tree, and the flora compilation attaches it to Areca catechu. Genuine Sanskrit name, but पूगः is the standard lemma, so not preferred.

verdicts.name: गुवाकः
verdicts.corroboratingSource: eFloraofIndia, Areca catechu, Sanskrit: अकोटः, चामरपुष्प, गुवाकः (guvakah), पूगफल, उद्वेग; Names of Plants in India gives the same Sanskrit list including गुवाकः.
verdicts.reason: Attested Sanskrit lemma for Areca catechu in the flora compilation, consistent with the Hindi/Bengali reflexes guva/guya. Not preferred, since API's and the lexica's primary Sanskrit name is पूगः (also the page name).

verdicts.name: पूगवृक्षः
verdicts.reason: Retrieved the Sanskrit lists for Areca catechu from eFloraofIndia and Names of Plants in India (अकोटः, चामरपुष्प, गुवाकः, खपुर, पूगफल, पूगः, पूगी, उद्वेग, वल्कतरुः) and the dictionary aggregation on kosha.sanskrit.today (क्रमुकफल, वल्कतरु, राजताल); API gives Kramuka and Ghonta plus the monograph name Puga. पूगवृक्ष is not in any of them. It reads as a transparent ad-hoc compound ('puga tree'), not an attested lemma. The attested forms पूगः and पूगफल should be used instead.

verdicts.name: रक्त चंदन
